metadata.title: On sampling two spin models using the local connective constant

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Theorem 1.4 (Sec. 15.3) concludes with 'Theorem 1.4 implies ...' where Theorem 1.5 (Ising4SPRadiusHash) is meant; an inferred uses edge TP5 -> PP_t14 was added.
The proof of Lemma 16.2 refers to \eqref{def:PotentialFunction} (psi, defined later in Sec. 16.1) where chi from (14.1) is meant; the resulting \ref edge is backward.

Section 2 gives an informal (partly k=1) overview of extensions, the extended influence matrix, T_SAW and the influence matrix; these copies were attached to the formal definitions via also_stated_at instead of separate special-case nodes, except the worked wb-extension example (ExP_ext) and the overview bounds (ClP_ov*).
Called 'folklore', 'standard to prove' or placed under 'Standard linear algebra' yet proved in the appendix; marked origin external (standard) with paper proofs.
The intro sketch of Theorem 1.1 is a proof node with rigor semi_formal as the proof-sketch rule requires, although the rigor rule excludes proofs; the finishing step warns about it.
Table 1 (cited spectral-radius bounds for planar, r-degenerate and bounded-genus graphs), the omitted proof-structure diagrams and the figures were not extracted.
Section 12 proves Theorem 11.1 in subsection 12.1 and Proposition 12.1 in 12.2; the three introductory sentences of Section 12 (pointing to a diagram) were left out of both proof nodes.

metadata.extraction_comment: Proofs written as whole (sub)sections titled 'Proof of X' are prose proof nodes (confidence 0.9) with steps; Theorem 1.6 has no proof in the paper ('almost identical' to Theorem 1.3) and Claims 12.3, 12.4 have omitted proofs, hence rigor semi_formal.

nodes.name: Optimum mixing for the Hard-core model below lambda_c of the radius-k connective constant
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, ${\Delta}>1$, $k\geq 1$ and $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}>1$ consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that the radius-$k$ connective constant is $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$. Also, let $\mu$ be the Hard-core model on $G$ with fugacity $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})$. There is a constant $C=C({\Delta}, k, \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon)$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.
nodes.statement_short: Glauber dynamics on the Hard-core model mixes in O(n log n) when $\lambda\le(1-\varepsilon)\lambda_c(\upd_k)$, $\upd_k$ the radius-$k$ connective constant.
assumptions: For any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, ${\Delta}>1$, $k\geq 1$ and $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}>1$ consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that the radius-$k$ connective constant is $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$
let $\mu$ be the Hard-core model on $G$ with fugacity $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})$
conclusions: There is a constant $C=C({\Delta}, k, \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon)$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.
nodes.label: thrm:HC4CCK

nodes.name: Optimum mixing for the Hard-core model in terms of the k-non-backtracking matrix norm
nodes.statement: For $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, for $\uprho>1$ and integers $k,N>0$, ${\Delta}>1$, consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$. Also, let $\mu$ be the Hard-core model on $G$ with fugacity $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\uprho)$. There is a constant $C={C({\Delta},\uprho,k,\varepsilon)}$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.
nodes.statement_short: Hard-core Glauber dynamics mixes in O(n log n) when $\lambda\le(1-\varepsilon)\lambda_c(\uprho)$, $\uprho=\|H_{G,k}^N\|_2^{1/N}$.
assumptions: For $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, for $\uprho>1$ and integers $k,N>0$, ${\Delta}>1$, consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$
let $\mu$ be the Hard-core model on $G$ with fugacity $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\uprho)$
conclusions: There is a constant $C={C({\Delta},\uprho,k,\varepsilon)}$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.
nodes.label: thrm:HC4SPRadiusHash

nodes.name: Hardness transition for the Hard-core model in terms of the k-non-backtracking matrix norm
nodes.statement: Unless ${\rm NP} = {\rm RP}$, for $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\Delta}\geq 3$, $N,k\geq 1$ and $\uprho > 1$, the following is true: For any $\lambda>(1+\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\lceil \uprho \rceil)$, there is no FPRAS for estimating the partition function of the Hard-core model for graphs $G$ of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$. For any $\lambda<(1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\uprho)$, there is an FPRAS for estimating the partition function of the Hard-core model for graphs $G$ of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$.
nodes.statement_short: Unless NP=RP: no FPRAS for the Hard-core partition function above $(1+\varepsilon)\lambda_c(\lceil\uprho\rceil)$; an FPRAS exists below $(1-\varepsilon)\lambda_c(\uprho)$.
assumptions: Unless ${\rm NP} = {\rm RP}$
for $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\Delta}\geq 3$, $N,k\geq 1$ and $\uprho > 1$
conclusions: For any $\lambda>(1+\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\lceil \uprho \rceil)$, there is no FPRAS for estimating the partition function of the Hard-core model for graphs $G$ of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$.

For any $\lambda<(1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\uprho)$, there is an FPRAS for estimating the partition function of the Hard-core model for graphs $G$ of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$.
nodes.label: thrm:HarndessTransHCNBM

nodes.name: Optimum mixing for the Ising model in terms of the radius-k connective constant
nodes.statement: For $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\Delta} >1$, $k\geq 1$, $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}>1$ and $\lambda>0$ consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that the radius-$k$ connective constant is $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$. Let $\mu$ be the Ising model on $G$ with external field $\lambda$ and inverse temperature $\beta\in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k},\varepsilon)$. There is a constant $C={C( {\Delta},\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon)}$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.

nodes.name: Hardness transition for the antiferromagnetic Ising model in terms of the k-non-backtracking matrix norm
nodes.statement: Unless ${\rm NP} = {\rm RP}$, for $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\Delta}\geq 3$, $N, k\geq 1$ and $\uprho > 1$ the following is true: For any $0<\beta \leq \frac{\uprho-1+\varepsilon}{\uprho+1-\varepsilon}$ and $\lambda$ such that we are not in the tree uniqueness region, there is no FPRAS for estimating the partition function of the {\em antiferromagnetic} Ising model for graphs $G$ of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$. For any $\frac{\uprho-1+\varepsilon}{\uprho+1-\varepsilon}\leq \beta\leq 1 $ and any $\lambda>0$, there is an FPRAS for estimating the partition function of the {\em antiferromagnetic} Ising model for graphs $G$ of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model
nodes.statement_short: Unless NP=RP: no FPRAS for antiferromagnetic Ising below $\beta=(\uprho-1+\varepsilon)/(\uprho+1-\varepsilon)$ outside tree uniqueness; FPRAS above it.
assumptions: Unless ${\rm NP} = {\rm RP}$
for $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\Delta}\geq 3$, $N, k\geq 1$ and $\uprho > 1$

nodes.name: Optimum mixing for the Hard-core model in terms of the adjacency spectral radius
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, for ${\Delta}, {\varrho}>1$, consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that $\norm{ {\UpA}_G}{2}={\varrho}$. Also, let $\mu$ be the Hard-core model on $G$ with fugacity $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}({\varrho})$. There is a constant $C={C({\Delta}, {\varrho}, \varepsilon)}$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.
nodes.statement_short: Hard-core Glauber dynamics mixes in O(n log n) when $\lambda\le(1-\varepsilon)\lambda_c(\|A_G\|_2)$.

nodes.name: Optimum mixing for the Ising model in terms of the adjacency spectral radius
nodes.statement: For $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, $\lambda>0$, ${\varrho}>1$ and integer ${\Delta} >1$, consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that $\norm{{\UpA}_G}{2}={\varrho}$. Let $\mu$ be the Ising model on $G$ with external field $\lambda$ and inverse temperature $\beta\in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}({\varrho},\varepsilon)$. There is a constant $C={C( {\Delta},{\varrho}, \varepsilon)}$ such that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on $\mu$ is at most $C n\log n$.

nodes.name: delta-contraction
nodes.statement: Let $\delta\geq 0$ and the integer ${\Delta}\geq 1$. Also, let $\beta,\gamma, \lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ be such that $0\leq \beta\leq \gamma$, $\gamma >0$ and $\lambda>0$. The set of functions $\{ H_d\}_{1\leq d <{\Delta}}$, defined as in \eqref{eq:DefOfH} with respect to the parameters $\beta,\gamma,\lambda$, exhibits {\em $\delta$-contraction } if it satisfies the following condition: For any $1\leq d < {\Delta}$ and any $({\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_1, \ldots, {\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_{d})\in [-\infty,+\infty]^{d}$, we have $\norm{\nabla H_{d} ({\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_1, \ldots, {\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_{d})}{\infty} \leq \delta.$
nodes.statement_short: $\{H_d\}$ exhibits $\delta$-contraction if $\|\nabla H_d\|_\infty\le\delta$ everywhere for all $1\le d<\Delta$.
nodes.label: def:HContraction

nodes.name: Spectral independence from delta-contraction via the adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\varrho} > 1$ and the integer ${\Delta} > 1$. Also, let $\beta,\gamma, \lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ be such that $0\leq \beta\leq \gamma$, $\gamma >0$ and $\lambda>0$. Consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that $\norm{{\UpA}_G}{2}={\varrho}$. Also, consider $\mu$ the Gibbs distribution on $G$, specified by the parameters $(\beta, \gamma, \lambda)$. For $\delta =\frac{1-\varepsilon}{{\varrho}}$, suppose the set of functions $\{ H_{d}\}_{1\leq d< {\Delta}}$ specified by $(\beta,\gamma,\lambda)$ exhibits $\delta$-contraction. For any $\Lambda\subset V$ and $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^{\Lambda}$, the influence matrix ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ induced by $\mu$ satisfies \begin{align}\nonumber \textstyle {\rho} \left( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} \right) &\leq \varepsilon^{-1} \enspace. \end{align}
assumptions: Let $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$, ${\varrho} > 1$ and the integer ${\Delta} > 1$.
let $\beta,\gamma, \lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ be such that $0\leq \beta\leq \gamma$, $\gamma >0$ and $\lambda>0$.

nodes.name: b-marginal boundedness
nodes.statement: For a number $b\geq 0$, we say that a distribution $\mu$ over $\{\pm 1\}^V$ is $b$-marginally bounded if for every $\Lambda\subset V$ and any $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^{\Lambda}$, we have the following: for any $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ and for any $x\in\{\pm 1\} $ which is in the support of $\mu_{u}(\cdot \ |\ \Lambda, \tau)$, we have $\mu_{u}(x\ |\ \Lambda, \tau)\geq b$.
nodes.statement_short: Every conditional marginal value in the support has probability at least $b$.

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon, b\in (0,1)$, $\uprho>1$ and the integers $k,N \geq 1$, ${\Delta} > 1$. Consider graph $G=(V,E)$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ such that $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2} =\uprho$. nodes.name: (s,delta,c)-potential function
nodes.statement: Let $s\geq 1$, $\delta,c>0$ and let the integer ${\Delta}> 1$. Also, let $\beta,\gamma, \lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ be such that $0\leq \beta\leq \gamma$, $\gamma >0$ and $\lambda>0$. Consider $\{ H_{d}\}_{1\leq d< \Delta}$, defined in \eqref{eq:DefOfH} with respect to $(\beta,\gamma,\lambda)$. The differentiable, strictly increasing function ${\Psi}$, with image $S_{{\Psi}}$, is called $(\darkmagenta{s}, \delta, c)$-potential if it satisfies the following two conditions: \begin{description} \item[Contraction] For $1\leq d< {\Delta}$, for $(\widehat{\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_1, \ldots, \widehat{\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_{d})\in (S_{{\Psi}})^{d}$, and ${\bf m}=({\bf m}_1, \ldots, {\bf m}_{d})\in \mathbb{R}^{d}_{ \geq 0}$ we have that \begin{align} \chi( H_d({\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_1, \ldots, {\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_{d}) ) \cdot \sum^{d}_{j=1} \frac{ \abs{ h\left({\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_j \right)}}{ \chi\left( {\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_j \right)} \cdot {\bf m}_j \leq \delta^{\frac{1}{\darkmagenta{s}}} \cdot \norm{ {\bf m}}{\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace , \end{align} where $\chi={\Psi}'$, ${\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_j={\Psi}^{-1}(\widehat{\bf \cadmiumgreen{y}}_j)$, while $h(\cdot)$ is the function defined in \eqref{eq:DerivOfLogRatio}. \item[Boundedness] We have that \begin{align} \max_{z,x\in J}\left\{ \chi(z) \cdot \frac{\abs{h(x)}}{\chi(x)} \right\} & \leq c \enspace. \end{align} \end{description}
nodes.statement_short: A strictly increasing $\Psi$ whose derivative $\chi$ makes the weighted tree recursion contract in $\ell_s$ (Contraction) and keeps $\chi(z)|h(x)|/\chi(x)\le c$ (Boundedness).
nodes.label: def:GoodPotential

nodes.statement: For graph $G=(V,E)$ and a Gibbs distribution $\mu$ on $\{\pm 1\}^V$, for $\Lambda\subset V$ and $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^V$, let $\UpM$ be the $(V\setminus \Lambda)\times (V\setminus \Lambda)$ diagonal matrix such that \begin{align}\nonumber \UpM(v,v) &\textstyle =\sqrt{\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_{v}(+1)\cdot \mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_{v}(-1)} &\forall v\in V\setminus \Lambda \enspace. \end{align} Then, for the influence matrix ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ induced by $\mu$, the following is true: if $\UpM$ is non-singular, then matrix $\UpM\cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G \cdot \UpM^{-1}$ is symmetric.

nodes.name: Spectral independence implies polynomial mixing

nodes.name: Optimal mixing from spectral independence and marginal boundedness
nodes.statement: Let the integer ${\Delta}\geq 3$ and $b,\eta\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$. Consider graph $G=(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices and maximum degree ${\Delta}$. Also, let $\mu$ be a totally connected Gibbs distribution on $\{\pm 1\}^V$. If $\mu$ is both $b$-marginally bounded and $\eta$-spectrally independent, then there are constants $C_1, C_2>0$ such the Glauber dynamics for $\mu$ exhibits mixing time \begin{align}\nonumber {\rm T}_{\rm mix} &\leq C_1\times \left( {{\Delta}}/{b} \right)^{C_2\left ( \frac{\eta-1}{b^2}+1 \right)} \times \left( n \log n \right) \enspace. \end{align}

olimits_{ \ell \geq 0} (\delta \cdot {\varrho})^{{\ell}/{\darkmagenta{s}}} \enspace. \end{align} Then, \Cref{thrm:AdjacencyPotentialSpIn} follows by substituting $c= rac{\zeta}{{\varrho}}$ and $\delta= rac{1-\varepsilon}{{\varrho}}$ and noting that the norm on the l.h.s. is an upper bound for ${ho}( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G})$. nodes.name: Proof of Claim 7.3
nodes.statement:
For brevity, we let  egin{align}
onumber {	t Max}& =\max_{ ar{e}, \hat{e} \in T} \left\{ {	extstyle \uppsi( ar{e}) \cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(\hat{e})} }{\uppsi(\hat{e})}} ight\} \enspace. \end{align} Recall that $\ell>1$. From the definition of $\mathcal{H}_{\ell} $ in \eqref{eq:DefOfCalHL} and \Cref{claim:AddPotentialA} we have  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} &= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_\ell) \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \left( \uppsi(e_{\ell})\cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(e_1)} }{\uppsi(e_1)} ight)\cdot \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell} rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} For $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $\ell\geq 0$, recall that ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$ is the set of paths $P$ from the root of $T$ to the set of copies of vertex $u$ which are at level $\ell$ of the tree such that ${	t weight}(P)
eq 0$. Also, recall that ${	t A}(u,\ell)$ is the set of copies of $u$ at level $\ell$ in $T$ that are connected to the root with a path $P\in {\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$. Noting that $\left( \uppsi(e_{\ell})\cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(e_1)}}{\uppsi(e_1)} ight)\leq {	t Max}$, we get  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} &\leq {	t Max}\cdot \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_\ell) \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell} rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})}\cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} As far as ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root}$ is concerned, recalling \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeights}, we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root} &= {	t Max}\cdot \sum
olimits_{1\leq j\leq r} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} \enspace, \end{align} where $z_1, \ldots, z_{r}$ are the children of the root, for some integer $r>0$. We show that for any vertex $v$ at level $h=1,\ldots, \ell-1$ of the tree $T$, we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &=\sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, \end{align} where ${\mathcal{P}}(v,u, \ell)$ is the set of paths of length $\ell-h+1$ from the parent of vertex $v$ to ${	t A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{v}$. Before proving that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true, let us show how it implies \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD}. For every child $z_{j}$ of the root, \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} implies  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} & = \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}) \in {\mathcal{P}}(z_{j}, u, \ell) } \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} Summing the above over all the children of the root, we get  egin{align} \sum
olimits_{z_{j}} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} & = \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots e_{\ell}) \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} For the above, we use the observation that the sets ${\mathcal{P}}(z_j,u,\ell)$'s partition ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$, i.e., we have $\cup_{z_{j}}{\mathcal{P}}(z_{j},u,\ell)={\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$, while for distinct ${j}, i$ the sets ${\mathcal{P}}(z_{j},u,\ell)$ and ${\mathcal{P}}(z_{i},u,\ell)$ do not intersect. Plugging \eqref{eq:GoodExpression4Rzj} into \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeightsRepeat4HlVsRroot}, we see that ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root}$ is equal to the r.h.s. of the inequality in \eqref{eq:basis4HlAtHlVsRroot}. This implies that $\mathcal{H}_{\ell} \leq {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root}$, which also proves the claim. We conclude the proof of \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} by showing that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true. To this end, we use induction on the level $h$ of vertex $v$ in \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl}. The basis of the induction corresponds to taking $h=\ell-1$. For the inductive step, we assume that there is $h\leq \ell-1$ such that that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true. We then prove that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is also true for any vertex $v$ at level $h-1$ of tree $T$. We start with the basis and show \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} for a vertex $v$ at level $\ell-1$. As per standard notation, let $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ be the children of $v$. These children are vertices at level $\ell$. From \eqref{eq:SRecurBaseWeights} and \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821}, we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &= \sum
olimits_{j} rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{ \upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} 
onumber\ &=\sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{j} rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{ \upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \mathds{1}\{v_{j} \in {	t A} (u,\ell )\}\cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, \end{align} where we let $b_{v}$ be the edge that connects $v$ to its parent at $T$, while edge $b_{j}$ connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. For the second equality, we substitute ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}}$ by using \eqref{eq:SRecurBaseWeights}. For each $u \in V\setminus \Lambda$ in \eqref{eq:FinalofBaseHlVsRvInter}, the summand $ rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \mathds{1}\{v_{j} \in {	t A} (u,\ell )\}$ is non-zero only if the edges $b_{v}$ and $b_{j}$ form a path which belongs to set ${\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$, i.e., we have $(b_{v},b_{j})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$. We use this observation and write \eqref{eq:FinalofBaseHlVsRvInter} as follows:  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&=\sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,e_2) \in {\mathcal{P}}(v, u, \ell)}  rac{\uppsi(e_{1}) }{\uppsi(e_2)} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_2)} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} It is not hard to see that \eqref{eq:FinalofBaseHlVsRv} corresponds to \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} for $h=\ell-1$. This concludes the proof of the base of the induction. The induction hypothesis is that there exists $1<h\leq \ell-1$, such that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true for any vertex at level $h$ of tree $T$. We show that the hypothesis implies that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true for any vertex $v$ at level $h-1$. As per standard notation, we let $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ be the children of $v$, while edge $b_{v}$ connects $v$ to its parent and edge $b_{j}$ connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. From \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821} we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &= \sum
olimits_{j}  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} The children of $v$ are at level $h$. Using the hypothesis, we substitute each ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}}$ using \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} and get  egin{align}
onumber {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{j}  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})}\cdot \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v_{j}, u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} It is elementary that for any $1\leq j\leq d$ and for every path $P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v_{j}, u, \ell)$, there is exactly one path $Q=(\overline{e}_1, \ldots, \overline{e}_{\ell-h+2})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$, with $\overline{e}_2=\{v,v_{j} \}$, such that  egin{align} 
onumber \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+2}  rac{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(\overline{e}_{i})} &=  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace \end{align} and vice versa. Combining the two relations above, we get  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{Q=(\overline{e}_1,\ldots, \overline{e}_{\ell-h+2})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v, u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+2}  rac{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, 
onumber \end{align} which proves the inductive steps and concludes the inductive proof. \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} follows.

nodes.statement:
For what follows, we abbreviate $\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k}$ to $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$. Consider $P, Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ which are compatible. Let $w$ and $u$ be the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Then, as already noticed in \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrixEquivalent}, we have  egin{align} osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)&={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(w,u), & 	extrm{and} && osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)&={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(u, w)\enspace, \end{align} where the influence matrix ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ is with respect to $\upzeta^{P,Q}$, the $\{P, Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$. Note that ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{Q,P}$ correspond to the same influence matrix. A useful observation is that \Cref{claim:InfSymmetrisation} and \eqref{eq::InfNormHStartVsH-HVsI} imply that if $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)
otin \{0,1\}$, then we have  egin{align} \sqrt{  rac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1) } }\cdot osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)&= \sqrt{ rac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} } \cdot osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)\enspace. \end{align} If at least one of $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)$ is in $\{0,1\}$, then we have $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)=osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)=0$. Let the $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}	imes \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ matrix ${\mathcal{M}}$ be defined as follows: For $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ with starting vertex $w$ and $Q \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ with starting vertex $u$, such that $P$ and $Q$ are compatible while $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)
otin \{0,1\}$, we let  egin{align} {\mathcal{M}}(P,Q)&= \sqrt{  rac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1) } } \cdot \abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q)} \enspace. \end{align} On the other hand, if at least one of $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)$ is in $\{0,1\}$, then we let ${\mathcal{M}}(P,Q)=0$. Also, we let ${\mathcal{M}}(P,Q)=0$ when $P$ and $Q$ are not compatible. ${\mathcal{M}}$ has non-negative entries, while \eqref{eq::InfNormHStartVsH-HVsIBB} implies that it is symmetric. Furthermore, we have  egin{align}

The second inequality follows since ${\mathcal{M}}$ is symmetric. Similarly to the first inequality, the third inequality follows by noting that \eqref{eq:DefOfHatL} and the $b$-marginal boundedness assumption imply that ${\mathcal{M}}$ has non-negative entries, while ${\mathcal{M}} \leq b^{-2}\cdot \abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}}$, where the comparison is entry-wise. \Cref{claim:Ll2VsLl2s} follows for $c_3=b^{-4}$.

nodes.statement:
We consider path $W=e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}$ from the root of $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P}, u)$ to a copy of vertex $w$. Note that we specify $W$ it terms of its edges. Also, recall that set $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ consists of each vertex in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ which is either a copy of a vertex $v\in P$, or a copy of a split-vertex of $v\in P$. Let $\upalpha_{m min}=\min_{e}\{ \abs{\upalpha_{P} (e)}, \abs{{\upalpha}(e)} \}$, where $e$ varies over the set of edges in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ such that $ \upalpha_{P} (e), \upalpha(e)
eq 0$. Similarly, we define $\upalpha_{m max}=\max_{e}\{\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e)}, \abs{\upalpha(e)}\}$ where $e$ varies over the same set of edges. It is an easy exercise to show that our assumption about $b$-marginal boundedness, for fixed $b>0$, implies that $\upalpha_{m min}$ and $\upalpha_{m max}$ are constants bounded away from zero. Consider $\ell_0$ as specified in \Cref{prop:StableSSM}. Let set $H$ consist of the edges $e_{i} \in W$ such that $i>\ell-k$. Also, let set $K$ consist of the edges $e_{i}\in W$ such that $1\leq i \leq \ell-k$ and ${m dist}(e_{i}, \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P} )<\ell_0$. Similarly, let set $R$ consist of the edges $e_{i}\in W$ such that $1\leq i \leq \ell-k$ and ${m dist}(e_{i}, \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P} )\geq \ell_0$. We have  egin{align} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} &= \prod
olimits_{e_{i}\in H}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{e_{i} \in K}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{e_{i} \in R}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \enspace. \end{align} For our subsequent arguments, we use the following result.  egin{claim} For $W=e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}$ and $\{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})\}$, $\{\upalpha(e_{i})\}$, the following is true: if $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})
eq 0$, then we have $\upalpha(e_{i})
eq 0$, for each $e_{i}\in K\cup R$. \end{claim} For $\upalpha_{P}(e_i)$ such that $e_{i}\in H$, we use the standard bound  egin{align} \abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} &\leq 1\enspace. \end{align} For each edge $e_{i}\in K$, we have  egin{align} \abs{ \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) } \leq  rac{\upalpha_{m max}}{\upalpha_{m min}} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \ \leq \ (1+\varepsilon/3)^{{1}/{\darkmagenta{s}}} \cdot  rac{\upalpha_{m max}}{\upalpha_{m min}} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace. \end{align} We use \Cref{claim:SupportOfWeiS} for the first inequality. The second inequality uses that $1<(1+\varepsilon/2)^{{1}/{\darkmagenta{s}}}$ for $\varepsilon, \darkmagenta{s}>0$. \Cref{prop:StableSSM} implies that, for every $e_{i} \in R$, we have  egin{align} \abs{ \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) } \leq (1+\varepsilon/3)^{{1}/{\darkmagenta{s}}}\cdot \abs{ \upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace. \end{align} Plugging \eqref{eq:WeightEllUBound}, \eqref{eq:WeightPVsWeightClose3LM} and \eqref{eq:WeightPVsWeightFarfromLM} into \eqref{eq:splitProdHatBetas}, we get  egin{align} \prod^{\ell}_{i=1} \abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} &\leq \left(  rac{\upalpha_{m max}}{\upalpha_{m min}} ight)^{\abs{K}} \cdot \prod^{\ell-k}_{i=1} (1+\varepsilon/3)^{{1}/{s}} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})}\enspace. \end{align} For the cardinality of set $K$, we use the following claim.  egin{claim} There are at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$ edges in path $W$ that are at distance $<\ell_0$ from set $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. \end{claim} The above implies that $\abs{K}\leq (k+1) \cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$. Hence, \Cref{thrm:ProdWideHatBetaVsBeta} follows from \eqref{eq:Final4thrm:ProdWideHatBetaVsBeta} by setting $\widehat{c}_1=\left(  rac{\upalpha_{m max}}{\upalpha_{m min}} ight)^{(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 13.3
nodes.statement:
We use \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} and identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}=T_{m SAW}(G,u)$ such that both trees have the same root. Then, $W$ is also a path in $\applegreen{T}$ starting from the root. Having $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}$, we endow the subset of edges of $\applegreen{T}$ that correspond to those of $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ with the edge weights $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}$. Note that we do not necessarily have $\upalpha_{P}(e)$ for all edges $e\in \applegreen{T}$. Also, recall that the set of weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ and $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ are induced by $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ and $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$, respectively. For $e_{i}\in W$, let $e_{i}=\{x_{i},z_{i}\}$ while let $\uppi_{i}$ be the set that consists of $x_{i}, z_{i}$ and their children in $\applegreen{T}$. Furthermore, we have the following observations:  egin{enumerate}[(i)] \item \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $ yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, \item \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} implies that each vertex in $\applegreen{T} \setminus \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ corresponds to a descendant of a vertex in $ yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$, \item \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $M \cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}} \subseteq L$, \item \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that the pinnings $\sigma$ and $\eta$ agree on the assignment in $L\cap M$. \end{enumerate} Since we assume that our Gibbs distributions are $b$-marginally bounded, we can have $\upalpha(e_{i})=0$ (resp. $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})=0$) only if at least one vertex in $\uppi_{i}$ has a fixed configuration under $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ (resp. $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$). Note that for Gibbs distributions with parameter $ eta=0$, it is possible that a pinning on a child of $x_{i}$ or $z_{i}$ determines the configuration of its parent with probability 1, implying that $\upalpha(e_{i})=0$ (resp. $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})=0$). Consider $1\leq i \leq \ell-k$. If there is $v\in \uppi_{i}$ which is not in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, this means that at least one of $x_{i}$ and $z_{i}$ is in $ yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$, i.e., due to observation ef{obs:TminusBarTVsAp}. But then, since $x_{i},z_{i}\in \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, observation ef{obs:APBarTVsBarAp} implies that the parent of $v$, i.e., one of $x_{i}, z_{i}$, is in $ yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. Since $i\leq \ell-k$, if any of $x_{i},z_{i}$ is in $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, then it should be a split-vertex in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$, which means that is of degree $1$. This can only happen if $i=1$, however in this case we have $x_{i},z_{i}
otin \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ because the root is a copy of vertex $u$ which is at distance at least $k$ from any copy of a vertex $v\in \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. We then conclude that this event cannot happen. Hence, all elements in $\uppi_{i}$ are vertices in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. The fact that $e_{i}\in \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ and observations ef{obs:PinMVsBarTVsPinL} and ef{obs:PinMVsPinLIntesection} imply that if any vertex in $\uppi_{i}$ is pinned, then the pinning is the same under both $\sigma,\eta$. Hence, if $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})
eq 0$, then we also have that $\upalpha(e_{i})
eq 0$. \Cref{claim:SupportOfWeiS} follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 13.4
nodes.statement: It is not hard to verify that the number of edges at distance $\ell$ from the vertices in $P\cup \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ in $\gext{G}{P}$ is the same as the number of edges at distance $\ell$ from the vertices in $P$ in graph $G$. Furthermore, it is not hard to check that there are at most ${\Delta}^{\ell+1}$ edges in $G$ which are at distance $\ell$ a from vertex $v\in P$. A simple geometric series calculation implies that the total number of edges at distance $<\ell_0$ from all vertices $v\in P$ is at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$. Recall that there are in total $k+1$ vertices in $P$. Hence, we conclude that the number of edges at distance $<\ell_0$ from the vertices in $P\cup \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ in $\gext{G}{P}$ is at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$. The claim follows by noting that each one of these, at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$ edges can have at most one copy in path $W$.
nodes.statement_short: Count edges within distance $\ell_0$ of the $k+1$ vertices of $P$ by a geometric series.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 16.2
nodes.statement: Using the definitions of the functions $\chi$ and $h$ from \eqref{def:PotentialFunction} and \eqref{def:GradientRecHC}, respectively, we have {\small \begin{align} \max_{\cadmiumgreen{y}_1,\cadmiumgreen{y}_2\in J }\left\{ \chi(\cadmiumgreen{y}_2) \cdot \frac{|h(\cadmiumgreen{y}_1)|}{\chi(\cadmiumgreen{y}_1)} \right\} &= \max_{\cadmiumgreen{y}_1,\cadmiumgreen{y}_2\in J} \left\{\sqrt{h(\cadmiumgreen{y}_1)h(\cadmiumgreen{y}_2) } \right\} \ =\ \max_{\cadmiumgreen{y}_1,\cadmiumgreen{y}_2\in J} \left\{\sqrt{ \frac{e^{\cadmiumgreen{y}_1}}{1+e^{\cadmiumgreen{y}_1}}\frac{e^{\cadmiumgreen{y}_2}}{1+e^{\cadmiumgreen{y}_2}} } \right\} \ =\ { \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}} \enspace. \nonumber \end{align} } The last inequality follows from the observation that the function $g(x)=\frac{e^{x}}{1+e^{x}}$ is increasing in $x$, while, from \eqref{eq:RangeJ4HC}, we have that $e^{\cadmiumgreen{y}_1},e^{\cadmiumgreen{y}_2}\leq \lambda$. The claim follows.

nodes.statement:
The claim follows by using simple rearrangements. We have  egin{align} {\mathcal{J}}_{d}({ f m}, { f z}) &= \chi\left(\log F_{d}({ f z}) ight) \sum
olimits_{j\in [d]}  rac{ \abs{ h(\log { f z}_j )}}{ \chi\left( \log { f z}_j ight)} 	imes { f m}_j 
onumber\ &= \sqrt{ rac{F_{d}({ f z})}{1+F_{d}( f z)}} \sum^{d}_{j=1} \sqrt{ rac{{ f z}_j}{1+{ f z}_j}}	imes { f m}_j \ &= \sqrt{ rac{1}{F_{d}({ f z})(1+F_{d}( f z))}} \sum^{d}_{j=1} \sqrt{{ f z}_j(1+{ f z}_j) }	imes rac{ F_{d}( f z)}{1+{ f z}_j} 	imes { f m}_j \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} In \eqref{eq:AppOfFX}, we substitute $\chi$ and $h$ according to \eqref{def:XPotentialFunction} and \eqref{def:GradientRecHC}, respectively. Using the definition of ${\psi} $ from \eqref{def:PotentialFunction}, we get that  egin{align} {\mathcal{J}}_{d}({ f m}, { f z}) &= {\psi}(F_{d}({ f z})) \sum
olimits_{j\in [d]} rac{1}{ {\psi}({ f z}_j)} 	imes  rac{ F_{d}( f z)}{1+{ f z}_i} 	imes { f m}_j \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} The above implies \eqref{eq:SubCondVsPotentials}, i.e., since $\left|  rac{\partial }{\partial { f x}_i}F_{d}({ f x}) ight|= rac{F_{d}({ f x})}{1+{ f x}_i}$, for any $i\in [d]$. The claim follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 18.3
nodes.statement: The claim follows by utilising the equality in \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalI2CalF} from the proof of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. We apply this equality with respect to the influence matrices ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$, ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$, i.e., instead of matrices ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$ that are considered there. More specifically, we have \begin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{P}(u,w) &=\sum\nolimits_{Q} \widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q, w) \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(u,w) \enspace, \end{align} where $Q$ varies over the walks in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanate from vertex $u$ and matrix $\widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A$ is defined as in \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}, with respect to the Gibbs distributions $\upzeta^{P}$ and $\upzeta^{P,Q}$. Applying the same arguments as in the proof of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}, we obtain $\max_{Q,z}\{ |\widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q,z)\}| \leq C_A$, where $C_A$ is specified in the statement of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. Note that the bound $C_A$ depends only on the parameters $k$ and $b$ for the marginal boundedness. \Cref{claim:CFReverseSplit} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Apply equality (18.8) from the proof of Lemma 18.1 to $\mathcal{I}^P$ and $\mathcal{I}^{P,Q}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.1
nodes.statement: Our result follows by showing that there is an appropriate bijection $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ from the vertex set of $\capri{t}_{P}$ to that of $\blue{T_{P}}$ that allows us to identify $\capri{t}_{P}$ with $\blue{T_{P}}$. Since the vertices in $\capri{t}_{P}$ correspond to the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}$ and the vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$ correspond to the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$, we equivalently establish the bijection $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ from set $\magenta{\Omega}$ to $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. For concreteness, let $P=x_0, \ldots, x_{k}$, while $x_0=w$. Let set ${\mathcal{O}}$ consist of each edge $e$ in $G$, which does not connect two consecutive vertices in $P$ but has at least one end in the set $\{x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k-1}\}$. Similarly, let set ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$ consist of each edge in $\gext{G}{P}$ which is between a split-vertex in set $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ and another vertex of $\gext{G}{P}$. The only edges in $G$ that do not appear in $\gext{G}{P}$ are exactly those in set ${\mathcal{O}}$. Similarly, the only edges in $\gext{G}{P}$ that do not appear in $G$ are exactly those in set ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$. This implies that the elements in $\magenta{\Omega} \cap \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ correspond to the walks that do not use edges from sets ${\mathcal{O}}$ and ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$. The definitions of the two trees $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$ imply that \begin{align}\nonumber \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}&=\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P} & \textrm{and} &&\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}&=\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P} \enspace. \end{align} To see this, recall that we have $P=x_0, \ldots, x_{k}$. Then each $W=v_{0}, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}$ corresponds to a self-avoiding walk that emanates from vertex $w$, while $v_{i}=x_{i}$, for $i=0,\ldots, \min\{k,r \}$. It is immediate to check that each such walk $W$ also belongs to $\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P}$ and vice versa. This implies that $\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}=\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P}$. With a very similar argument, we also get $\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}=\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$. It is only the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ and $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ that use edges from ${\mathcal{O}}$ and ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$, respectively. For each walk $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$, there is a walk $W_{P}=z_0, \ldots, z_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ such that $v_{i}=z_{i}$ for $i=0,\ldots, r-1$, while $z_{r}$ is a split-vertex that is generated by vertex $v_{r}$ and vice versa. This holds since the definition of $\gext{G}{P}$ implies that when constructing $\gext{G}{P}$, we substitute the edge $\{v_{r-1}, v_{r}\}\in{\mathcal{O}}$ with the edge $\{z_{r-1}, z_{r}\}\in {\mathcal{O}}_{P}$. Considering all the above, we specify $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ that \begin{align} \cadmiumorange{\uph}(W) &= \left\{ \begin{array}{lcl} W && \textrm{if } W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}\enspace, \\ W_{P} && \textrm{if } W \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)} \enspace, \\ \end{array} \right . \end{align} where $W_{P}$ is as described in the paragraph above \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}. It is easy to check that for each $W_{P}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ there is a unique $W \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ such that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}$. This observation and \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection} imply that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ is a bijection from $\magenta{\Omega}$ to $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. Using the correspondence between sets $\magenta{\Omega}$, $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ and the sets of vertices of trees $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$, respectively, we identify $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ as a bijection from the set of vertices in $\capri{t}_{P}$ to those in $\blue{T_{P}}$. For vertex $u$ in $\capri{t}_{P}$ that corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, we have that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(u)$ is a vertex in $\blue{T_{P}}$ that corresponds to walk $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. From \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}, it is easy to verify that if $u$ is a copy of $v$ in $G$, then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(u)$ must be a copy of $v$ or a split-vertex in $\gext{G}{P}$ generated by $v$. We now show that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ preserves adjacencies. That is, for two vertices $x$, $z$ in $\capri{t}_{P}$ which are adjacent, we have that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ are two adjacent vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$. Suppose $x$ and $z$ correspond to walks $W, \overline{W}\in \magenta{\Omega}$, respectively. W.l.o.g., suppose walk $ W$ extends walk $\overline{W}$ by one vertex. Then, the vertices $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ correspond to walks $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})$, respectively. The definition of $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ implies that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)$ extends $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})$ by one vertex. To see this, note that in this setting we have $\overline{W}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}$ while $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, hence we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})=\overline{W}$. If $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$, then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W$ implying that $W$ extends $\overline{W}$. If on the other hand we have $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}$, where $W_{P}$ is defined as in the paragraph above \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}. It is easy to verify that $W_{P}$ extends $\overline{W}$ in this case too. Hence, $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ are two adjacent vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$. This implies that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ preserves adjacencies between the two trees, $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$. From all the above, we conclude that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ has all the necessary properties to allow us to identify $\capri{t}_{P}$ with $\blue{T_{P}}$. \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Construct an explicit bijection between the walks of $t_P$ and $T_P$ (swapping last vertices with split-vertices) and check it preserves adjacency.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.2
nodes.statement: Let $\mu^{M,\sigma}$ be the Gibbs distribution on $T=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$ induced by the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction on $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Similarly, let the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{K,\eta}_P$ on $\blue{T_{P}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P},w)$ be induced by the same construction with respect to the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Consider the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ and $\{ \upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ induced by the two Gibbs distributions $\mu^{M,\sigma}$ and $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ respectively. Note that the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ are on the edges of $T$, while the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ are on the edges of $\blue{T_{P}}$. Using \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw}, we identify $\blue{T_{P}}$ as a subtree of $T$, and we endow the edges of $\blue{T_{P}}$ with the edge-weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}_{e\in \blue{T_{P}}}$. Fix an edge $e=\{x,z\}$ in $\blue{T_{P}}$ such that $z$ is the child of $x$. Suppose $e$ is at distance $\geq k$ from the root. \Cref{lemma:GibbsWeightsTpVsP} follows by showing that $\upalpha(e)=\upalpha_{P}(e)$. The edge weights $\upalpha(e)$ and $\upalpha_{P}(e)$ only depend on the parameters of the initial Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and the pinnings $(M,\sigma)$ and $(K,\eta)$ that the two Gibbs distributions $\mu^{M,\sigma}$, $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ impose, respectively, at the vertices of $T_{z}$. As per standard notation, $T_{z}$ is the subtree of $\blue{T_{P}}$ that consists of vertex $z$ and its descendants. Since $z$ is also a vertex in $T$, it is not hard to verify that the subtree of $T$ which consists of $z$ and its descendants is exactly the same as $T_{z}$. This is due to the assumption that edge $e$ is at distance $\geq k$ from the root of $T$. Since, by definition, both $\mu^{M,\sigma}$ and $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ have the same parameters, it suffices to show the pinnings $(M\cap \blue{T_{P}},\sigma)$ and $(K,\eta)$ are identical. Here, we let $(M\cap \blue{T_{P}},\sigma)$ stand for the restriction of pinning $(M,\sigma)$ to the vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$. Let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}$ consist of the self-avoiding walks in $\magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}$ whose last vertex is in set $\Lambda$. Similarly, we define $\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P} \subseteq \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}_{P}$. The $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction implies that set $M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$ consists of the vertices that correspond to the walks in $ \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda} \cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$. Similarly, set $K$ in $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ consists of the vertices that correspond to the walks in $ \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$. We start by showing that $M\cap \blue{T_{P}} \subseteq K$ while for every $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, we have $\sigma(v)=\eta(v)$. Since we identify $\blue{T_{P}}$ as a subtree of $T$, each vertex in $\blue{T_{P}}$ corresponds to two walks, one from set $\magenta{\Omega}$ and one from set $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. Particularly, for vertex $v\in \blue{T_{P}}$ which corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, it also corresponds to walk $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$, where $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ is the bijection between $\magenta{\Omega}$ and $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ described in \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}, i.e., the proof of \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw}. Each vertex $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, which corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}$, also corresponds to the same walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_P$ since \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection} implies $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}$. We then obtain that vertex $v\in K$. Furthermore, the pinning rules of the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction imply $\eta(v)=\sigma(v)=\tau(v)$. Recall that $\tau$ is from the pinning of the initial Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Arguing as above, for each vertex $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, which corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$, we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$. Hence, we obtain that $v\in K$. For such vertex $v$, the pinning rules of the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction imply that $\eta(v)=\sigma(v)$. Each vertex $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$ which corresponds to walk $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ also corresponds to walk $W_{P}=z_0, \ldots, z_{r}$ such that $v_{i}=z_{i}$ for $0\leq i \leq r-1$, while $z_{r}$ is a split-vertex in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P} $generated by vertex $v_{r}$. That is, we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$. This implies that $v\in K$. For vertex $v$ in the paragraph above, the pinning $\sigma(v)$ is induced by the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction on $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, while the pinning $\eta(v)$ is because we consider the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, which pins the split-vertices in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$. From the description of the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction and the definition of the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ it not hard to verify that $\eta(v)=\sigma(v)$, e.g., see \eqref{eq:DefOfTau_x}. All the above imply that $M\cap \blue{T_{P}} \subseteq K$, while for each $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, we have $\sigma(v)=\eta(v)$. With a very similar line of arguments, we also deduce that $K \subseteq M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, while for each $v\in K$, we have $\sigma(v)=\eta(v)$. We omit these arguments because they are almost identical to those we presented above. We conclude that the two pinnings $(M\cap \blue{T_{P}},\sigma)$ and $(K,\eta)$ are identical. Consequently, we have that $\upalpha(e)=\upalpha_{P}(e)$ for any edge $e$ at distance $\geq k$ from the root of $\blue{T_{P}}$. \Cref{lemma:GibbsWeightsTpVsP} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Weights depend only on the subtree below an edge; show the two pinnings coincide there by walk-type analysis.

For the last inequality we note that $\frac{R+1}{R-1}$ is decreasing in $R$, hence, for $R\geq 2$, we have that $\frac{R+1}{R-1}\leq 3$. nodes.name: Two-spin Gibbs distribution and partition function
nodes.statement: We parametrise $\mu$ by using the numbers $\beta \geq 0$ and $\gamma, \lambda >0$, while each configuration $\sigma\in \{\pm 1\}^V$ gets probability mass \begin{align} \mu(\sigma) &=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}} \times \lambda^{\# \textrm{assignments ``1" in $\sigma$ } } \times \beta^{\# \textrm{edges with both ends ``1" in $\sigma$ } } \times \gamma^{\# \textrm{edges with both ends ``-1" in $\sigma$} } \enspace, \end{align} where $\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{Z}(G,\beta,\gamma, \lambda)$ is the normalising quantity called the {\em partition function}.

nodes.name: Hard-core model
nodes.statement: The Hard-core model is a probability distribution over the {\em independent sets} $\sigma$ of an underlying graph $G$ such that each $\sigma$ gets probability mass $\mu(\sigma)$, which is proportional to $\lambda^{\abs{\sigma}}$, where $\abs{\sigma}$ is the cardinality of the independent set $\sigma$. Using the formulation in \eqref{def:GibbDistr}, this distribution corresponds to having $\beta=0$, $\gamma=1$ and $\lambda>0$.
differentia: $\sigma$ gets probability mass $\mu(\sigma)$, which is proportional to $\lambda^{\abs{\sigma}}$

nodes.name: fugacity
nodes.statement: Typically, the parameter $\lambda>0$ is called {\em fugacity}.

nodes.name: Computational phase transition for the Hard-core model at lambda_c(Delta-1)
nodes.statement: This connection implies that for graphs $G$ of maximum degree ${\Delta}$ and the Hard-core model with fugacity $\lambda$ on such graphs, there exists a critical value ${\lambda_c}({\Delta}-1)$ such that following is true: for any fugacity $\lambda<{\lambda_c}({\Delta}-1)$, there exists an FPTAS for estimating the partition function, whereas, for $\lambda>{\lambda_c}({\Delta}-1)$ it is NP-hard to estimate the partition function even within an exponentially large factor.
nodes.origin_citation: Weitz 2006; Sly 2010; Sly & Sun 2014; Galanis, Štefankovič & Vigoda 2016
nodes.statement_short: FPTAS for the Hard-core partition function below $\lambda_c(\Delta-1)$, NP-hard above.

nodes.name: critical fugacity lambda_c(k) (tree uniqueness threshold)
nodes.statement: Recall that, for integer $k>1$, the critical value ${\lambda_c}(k)=\frac{k^{k}}{(k-1)^{(k+1)}}$ signifies the uniqueness/non-uniqueness phase transition for the Hard-core model on the $k$-ary tree, established by Kelly in \cite{Kelly85}.

nodes.name: FPTAS
nodes.statement: Also, recall that FPTAS stands for Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme. An FPTAS computes an estimation which is within a factor $(1\pm \upepsilon)$ from $\mathcal{Z}$ in time which is polynomial $n$ and $\log \frac{1}{\upepsilon}$.

nodes.name: FPTAS for the Hard-core model below lambda_c of the connective constant
nodes.statement: These works propose an FPTAS for estimating the partition function of the Hard-core model for any fugacity $\lambda<{\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd})$, where $\goldenbrown{\upd}$ is the {\em connective constant} of the underlying graph $G$.
nodes.origin_citation: Sinclair, Srivastava, Yin 2013; Sinclair, Srivastava, Štefankovič, Yin 2017
nodes.statement_short: FPTAS for the Hard-core partition function for $\lambda<\lambda_c(\upd)$, $\upd$ the connective constant.

nodes.name: FPRAS
nodes.statement: An FPRAS computes with probability $1-\updelta$ an estimation which is within a factor $(1\pm \upepsilon)$ from $\mathcal{Z}$, in time which is polynomial in $n$, $\log \frac{1}{\upepsilon}$ and $\log\frac{1}{\updelta}$.

nodes.name: Optimum mixing of Glauber dynamics for the Hard-core model up to lambda_c(Delta-1)
nodes.statement: Advances in the area, such as the work of Anari, Liu and Oveis-Gharan in \cite{OptMCMCIS}, which introduces the well-known {\em Spectral Independence} method, as well as the subsequent work of Chen, Liu and Vigoda in \cite{VigodaSpectralIndB}, establish {\em optimum} mixing for Glauber dynamics on the Hard-core model for any $\lambda<{\lambda_c}({\Delta}-1)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Anari, Liu, Oveis Gharan 2020; Chen, Liu, Vigoda 2021
nodes.statement_short: Glauber dynamics on the Hard-core model mixes optimally for $\lambda<\lambda_c(\Delta-1)$.

nodes.name: optimum mixing
nodes.statement: Recall that Glauber dynamics exhibits optimum mixing when the mixing time attains its (asymptotically) minimum value, which is $O(n\log n)$; see Hayes and Sinclair \cite{OptMixingTime}.

nodes.name: Optimum mixing yields an O*(n^2) FPRAS
nodes.statement: Optimum mixing for Glauber dynamics implies an $O^*(n^2)$ time FPRAS for the partition function (where $O^*(\cdot)$ omits the poly-logarithmic terms).

nodes.name: Optimum mixing on amenable graphs below lambda_c of the connective constant
nodes.statement: Using standard arguments like those in \cite{CesiAmenable,MixingTimeSpaceRSA}, one can show that \cite{ConnectiveConstFirst,ConnectiveConst} imply $O(n\log n)$ mixing for Glauber dynamics on the Hard-core model with $\lambda<{\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd})$ on {\em amenable graphs} \footnote{Roughly speaking, an infinite graph $G=(V,E)$ is amenable if $\inf\frac{\abs{ \partial W}}{\abs{W}}=0$, where the infimum ranges over all finite $W\subset V$, while $\partial W$ is the boundary of $W$. If $G$ is finite, we typically have $\abs{ \partial W}\ll \abs{W}$, for sufficiently large blocks $W\subset V$.}.
nodes.origin_citation: Sinclair, Srivastava, (Štefankovič,) Yin; Cesi 2001; Dyer, Sinclair, Vigoda, Weitz 2004

nodes.name: Mixing of Glauber dynamics for the Hard-core model on G(n,d/n)
nodes.statement: The state-of-the-art bound for this distribution is from the work of Efthymiou and Feng in \cite{EfthFeng23} which obtains $O(n^{1+\frac{C}{\log\log n}})$ mixing of Glauber dynamics for any $\lambda<{\lambda_c}(d)$, improving on the works in \cite{SIGnp,Efth19}.

nodes.name: Connective constant as the limit of radius-k connective constants (intro)
nodes.statement: The connective constant $\goldenbrown{\upd}$ corresponds to $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$ for $k\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 1.1 from Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: \Cref{thrm:HC4CCK} follows easily from \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusHash}. Specifically, it suffices to use the fact that for large $N$ we essentially have $\nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}\leq \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$ (see \Cref{prop:HSPRadCCLCC} for the exact relation) and note that the function ${\lambda_c}(z)$ is decreasing in $z$.

nodes.name: Hashimoto non-backtracking matrix
nodes.statement: Recall that $\byzantine{\UpH}_G$ is a 0/1 matrix indexed by the {\em ordered pairs} of the adjacent vertices in $G$ such that for any $e=uw$ and $f=z \cadmiumgreen{y}$, we have \begin{align}\nonumber \byzantine{\UpH}_G(e, f) =\mathds{1}\{w=z \}\times \mathds{1}\{u\neq \cadmiumgreen{y}\} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Ising model
nodes.statement: Using the formalism in \eqref{def:GibbDistr}, the Ising model corresponds to taking $\beta=\gamma$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model

nodes.name: inverse temperature and external field
nodes.statement: Usually, we refer to the parameters $\beta$ as the {\em inverse temperature} and $\lambda$ as the {\em external field}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model

nodes.name: ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising model
nodes.statement: Recall that when $\beta>1$, the Ising model is called {\em ferromagnetic}, while for $\beta<1$, it is called {\em antiferromagnetic}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model

nodes.name: Ising uniqueness on the k-ary tree
nodes.statement: For integer $k\geq 2$, it is well-known that the Ising model on the infinite $k$-ary tree, with external field $\lambda>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta\geq 0$, exhibits uniqueness for \begin{align}\nonumber \frac{k-1}{k+1} <\beta< \frac{k+1}{k-1} \enspace . \end{align}
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model
nodes.statement_short: Ising on the infinite $k$-ary tree is in uniqueness iff $\frac{k-1}{k+1}<\beta<\frac{k+1}{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Ising uniqueness interval U_Ising(z,delta)
nodes.statement: For $z>1$ and $\delta\in (0,1)$, we let the interval \begin{align} {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(z,\delta) =\textstyle \left [ \frac{z-1+\delta}{z+1-\delta}, \frac{z+1-\delta}{z-1+\delta}\right] \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model

nodes.name: Rapid mixing for the Ising model on G(n,d/n)
nodes.statement: It is known that Glauber dynamics on typical instances of this distribution is rapidly mixing for any $\beta\in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\goldenbrown{\upd},\varepsilon)$ and any $\varepsilon>0$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model
nodes.origin_citation: Mossel & Sly 2013; Efthymiou, Hayes, Štefankovič & Vigoda 2018; Efthymiou & Zampetakis 2024

nodes.name: No hardness region for the ferromagnetic Ising model (Jerrum-Sinclair)
nodes.statement: There is no hardness region for the ferromagnetic Ising model. This is due to the algorithm of Jerrum and Sinclair in \cite{JerSincIsing93}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Further results for the Ising model

nodes.name: marginal mu_Lambda
nodes.statement: For $\Lambda\subset V$, we let $\mu_{\Lambda}$ denote the marginal of $\mu$ at set $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: conditional distribution given a pinning
nodes.statement: We also let $\mu_G(\cdot \ |\ M, \sigma)$ and $\mu^{M,\sigma}_G$ denote the distribution $\mu$ conditional on the configuration at $M\subset V$ being $\sigma$.

nodes.name: pinning
nodes.statement: Sometimes, we use the term ``pinning" to refer to $(M,\sigma)$.

nodes.name: neighbourhood N_G(w)
nodes.statement: For vertex $w\in V$, we let $N_G(w)$ be the set of vertices which are adjacent to $w$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Spectral radius bounded by a similarity-transformed infinity norm
nodes.statement: From standard linear algebra, we have \begin{align*} {\rho}\left( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} \right) &\leq \norm{ \UpD^{-1} \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} \cdot \UpD }{\infty} \enspace, \end{align*} for any non-singular matrix $\UpD$ such that $\UpD$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ are conformable for multiplication.

nodes.name: influence of a path in T_SAW (overview)
nodes.statement: Each path in $T=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$ is associated with a real number that we call {\em influence}. The influences depend on the parameters of the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}$. For the path of length $1$, which corresponds to edge $e$ in $T$, we let $\upalpha(e)$ denote its influence. For a path $P$ of length $>1$, the influence $\upalpha(P)$ is given by \begin{align}\nonumber \upalpha(P) &= \prod\nolimits_{e\in P}\upalpha(e) \enspace, \end{align} i.e., $\upalpha(P)$ is equal to the product of influences of the edges in this path\footnote{In the related literature, influences are defined w.r.t. the vertices of the tree, not the edges. Our formalism here is equivalent.}.

nodes.name: Example of a wb-extension
nodes.statement: For our example, let $P=wb$. Then, $\gext{G}{P}$ is a new graph obtained by applying the following operations on $G$: \begin{enumerate}[(a)] \item remove all the edges that are incident to vertex $w$, apart from the one that connects $w$ and $b$, \item for each neighbour $z$ of vertex $w$ that has been disconnected, insert a new vertex $wz$ and connect it only to vertex $z$. \end{enumerate} \Cref{fig:ADExtGNew} shows the resulting graph after applying the above operations to graph $G$ in \Cref{fig:Base4TSAWIntro}. Compared to $G$, graph $\gext{G}{P}$ has an extra vertex which we denote with two letters, i.e., vertex $wd$.

nodes.name: ratio of marginals at the root
nodes.statement: For $K \subseteq V\setminus\{r\}$ and $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^{K}$, let the {\em ratio of marginals} at the root ${R}^{K, \tau}_{r}$ be defined by \begin{align} {R}^{K, \tau}_{r}=\frac{\mu^{K,\tau}_{r}(+1)}{\mu^{K,\tau}_{r}(-1)} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: subtree T_u
nodes.statement: For vertex $u\in V$, we let $T_{u}$ be the subtree of $T$ that includes $u$ and all its descendants. We always assume that the root of $T_{u}$ is vertex $u$.

nodes.name: ratio of marginals for a subtree
nodes.statement: With a slight abuse of notation, we let ${R}^{K, \tau}_{u}$ denote the ratio of marginals at the root for the subtree $T_{u}$, where the Gibbs distribution is with respect to $T_{u}$, while we impose pinning $\tau(K\cap T_{u})$.

nodes.name: tree recursion F_d
nodes.statement: Suppose that the vertices $v_1, \ldots, v_{d}$ are the children of the root $r$, for an integer $d>0$. It is standard to express ${R}^{K, \tau}_{r}$ in terms of ${R}^{K, \tau}_{v_{i}}$'s by having ${R}^{K, \tau}_{r}=F_{d} ({R}^{K, \tau}_{v_1}, \ldots, {R}^{K, \tau}_{v_{d}} )$, where \begin{align} F_{d}:[0, +\infty]^{d}\to [0, +\infty] & &\textrm{s.t.}& & (x_1, \ldots, x_{d})\mapsto \lambda \prod^{d}_{i=1}\frac{\beta {x}_{i}+1}{{x}_{i}+\gamma} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: log-ratio recursion H_d
nodes.statement: Let $H_{d}=\log \circ F_{d} \circ \exp$, which means that \begin{align} H_{d}:[-\infty, +\infty]^{d}\to [-\infty, +\infty] &&\textrm{s.t.}&& (x_1, \ldots, x_{d})\mapsto \log \lambda+\sum^{d}_{i=1} \log\left( \frac{\beta \exp(x_{i})+1}{\exp(x_{i})+\gamma} \right) \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Log-ratio recursion
nodes.statement: From \eqref{eq:BPRecursion}, it is elementary to verify that $\log {R}^{K, \tau}_{r}=H_{d}(\log {R}^{K, \tau}_{v_1}, \ldots, \log {R}^{K, \tau}_{v_{d}})$.
