nodes.name: delta-contraction equivalent to a bound on h
nodes.statement: The $\delta$-contraction condition is equivalent to having $h(z)\leq \delta$, for any $z\in [-\infty,+\infty]$, where $h(z)$ is defined in \eqref{eq:DerivOfLogRatio}.

nodes.name: Glauber dynamics
nodes.statement: We use the discrete-time, (single site) {\em Glauber dynamics} ${\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}}$ to approximately sample from $\mu$. Glauber dynamics is a very simple to describe Markov chain. The state space is the support of $\mu$. We assume that the chain starts from an arbitrary configuration $X_0$. For $t\geq 0$, the transition from the state $X_{t}$ to $X_{t+1}$ is according to the following steps: \begin{enumerate}[(a)] \item Choose uniformly at random a vertex $v\in V$. \item For every vertex $w$ different than $v$, set $X_{t+1}(w)=X_{t}(w)$. \item Set $X_{t+1}(v)$ according to the marginal of $\mu$ at $v$, conditional on the neighbours of $v$ having the configuration specified by $X_{t+1}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Single-site heat-bath Markov chain: pick a uniform vertex and resample its spin from the conditional marginal.

nodes.name: total variation distance
ergodic Markov chain
nodes.statement: Recall that $\UpP$ is called ergodic if it is irreducible and aperiodic.

nodes.name: mixing time
nodes.statement: For $t\geq 0$ and $\sigma\in \Omega$, we let $\UpP^{t}(\sigma, \cdot)$ be the distribution of $X_{t}$ when $X_0=\sigma$. Then, the {\em mixing time} of $\UpP$ is defined by \begin{align}\nonumber {\rm T}_{\rm mix}(\UpP)=\min\{t\geq 0\ :\ \forall \sigma\in \Omega \ \ \norm{\UpP^{t}(\sigma, \cdot)-\mu(\cdot)}{tv}\leq 1/4\} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: pairwise influence matrix
nodes.statement: Let graph $G=(V,E)$ and a Gibbs distribution $\mu$ on $\{\pm 1\}^V$. For $\Lambda\subset V$ and a configuration $\tau$ at $\Lambda$, the {\em pairwise influence matrix} ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ is indexed by the vertices in $V\setminus \Lambda $ such that, for $u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have \begin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}(w,u) & = \mu_{u}(+1 \ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, +1))- \mu_{u}(+1 \ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, -1)) \enspace, \end{align} where $\mu_{u}(+1 \ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, +1))$ is the probability of the event that vertex $u$ has configuration $+1$, conditional on that the configuration at $\Lambda$ is $\tau$ and the configuration at $w$ is $+1$. We have the analogous for $\mu_{u}(+1 \ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, -1))$.
also_stated_at: Let graph $G=(V,E)$ and a Gibbs distribution $\mu$ on $\{\pm 1\}^V$. For $\Lambda\subset V$ and a configuration $\tau$ at $\Lambda$, the ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ is a matrix indexed by the vertices in $V\setminus \Lambda$ such that for any $w,u\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have \begin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}(w,u) &= \mu_{u }(+1\ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, +1))- \mu_{u }(+1\ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, -1)) \enspace. \end{align} The Gibbs marginal $\mu_{u }(+1 \ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, +1))$ indicates the probability that vertex $u$ gets $+1$, conditional on the configuration at $\Lambda$ being $\tau$ and the configuration at $w$ being $+1$. We have the analogous for the marginal $\mu_{u }(+1 \ |\ (\Lambda, \tau), (w, -1))$.

nodes.name: totally connected distribution
nodes.statement: Let graph $G=(V,E)$. For a non-empty set $S\subset V$, let ${\tt H}_S$ be the graph whose vertices correspond to the configurations in $\{\pm 1\}^S$. Two configurations in $\{\pm 1\}^S$ are considered adjacent if and only if they differ at the assignment of a single vertex. Similarly, any subset $\Omega_0\subseteq \{\pm 1\}^S$ is considered to be connected if the subgraph induced by $\Omega_0$ is connected.

nodes.name: Two-spin Gibbs distributions considered are totally connected
nodes.statement: We remark here that all Gibbs distributions with soft-constraints such as the Ising model are totally connected in a trivial way. The same holds for the Hard-core model and this follows from standard arguments.

nodes.name: locally finite graph
nodes.statement: Locally finite means that all vertices have finite degree.

nodes.name: number of self-avoiding walks pi(v,k)
nodes.statement: For a vertex $v$ of graph $G$, we denote by $\pi(v,k)$ the number of {\em self-avoiding walks} of length $k$ starting at $v$.

nodes.name: self-avoiding walk
nodes.statement: Recall that a walk is called self-avoiding if it does not repeat vertices.
also_stated_at: Recall that a walk is {\em self-avoiding} if it does not repeat vertices.

nodes.name: c_k
nodes.statement: We let \begin{align}\nonumber c_{k}=\sup\{ \pi(v,k)\ |\ v\in V\}\enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: The connective-constant limit exists
nodes.statement: It is well-known that the above limit always exists.

nodes.name: Connective constant is the limit of radius-k connective constants
nodes.statement: The above definitions imply that $\goldenbrown{\upd}=\lim_{k \to\infty} \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$.

nodes.name: adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: For graph $G=(V,E)$, the {\em adjacency matrix} ${\UpA}_G$ is a zero-one, $V\times V$ matrix such that, for any $u,w\in V$, we have \begin{align}\nonumber {\UpA}_G(w,u)= \mathds{1}\{\textrm{$u, w$ are adjacent in $G$}\} \enspace. \end{align}
also_stated_at: Recall that ${\UpA}_G$ is a 0/1 matrix indexed by the vertices of $G$ such that for any $u,w$, we have \begin{align}\nonumber {\UpA}_G( u,w)= \mathds{1}\{\textrm{$u, w$ are adjacent in $G$}\} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: walk
nodes.statement: Recall that a {\em walk} in graph $G$ is any sequence of vertices $w_0, \ldots, w_{\ell}$ such that each consecutive pair $(w_{i-1}, w_{i})$ is an edge.

nodes.name: length of a walk
nodes.statement: The length of the walk is equal to the number of consecutive pairs $(w_{i-1}, w_{i})$.

nodes.name: eigenvectors phi_j of A_G
nodes.statement: We denote with $\upphi_{j} \in \mathbb{R}^V$ the eigenvector of ${\UpA}_G$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\upxi_{j}({\UpA}_G)$.

nodes.name: Perron-Frobenius Theorem (for the adjacency matrix)
nodes.statement: When $G$ is connected, then ${\UpA}_G$ is irreducible. Then, the Perron-Frobenius Theorem implies that \begin{align} {\rho}({\UpA}_G)&=\upxi_1({\UpA}_G)& \textrm{and} && \upphi_1(u) &>0 \qquad \forall u\in V \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: For connected $G$, $\rho(A_G)=\xi_1(A_G)$ and the principal eigenvector is strictly positive.

nodes.name: Spectral radius of the adjacency matrix between sqrt(Delta) and Delta
nodes.statement: It is an easy exercise to show that $\sqrt{{\Delta}} \leq {\rho}({\UpA}_G)\leq {\Delta}$.

nodes.name: set of self-avoiding walks of length k
nodes.statement: For graph $G=(V,E)$ and integer $k>0$, we let $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$ be the set of self-avoiding walks of length $k$.

nodes.name: reversed walk P^{-1}
nodes.statement: For $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$, we let $P^{-1}$ denote the walk with the opposite direction.

nodes.name: reversal-closed walk set L
nodes.statement: Let $L\subseteq \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$ be such that if $P \in L$, then $P^{-1}\in L$, too.

nodes.name: reversed vector x-check
nodes.statement: For ${\bf x}\in \mathbb{R}^{L}$, let the vector $\PTV{\bf x}$ be such that \begin{align} \PTV{\bf x}(P) &={\bf x}(P^{-1}) &\forall P\in L \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: reversal involution R_L
nodes.statement: Also, let $\UpR_L$ be the involution on $\mathbb{R}^{L}$ such that \begin{align} \UpR_L \cdot {\bf x}=\PTV{\bf x} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: PT-invariant matrix
nodes.statement: The $L\times L$ matrix $\UpZ$ is PT-invariant if we have \begin{align} \UpZ\cdot \UpR_L &=\UpR_L \cdot \MTR{\UpZ}\enspace, \end{align} where $\MTR{\UpZ}$ is the matrix transpose of $\UpZ$.

nodes.name: PT-invariance implies Z R_L symmetric
nodes.statement: The above implies that $\UpZ\cdot \UpR_L$ is symmetric, while we also have \begin{align} \UpZ(P,Q) &=\UpZ(Q^{-1},P^{-1}) \enspace, & \forall P,Q \in L \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: k-non-backtracking matrix
nodes.statement: For graph $G=(V,E)$ and integer $k>0$, recall that $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$ is the set of self-avoiding walks of length $k$. The (order) $k$-non-backtracking matrix $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}$ is an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k} \times \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$, zero-one matrix such that for any $P=x_0,\ldots, x_{k}$ and $Q=z_0, \ldots, z_{k}$ in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$, we have \begin{align} \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}(P, Q) &=\mathds{1}\{x_0 \neq z_{k} \}\times \prod\nolimits_{0\leq i <k}\mathds{1}\{z_{i} = x_{i+1}\} \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Zero-one matrix on length-$k$ self-avoiding walks: $H_{G,k}(P,Q)=1$ iff $Q$ is $P$ shifted by one vertex without repeating vertices.
also_stated_at: $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}$ is a generalisation of $\byzantine{\UpH}_G$. It is a 0/1 matrix indexed by the $k$-non-backtracking walks in $G$. For $e$ and $f$, two $k$-non-backtracking walks, we have $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}(e,f)=1$ if walk $f$ extends walk $e$ by one vertex without creating a loop. Otherwise, the entry is zero.

nodes.name: Example of entries of H_{G,3}
nodes.statement: For the graph $G$ in \Cref{fig:OrientedEdges}, consider $\byzantine{\UpH}_{G,3}$. Then, for $P=abx$, $Q=bx d$ and $R=x d e$ we have $\byzantine{\UpH}_{G,3}(P, Q)=1$, also, we have $\byzantine{\UpH}_{G,3}(Q,R)=1$, while note that we have $\byzantine{\UpH}_{G,3}(P, R)=0$.

nodes.name: k-non-backtracking walk
nodes.statement: For any integer $r>k$, we say that walk $R=w_{0},\ldots, w_{r}$ is a {\em $k$-non-backtracking walk} in $G$, if every $(k+2)$-tuple of consecutive vertices $w_{i}, \ldots, w_{i+k+1}$ in $R$ is a self-avoiding walk.

nodes.name: PT-invariance of powers of H_{G,k}
nodes.statement: It is elementary to show that it is PT-invariant. More specifically, for any integer $\ell\geq 0$, we have \begin{align} \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR &= \UpR \cdot\MTR{\byzantine{\UpH}}^{\ell}_{G,k}\enspace, \end{align} where $\UpR $ is the involution on $\mathbb{R}^{\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}}$ defined as in \eqref{def:OfInvolutation}.

nodes.name: Justification of PT-invariance of H_{G,k}
nodes.statement: The PT-invariance emerges from the simple observation that for any two $P,Q \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$, the number of $k$-non-backtracking walks of length $\ell$ from $P$ to $Q$ in graph $G$ is the same as the number of $k$-non-backtracking walks of length $\ell$ from $Q^{-1}$ to $P^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reversing walks gives a bijection between $k$-non-backtracking walks from $P$ to $Q$ and from $Q^{-1}$ to $P^{-1}$.

nodes.name: top singular value sigma_{k,ell}
nodes.statement: For integers $k,\ell>0$, let $\upsigma_{k,\ell}$ be the maximum {\em singular value} of matrix $(\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}$, i.e., $\norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2}=\upsigma_{k,\ell}$.

nodes.name: tree of self-avoiding walks T_SAW(G,w)
nodes.statement: For each vertex $w$ in $G$, we define $T=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$, the tree of self-avoiding walks starting from $w$, as follows: Consider the set consisting of every walk $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ in graph $G$ that emanates from vertex $w$, i.e., $v_0=w$, while one of the following two holds \begin{enumerate} \item $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ is a self-avoiding walk, \item $v_0, \ldots, v_{r-1}$ is a self-avoiding walk, while there is $j\leq r-3$ such that $v_{r}=v_{j}$. \end{enumerate} Each of these walks corresponds to a vertex in $T$. Two vertices in $T$ are adjacent if the corresponding walks are adjacent, i.e., one walk extends the other by one vertex.
also_stated_at: For vertex $w$ in $G$, we define $T=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$, the tree of self-avoiding walks starting from $w$, as follows: Consider the set of walks $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ in graph $G$ that emanates from vertex $w$, i.e., $v_0=w$, while one of the following two holds \begin{enumerate} \item $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ is a self-avoiding walk, \item $v_0, \ldots, v_{r-1}$ is a self-avoiding walk, while there is $j\leq r-3$ such that $v_{r}=v_{j}$. \end{enumerate} Each of these walks corresponds to a vertex in $T$. Two vertices in this tree are adjacent if the corresponding walks are adjacent, i.e., one extends the other by one vertex.

nodes.name: copy of a vertex in T_SAW
nodes.statement: The vertex in $T$ that corresponds to the walk $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$, is called ``copy of vertex $v_{r}$", i.e., $v_{r}$ is the last vertex in the path.
also_stated_at: The vertex $z$ in $T$ corresponding to walk $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ in $G$ is called a {\em copy} of vertex $v_{r}$ in tree $T$.

nodes.name: set of copies A(v)
nodes.statement: For each vertex $v$ in $G$, we let ${\tt A}(v)$ be the set of its copies in $T$.

nodes.name: Gibbs distribution and pinning on T_SAW
nodes.statement: Let $\mu_T$ be a Gibbs distribution on $T$ which has the same specification as $\mu_G$. Each $z \in {\tt A}(x)$ in the tree $T$, such that $x \in \Lambda$, is pinned to configuration $\tau(x)$. Furthermore, if vertex $z$ in $T$ corresponds to walk $v_0, \ldots, v_{\ell}$ in $G$ such that $v_{\ell}=v_j$, for $0\leq j \leq \ell-3$, then we set a pinning at vertex $z$, as well. This pinning depends on the total ordering of the vertices. Particularly, we set at $z$ \begin{enumerate}[(a)] \item $-1$ if $v_{j+1}>v_{\ell-1}$, \item $+1$ otherwise. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: pinned set Gamma and pinning sigma in T_SAW
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=\Gamma(G,\Lambda)$ be the set of vertices in $T$ which have been pinned in the above construction, while let $\sigma=\sigma(G,\tau)$ be the pinning at $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: influence weights alpha(e) on T_SAW edges
nodes.statement: For each edge $e$ in $T$, we specify weight $\upalpha(e)$ as follows: letting $e=\{x,z\}$ be such that $x$ is the parent of $z$ in $T$, we set \begin{align} \upalpha(e)=\left \{ \begin{array}{lcl} 0 & \quad&\textrm{if there is a pinning at either $x$ or $z$},\\ \textstyle h\left(\log {R}^{\Gamma, \sigma}_{z}\right) & & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{array} \right . \end{align} The function $h(\cdot)$ is from \eqref{eq:DerivOfLogRatio}, while ${R}^{\Gamma, \sigma}_{z}$ is a ratio of Gibbs marginals at $z$ (see definitions in Section \ref{sec:RecursionVsSpectralIneq}).
nodes.origin_citation: Anari, Liu, Oveis Gharan 2020; Chen, Liu, Vigoda 2020
nodes.statement_short: Edge weight 0 at pinned endpoints, else $h(\log R^{\Gamma,\sigma}_z)$ at the child $z$.

nodes.name: edge-to-vertex matrix C
nodes.statement: Consider the zero-one $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}\times V$ matrix $\UpC$ such that, for any $wx\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}$ and any $u\in V$, we have \begin{align} \UpC(wx,u)&=\mathds{1}\{x=u\}\enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: P-extension of a graph
nodes.statement: We consider graph $G=(V,E)$ and a self-avoiding walk $P$ of length $k \geq 1$ in this graph. We introduce the notion of $P$-extension of $G$, denoted as $\gext{G}{P}$. This is a graph obtained after a set of operations on $G$. We use induction on the length $k$ of walk $P$ to define $\gext{G}{P}$. First, consider $P$ of length $1$, while let $P=u, v$. Let $\byzantine{\partial \UpS}$ be the set of all neighbours of vertex $u$ in graph $G$ apart from vertex $v$, i.e., $\byzantine{\partial \UpS}=N_G(u)\setminus\{v\}$. Graph $\gext{G}{P}$ is obtained by working as follows: \begin{enumerate}[(a)] \item remove each edge of $G$ that connects $u$ to a vertex $z\in \byzantine{\partial \UpS}$, \item for each $z\in \byzantine{\partial \UpS}$, insert the new vertex $uz$ in the graph which is only connected to $z$. \end{enumerate} \Cref{fig:GBeforeExt,fig:GAtRoot} show an example of the above operations. \Cref{fig:GBeforeExt} shows the initial graph $G$. \Cref{fig:GAtRoot} shows the $P$-extension of $G$, for walk $P=w,b$. We call {\em split-vertices} all vertices introduced in step (b). We let $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_P$ denote the set of split-vertices in $\gext{G}{P}$. In the example shown in \Cref{fig:GBeforeExt,fig:GAtRoot}, we have $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}=\{ w a, wx\}$. Suppose, now, that $P x$ is a self-avoiding walk in $G$, which is of length $k>1$. With $Px$, we indicate that vertex $x$ is the last vertex of the walk, while $P$ corresponds to the first $k$ vertices. $P$ is a self-avoiding walk of length $k-1$ in $G$. We show how to obtain $\gext{G}{Px}$ using $\gext{G}{P}$. It is easy to see that $Px$ is also a self-avoiding walk in $\gext{G}{P}$. Let $u$ be the last vertex in $P$, i.e., vertex $u$ is just before $x$ in $Px$. Let $\byzantine{\partial \UpS}$ contain all neighbours of $u$ in $\gext{G}{P}$ apart from $x$, the vertex in $P$ prior to $u$ and the vertices in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$. If $\byzantine{\partial \UpS}\neq \emptyset$, then $\gext{G}{Px}$ is the result of the following operations on $\gext{G}{P}$: \begin{enumerate}[(a)] \setcounter{enumi}{2} \item remove each edge in $\gext{G}{P}$ that connects $u$ to a vertex $z\in \byzantine{\partial \UpS}$, \item for each $z\in \byzantine{\partial \UpS}$, we insert the split-vertex $uz$, which is only connected to $z$. \end{enumerate} If $\byzantine{\partial \UpS}= \emptyset$, graphs $\gext{G}{P}$ and $\gext{G}{Px}$ are identical. For graph $\gext{G}{Px}$, the set of split vertices $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{Px}$ corresponds to the union of the split-vertices $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ and the newly introduced split-vertices at step (d).
nodes.statement_short: Inductively cut the edges from each walk vertex to its off-walk neighbours and attach a fresh degree-one split-vertex to each such neighbour.
also_stated_at: Every extension of graph $G$ is specified with respect to a self-avoiding walk $P$ of length $k$ in this graph (here $k=1$). The resulting graph is called the $P$-extension of $G$ and is denoted as $\gext{G}{P}$.

nodes.name: split-vertices
nodes.statement: We call {\em split-vertices} all vertices introduced in step (b).
also_stated_at: This new vertex is called {\em split-vertex}.

nodes.name: set of split-vertices S_P
nodes.statement: We let $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_P$ denote the set of split-vertices in $\gext{G}{P}$.

nodes.name: naming convention uz for split-vertices
nodes.statement: We follow the convention to denote with $uz$ the split-vertex obtained from vertex $u$ of the initial graph $G$ and is connected to vertex $z$.

nodes.name: compatible walks
nodes.statement: For integer $k\geq 1$, let $P$ and $Q$ be two self-avoiding walks in $G$, each of length $k$. Let $w$ and $u$ be the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. We say that $P$ and $Q$ are {\em compatible} when ${\rm dist}_G(u,w)\geq 2k$.

nodes.name: {P,Q}-extension of a graph
nodes.statement: For compatible $P$ and $ Q$, the $\{P,Q \}$-extension of graph $G$, denoted as $\gext{G}{P,Q}$, is obtained by taking the $Q$-extension of graph $\gext{G}{P}$.
also_stated_at: For two self-avoiding paths $P,Q$ in $G$, each of length $k= 1$, which do not intersect with each other, we also consider the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of graph $G$. We obtain this graph by first getting $\gext{G}{P}$, i.e., the $P$-extension of $G$, and then we take the $Q$-extension of graph $G_{P}$.

nodes.name: Order independence of the {P,Q}-extension of a graph
nodes.statement: The order in which we consider $P$ and $Q$ to obtain the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of graph $G$ does not matter. It is easy to check that, as long as $P$ and $Q$ are compatible, one obtains the same graph $\gext{G}{P,Q}$ by either taking the $P$-extension of $\gext{G}{Q}$ or the $Q$-extension of $\gext{G}{P}$.
also_stated_at: The order in which we consider $P$ and $Q$ to obtain the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of graph $G$ does not matter. As long as $P$ and $Q$ do not intersect, one obtains the same graph $\gext{G}{P,Q}$ by either taking the $P$-extension of $\gext{G}{Q}$ or the $Q$-extension of $\gext{G}{P}$. Similarly for $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$.

nodes.name: The {P,Q}-extension is well defined for compatible walks
nodes.statement: The notion of $\{P,Q\}$-extension is well-defined since the compatibility of $P,Q$ ensures that $Q$ is a self-avoiding walk of $\gext{G}{P}$ and $P$ is a self-avoiding walk of $\gext{G}{Q}$.

nodes.name: P-extension of a Gibbs distribution
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda\subset V$ and $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^{\Lambda}$. Also, let the self-avoiding walk $P$ in graph $G$, which is of length $k \geq 1$. We take $P$ such that it does not intersect with set $\Lambda$. Then, consider $\gext{G}{P}$, i.e., the $P$-extension of $G$. Recall that we follow the convention to call $uz$ the split-vertex in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ obtained from vertex $u$ of the initial graph $G$ and is connected with vertex $z$. The $P$-extension of the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ is a new Gibbs distribution with underlying graph $\gext{G}{P}$ having the same specifications as $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. More specifically, we let $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\gext{G}{P}}$ be the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ such that the set of pinned vertices $M=\Lambda\cup \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ while pinning $\sigma$ satisfies the following: for $s \in \Lambda\subseteq M$, we have $\sigma(s)=\tau(s)$, while for $qx\in \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$, we have \begin{align} \sigma(qx) &= \left\{ \begin{array}{lcl} +1& \quad & \textrm{if $z>x$}\enspace,\\ -1& \quad &\textrm{if $z<x$} \enspace, \end{array} \right. \end{align} where $z$ is the vertex after $q$ in path $P$. The comparison between $z$ and $x$ is with respect to the total ordering of the vertices in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Same specification on $G_P$, with split-vertices pinned to $\pm1$ according to the total order relative to the next walk vertex.
also_stated_at: The $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ is a new Gibbs distribution with underlying graph $\gext{G}{P}$, i.e. the $P$-extension of $G$, and it has the same specification as $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, i.e., the same parameters $\beta,\gamma$ and $\lambda$. Letting $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{G_{P}}$ be the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, the set of pinned vertices $M$ corresponds to the union of the vertices in $\Lambda$ and the split-vertices of graph $G_{P}$. The pinning $\sigma$ is specified as follows: for any $v\in \Lambda$, we have $\sigma(v)=\tau(v)$, while for each split-vertex $vz$, we have \begin{align} \sigma(v z) &= \left\{ \begin{array}{lcl} +1& \quad & \textrm{if $x>z$}\enspace,\\ -1& \quad &\textrm{if $x<z$} \enspace, \end{array} \right. \end{align} where $x$ is the vertex after $v$ in path $P$. The comparison between $x$ and $z$ is with respect to the total ordering of the vertices in $G$.

nodes.name: {P,Q}-extension of a Gibbs distribution
nodes.statement: For integer $k\geq 1$, let $P$ and $Q$ be two self-avoiding walks in $G$, each of length $k$. Let $w$ and $u$ be the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. We assume that $P$ and $Q$ are compatible, i.e., ${\rm dist}_{G}(u,w)\geq 2k$. We obtain the $\{P,Q \}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ by first taking $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\gext{G}{P}}$, i.e., the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, and then taking the $Q$-extension of $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\gext{G}{P}}$. The $\{P,Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ is a Gibbs distribution on graph $\gext{G}{P,Q}$.
also_stated_at: Similarly, we obtain the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. That is, we first take the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and then, apply the $Q$-extension to the resulting Gibbs distribution.

nodes.name: Order independence of the {P,Q}-extension of a Gibbs distribution
nodes.statement: As in the case of graphs, for $P$ and $Q$ which are compatible, the order in which we consider them to obtain the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ does not make any difference to the outcome.

nodes.name: self-avoiding walks avoiding Lambda
nodes.statement: We let $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$ be the set of all self-avoiding walks in $G$ of length $k$ and do not intersect with $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: root path R_P of a walk in T_SAW
nodes.statement: Consider $\magenta{T}=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$. For each walk $P=x_0,\ldots,x_k$ in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanates from $w$, there is a path $R_{P}=u_0,\ldots, u_{k}$ in tree $\magenta{T}$, which emanates from the root, while $u_{i}$ is a copy of $x_{i}$, for all $0\leq i \leq k $.

nodes.name: subtree t_P
nodes.statement: Let $\capri{t}_{P}$ be the subtree of $\magenta{T}$ induced by the following set of vertices: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item the vertices in path $R_{P}$, \item all neighbours of $R_{P}$ which are copies of a vertex in $P$, \item all the descendants of vertex $u_{k}$ in $\magenta{T}$, recall that $u_{k}$ is the last vertex in $R_{P}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: tree T_P = T_SAW(G_P, w)
nodes.statement: Also, let $\blue{T_{P}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P},w)$. Tree $\blue{T_{P}}$ is well-defined since $w$ is also a vertex in $\gext{G}{P}$.

nodes.name: identification of trees
nodes.statement: In what follows, we show that we can {\em identify} $\capri{t}_{P}$ with $\blue{T_{P}}$. This means that there is a bijection ${\uph}$ from the set of vertices in $\capri{t}_{P}$ and those in $\blue{T_{P}}$, such that the following holds: \begin{enumerate}[(a)] \item $\uph$ preserves adjacencies, i.e., if vertices $x$ and $z$ are adjacent in $\capri{t}_{P}$, then $\uph(x)$ and $\uph(z)$ are adjacent in $\blue{T_{P}}$, \item for a vertex $u$ in $\capri{t}_{P}$, which is a copy of vertex $v$ in $G$, we have that $\uph(u)$ is a copy of vertex $v$, or a copy of a split-vertex in $\gext{G}{P}$, generated by $v$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: P-extension weights alpha_P
nodes.statement: Applying the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction to the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ gives rise to the weights $\{\upalpha_{P} (e)\}$ over the edges of $\blue{T_{P}}$.

nodes.name: tree T_SAW(G,u) with its Gibbs distribution and weights
nodes.statement: Consider the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Using the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction for $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, we obtain the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ for tree $\applegreen{T}=T_{\rm SAW}(G,u)$. Also, let $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ be the collection of weights over the edges of $\applegreen{T}$ that arise from $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$.

nodes.name: tree T-bar = T_SAW(G_P,u) with extension weights
nodes.statement: We use the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction for the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and get the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ for tree $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$. Let $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ be the collection of weights over the edges of $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ that arise from $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$.

nodes.name: extended influence matrix
nodes.statement: The extended influence matrix $\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}=\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$ is an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}\times \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$ matrix such that for $P, Q \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$, we define the entry $\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q) $ as follows: We have \begin{align} \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q) &=0 \enspace, \end{align} if $P$ and $Q$ are not compatible, i.e., the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$ are at distance $< 2k$. Consider $P$ and $Q$ which are compatible, while let $w$ and $u$ be their starting vertices, respectively. Letting $\upzeta^{P,Q}$ be the $\{P, Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ we have \begin{align} \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q) &= \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1\ |\ (w,+1)) - \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1 \ |\ (w,-1)) \enspace, \end{align} where $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}$ is the marginal of $\upzeta^{P,Q}$ at vertex $u$. Letting $ {\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ be the influence matrix induced by $\upzeta^{P,Q}$, \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrix} implies \begin{align} \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q) &={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(w,u)\enspace, \end{align} where, as mentioned above, $w$ and $u$ are the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Indexed by length-$k$ walks avoiding $\Lambda$: zero for incompatible pairs, else the influence of $w$ on $u$ in the $\{P,Q\}$-extension.
also_stated_at: For $P$ and $Q$ self-avoiding walks in graph $G$, each of length $k=1$, which do not intersect with each other and do not intersect with $\Lambda$, for matrix $\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}=\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$, the following holds: letting $\zeta^{P,Q}$ be the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, we have \begin{align} \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)&=\zeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1\ |\ (w,+1))-\zeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1\ | \ (w,-1))\enspace, \end{align} where $w$ and $u$ are starting vertices of walks $P,Q$, respectively.

nodes.name: short-range influence matrix I_{<k}
nodes.statement: For integer $k>0$, let ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G, <k}$ be the $(V\setminus \Lambda)\times (V\setminus \Lambda)$ matrix such that, for any $u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have \begin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,<k}(u,w) &= \mathds{1}\{{\rm dist}_{G}(u,w)< k\} \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}(u,w) \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: vertex-to-walk matrix D_k
nodes.statement: Let $\UpD_{k}$ be the $(V\setminus \Lambda)\times \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, zero-one matrix such that for $r \in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, we have \begin{align} \UpD_{k}(r, P) &= \mathds{1}\{ \textrm{$r$ is the starting vertex of walk $P$} \} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: walk-to-vertex matrix C_k
nodes.statement: Also, let $\UpC_{k}$ be the $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}\times (V\setminus \Lambda)$, zero-one matrix, such that for $r \in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, we have \begin{align} \UpC_{k} (P, r) &= \mathds{1}\{ \textrm{$r$ is the last vertex of walk $P$}\} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: entrywise absolute value |D| of a matrix
nodes.statement: In what follows, for a matrix $\UpD \in \mathbb{R}^{ N \times N}$, we let $\abs{\UpD}$ denote the matrix having entries $\abs{\UpD_{i,j}}$.
also_stated_at: For $\UpD, \UpB, \UpC \in \mathbb{R}^{ N \times N}$, we let $|\UpD|$ denote the matrix having entries $|\UpD_{i,j}|$.

Recall that, for matrix $\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$, we let $\abs{\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}}$ denote the matrix having entries $\abs{\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}(P,Q)}$.

nodes.name: set A-bar_P of copies of P and split-vertices in T-bar
nodes.statement: Also, let set $\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$ consist of each vertex in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ which is either a copy of a vertex $v\in P$, or a copy of a split-vertex in $v\in \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$.

nodes.name: Hard-core potential function Psi
nodes.statement: We start by introducing the potential function ${\Psi}$. We define ${\Psi}$ in terms of $\chi={\Psi}'$ by having { \begin{align} \chi &: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R} & \textrm{such that} && y& \mapsto {\textstyle{\sqrt{\frac{e^y}{1+e^y}} }} \enspace, \end{align} } while ${\Psi}(0)=0$.
nodes.section: 14 Proof of rapid mixing results in 1 - Hard-core Model

nodes.name: inverse critical function Delta_c(lambda)
nodes.statement: For any given $\lambda>0$, we define, implicitly, function ${\Delta_c}(\lambda)$ to be the positive number $z>1$ such that $\frac{z^{z}}{(z-1)^{(z+1)}}=\lambda$.
nodes.section: 14 Proof of rapid mixing results in 1 - Hard-core Model

nodes.name: Delta_c is the inverse of lambda_c
nodes.statement: From its definition it is not hard to see that ${\Delta_c}(\cdot)$ is the inverse map of ${\lambda_c}(\cdot )$, i.e., we have that ${\Delta_c}(x)={\lambda_c}^{-1}(x)$. In that respect, ${\Delta_c}(x)$ is well-defined as ${\lambda_c}(x)$ is monotonically decreasing in $x$.
nodes.section: 14 Proof of rapid mixing results in 1 - Hard-core Model

nodes.name: Ising log-ratio recursion
nodes.statement: For the Ising model, this correspond to the function $H_d:[-\infty, +\infty]^d\to [-\infty, +\infty] $ such that {\small \begin{align} (x_1, \ldots, x_d)\mapsto \log\lambda+ \sum\nolimits_{i\in [d]} \log\left( \frac{\beta \exp(x_{i})+1}{\exp(x_{i})+\beta} \right) \enspace . \end{align}
nodes.section: 15 Proof of results in 1 - Ising Model

nodes.name: walk set Omega of t_P
nodes.statement: We let set $\magenta{\Omega}$ consist of all walks $W$ in $G$ that correspond to the vertices in $\capri{t}_{P}$.

nodes.name: walk set Omega_P of T_P
nodes.statement: Similarly, we define set $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ that consists of all walks that correspond to the vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$.

nodes.name: Type I and Type II walks
nodes.statement: Since each of $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$ is a (part of) tree of self-avoiding walks starting from vertex $w$, the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction implies that each walk $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ in $\magenta{\Omega}$ or $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ is such that $v_0=w$, while it is one of the following two types: \begin{description} \item[Type I] $v_0, \ldots, v_{r}$ is a self-avoiding walk, \item[Type II] $v_0, \ldots, v_{r-1}$ is a self-avoiding walk, while there is $j\leq r-3$ such that $v_{r}=v_{j}$. \end{description}

nodes.name: Omega^(a)
nodes.statement: Let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ consist of all the elements in $\magenta{\Omega}$ which are self-avoiding walks, i.e., they are of Type I.

nodes.name: Omega^(b)
nodes.statement: Let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ consist of all walks $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}$, which are of Type II such that $v_{r}\in P$.

nodes.name: Omega^(c)
nodes.statement: Finally, let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ consist of all walks $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}$ which is of Type II, while $v_{r}\notin P$.

nodes.name: Omega_P^(a)
nodes.statement: Similarly, let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P} \subseteq \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ consist of all the elements in $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$, which are of Type I, and do not use any of the split-vertices in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$.

nodes.name: Omega_P^(b)
nodes.statement: Let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ consist of all the elements in $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$, which are of Type I, such that the last vertex is in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$.

nodes.name: Omega_P^(c)
nodes.statement: Finally, let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ consist of all walks $W$ of Type II.

nodes.name: non-negative matrix
nodes.statement: For the matrix $\UpL \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ we follow the convention to call it non-negative, if all its entries are non-negative numbers, i.e., every entry $\UpL_{i,j}\geq 0$.

nodes.name: ordered eigenvalues xi_i
nodes.statement: For an $N\times N$ matrix $\UpL$, we let $\upxi_i(\UpL)$, for $i=1,\ldots, N$, denote the eigenvalues of $\UpL$ such that $\upxi_1(\UpL)\geq \upxi_2(\UpL) \geq \ldots \geq \upxi_N(\UpL)$.

nodes.name: spectrum
nodes.statement: Also, we let ${\Upphi}(\UpL)$ denote the set of distinct eigenvalues of $\UpL$. We also refer to ${\Upphi}(\UpL)$ as the {\em spectrum} of $\UpL$.

nodes.name: spectral radius
nodes.statement: We define the {\em spectral radius} of $\UpL$, denoted as ${\rho}(\UpL)$, to be the real number such that \begin{align}\nonumber {\rho}(\UpL)=\max_{}\{ |\upxi| \ : \ \upxi\in {\Upphi}(\UpL) \} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Spectral radius is a lower bound for every matrix norm
nodes.statement: It is a well-known result that the spectral radius of $\UpL$ is the greatest lower bound for all of its matrix norms, e.g. see Theorem 6.5.9 in \cite{MatrixAnalysis}. That is, letting $\enorm{\cdot} $ be a matrix norm on $N\times N$ matrices, we have that \begin{align} {\rho}(\UpL) \leq \enorm{ \UpL} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: matrix transpose
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we let $\MTR{\UpL}$ be the standard matrix transpose of $\UpL$.

nodes.name: Spectral radius equals 2-norm for symmetric matrices
nodes.statement: It is useful to mention that when $\UpL$ is symmetric, i.e., $\MTR{\UpL}=\UpL$, we have that ${\rho}(\UpL) = \norm{\UpL}{2}$.

nodes.name: entrywise matrix order
nodes.statement: For the matrices $\UpB, \UpC$ we define $\UpB\leq \UpC$ to mean that $\UpB_{i,j}\leq \UpC_{i,j}$ for each $i$ and $j$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement:
Recalling that $\delta=(1-\varepsilon)/{\varrho}$, let ${{\UpB}}$ be the $V	imes V$ matrix defined by  egin{align} {{\UpB}}&= \sum
olimits_{0\leq \ell \leq n} \left( \delta \cdot {\UpA}_Gight)^{\ell} \enspace. \end{align} Since the adjacency matrix ${\UpA}_G$ is symmetric, ${{\UpB}}$ is symmetric, as well. We have  egin{align}

Cauchy’s interlacing theorem, e.g., see \cite{MatrixAnalysis}, implies that  egin{align} {ho}\left ({{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda} ight )&\leq {ho}\left ({{\UpB}} ight ) \leq \varepsilon^{-1}\enspace. \end{align} \Cref{thrm:AdjacencyInfinityMixing} follows by showing that ${ho}( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G} ) \leq {ho}\left( {{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda} ight)$. Also, we have ${{\UpB}}(u,u)\geq 1$, as the summand in \eqref{eq:DefOfPowerAdj} for $\ell=0$ corresponds to the identity matrix. This proves that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:AdjacencyInfinityMixing} is true when $u=w$. Fix $w,u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ such that $w

The $\delta$-contraction assumption implies that $\abs{\upalpha(e)} \leq \delta$, for each $e\in T$. Then, from \eqref{eq:AdjacencyInfinityMixingTsawConstruction}, we have  egin{align} \abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G} (w,u)}&\leq \sum

Plugging the above bound into \eqref{eq:AdjacencyInfinityMixingInlEntryBoundDelta}, we get  egin{align}

nodes.statement_short: Dominate $|\mathcal{I}|$ entrywise by $B=\sum_\ell(\delta A_G)^\ell$ via the $T_{\rm SAW}$ path expansion and walk counting; $\rho(B)\le\varepsilon^{-1}$ and Cauchy interlacing.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.1
nodes.statement:
We abbreviate ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda, 	au}_G$ to ${\mathcal{I}}$ and the diagonal element $\UpD (u,u)$ to $\UpD (u)$. The following result is useful to involve the potential function ${\Psi}$ in our derivations.  egin{claim} For integer $\ell>1$ and any path $P=e_1, \ldots e_{\ell}$ such that ${	t weight}(P)

Using a simple telescopic trick, we get  egin{align} \abs{{	t weight}(P)}&= \prod^{\ell}_{i=1} rac{\uppsi(e_{i})}{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \ = \ \uppsi(e_{\ell})\cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(e_1)}}{\uppsi(e_1)}\cdot \prod^{\ell}_{i=2} rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} The claim follows. \end{proof} For $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $\ell\geq 0$, let ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$ be the set of paths $P$ from the root of $T$ to the set of copies of vertex $u$ which are at level $\ell$ of the tree such that ${	t weight}(P)

olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \abs{ {	t weight}(P ) } \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} Recalling that \Cref{prop:Inf2TreeRedaux} implies  egin{align} 	extstyle \left( \UpD^{-1}\cdot {\mathcal{I}}\cdot \UpD ight) (w,u) & = rac{1}{\UpD(w)} \cdot \sum
olimits_{\ell \geq 0} \sum
olimits_{P \in {\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)}{	t weight}(P) \cdot \UpD(u)\enspace, \end{align} we have  egin{align} \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda } \abs{\left( \UpD^{-1}\cdot {\mathcal{I}}\cdot \UpD ight) (w,u)} & \leq  rac{1}{\UpD(w)} \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} \enspace . \end{align} Fix $\ell> 1$. For a vertex $v$ at level $h$ of $T$, where $h=0, \ldots, \ell$, let the quantity ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}$ be defined as follows: For $h=\ell$, we let  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} & = \sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \mathds{1}\{v \in {	t A} (u,\ell)\} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} For a vertex $v$, which is at level $0< h <\ell$ such that vertices $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ are its children, we let  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \uppsi(b_{v})\cdot \sum
olimits_{j}  rac{\abs{\upalpha(b_{j})}}{\uppsi(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} \enspace, \end{align} where $b_{v}$ is the edge that connects $v$ to its parent, while $b_{j}$ is the edge that connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. Since we assume that $h>0$, $v$ has a parent, hence $b_{v}$ is well-defined. Also, recall $\uppsi(\cdot)$ from \Cref{claim:AddPotentialA}. Finally, for $h=0$, i.e., $v$ and the root of $T$ are identical, we let  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}\ = \ {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root} & = \max_{ ar{b},\hat{b}\in T} \left\{ {	extstyle \uppsi\left( ar{b}ight) \cdot  rac{\abs{ \upalpha\left(\hat{b}ight)}}{\uppsi\left(\hat{b}ight)}} ight\} \cdot \sum
olimits_{z_{j}} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} \enspace, \end{align} where $z_1, \ldots, z_{r}$ are the children of the root of $T$.  egin{claim} For any $\ell> 1$, we have $\mathcal{H}_{\ell} \leq {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root}$. \end{claim} The proof of \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} appears immediately after the proof of \Cref{thrm:InflNormBound4GeneralD}. The Boundedness property of the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential ${\Psi}$, together with \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeights} imply  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root} & \leq c \cdot \sum
olimits_{z_j} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_j} \enspace. \end{align} 
oindent The Contraction property of the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential ${\Psi}$ and \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821} imply that, for every vertex $v$ at level $0<h<\ell$, we have  egin{align} \left( {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} ight) ^{\darkmagenta{s}} & \leq \delta \cdot \sum
olimits_{v_j} \left( {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_j} ight)^{\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace, \end{align} where recall that $v_1,\ldots, v_d$ are the children of $v$. Then, \eqref{eq:SubContVsDeltaKWeights} and \eqref{eq:SRecurBaseWeights}, imply  egin{align} \left ( {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} ight)^{\darkmagenta{s}} & \leq \delta^{\ell - h }\cdot \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \abs{{	t A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{v}} \cdot \left ( \UpD(u)ight)^{\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace , \end{align} where, recall that ${	t A}(u,\ell)\subseteq {	t A}(u)$ is the set of copies of vertex $u$ in $T$ that are at level $\ell$. $T_{v}$ is the subtree of $T$ that includes $v$ and its descendants. Applying \eqref{eq:SubContVsDeltaKWeights1821} for the children of the root and plugging the result into \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeightsB}, we get  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root} & \leq c\cdot \sum
olimits_{z_{j}} \left( \delta^{\ell-1} \cdot \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \abs{{	t A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{z_{j} }} \cdot \left ( \UpD(u)ight )^{\darkmagenta{s}} ight )^{1/{\darkmagenta{s}}} \enspace, \end{align} where note that each $z_{j}$ is at level $h=1$ of $T$. Suppose that $z_{j}$ is a copy of vertex $z$ in $G$. Then, since $\ell>1$, we have  egin{align} \abs{{	t A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{z_j}} \leq \left( \UpC\cdot {\UpA}^{\ell-1}_Gight)(wz,u)\enspace, \end{align} where recall matrix $\UpC$ from \eqref{def:SingleEdgeM}, while ${\UpA}_G$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$. To see that \eqref{eq:CPUELLTzjVsMAlwzu} is true, we note that the l.h.s. considers only self-avoiding walks, while the r.h.s. considers simple walks., i.e., including the self-avoiding ones. Combining \eqref{eq:CPUELLTzjVsMAlwzu} with \eqref{eq:FinalBoundRroorAdj} and \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD}, for $\ell>1$, we have  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} & \leq c \cdot \sum
olimits_{z \in N_G(w)} \left( \delta^{\ell-1} \cdot \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \left( \UpC\cdot {\UpA}^{\ell-1}_Gight)(wz,u) \cdot \left ( \UpD(u)ight )^{\darkmagenta{s}} ight )^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace. \end{align} As far as $\mathcal{H}_1$ is concerned, note that for any edge $e\in T$, we have  egin{align} \abs{\upalpha(e)}=  rac{\uppsi(e)}{\uppsi(e)} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e)} \leq \max_{ ar{e}, \hat{e} \in T} \left\{ \uppsi( ar{e}) \cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(\hat{e})}}{\uppsi(\hat{e})} ight\} \leq c \enspace, \end{align} where the last inequality follows from the Boundedness condition of the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential function ${\Psi}$. Applying the definition of $\mathcal{H}_{\ell}$ for $\ell=1$, we get  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_1 &=\sum
