In light of all the above, we get \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:InflNormBound4GeneralD} by plugging \eqref{eq:FinalBoundCJLAdj} and \eqref{eq:FinalBoundCJ1Adj} into \eqref{eq:bCVsbCELL} and noting that $\mathcal{H}_0=\UpD(w)$. \Cref{thrm:InflNormBound4GeneralD} follows. \hfill $\square$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand weighted row sums over $T_{\rm SAW}$ paths, telescope with the potential, and run a level-by-level recursion using the Contraction and Boundedness properties.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10.1
nodes.statement_short: Combine Proposition 9.2 with the entrywise bound $|\mathcal{L}|\le\mathcal{J}$ (Lemma 10.2) and $\|\mathcal{J}\|_2$ bound (Proposition 10.3).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10.2
nodes.statement:
When there is no danger of confusion, in what follows we abbreviate matrix $\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k}$ to $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$. Let $P,Q \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$, while let $w$ and $u$ be their starting vertices, respectively. For non-compatible $P, Q$, the definitions of matrices $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$ and $ \mathcal{J}$ imply that $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)= \mathcal{J}(P,Q)=0$. We consider compatible $P$ and $Q$. It suffices to show that $\abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)} \leq \mathcal{J}(P,Q)$. We let $\upzeta^{P,Q}$ be the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$, while let ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ be the influence matrix induced by $\upzeta^{P,Q}$. Recall from \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrixEquivalent} that  egin{align} osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q)={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(w,u)\enspace, \end{align} where, as mentioned above, $w$ and $u$ are the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $T_{P,Q}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P,Q}, w)$. Also, let $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ be the collection of weights over the edges of $T_{P,Q}$ we obtain as described in \eqref{def:OfInfluenceWeights} with respect to the Gibbs distribution $\upzeta^{P,Q}$. We have  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(w,u)&=\sum
olimits_{\ell \geq 2k}\sum
olimits_{W\in T_{P,Q} : \abs{W}=\ell} \prod
olimits_{e\in W} \upalpha(e)\enspace, \end{align} where $W$ varies over the paths of length $\ell$ in $T_{P,Q}$ from the root to the copies of vertex $u$ corresponding to self-avoiding walks in $\gext{G}{P,Q}$. Any copies of $u$ in $T_{P,Q}$ that do not correspond to self-avoiding walk have a pinning. The influence of the root to vertices with pinning is zero. The assumption about $\delta$-contraction implies that $\upzeta^{P,Q}$ also exhibits $\delta$-contraction, i.e., it has the same specifications as $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$. Hence, we have $\abs{ \prod
olimits_{e\in W } \upalpha(e) } \leq \delta^{\ell}$ for each $W$ of length $\ell$. Combining this observation with \eqref{eq:IPQVsCalLPQ11-3} and \eqref{eq:IPQVsEdgeWeights11-3}, we obtain  egin{align}
onumber \abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q)}=\abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(w,u)}&\leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 2k}\sum
olimits_{W\in T_{P,Q} : \abs{W}=\ell} \delta^{\ell} =\sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 2k} \delta^{\ell} \cdot \abs{\widehat{	t A}(u,\ell)} = \mathcal{J}(P,Q) \enspace. \end{align} The above proves that indeed $\abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)} \leq \mathcal{J}(P,Q)$ for $P$ and $Q$ which are compatible. \Cref{lemma:eq:CLVsCJEntrywise} follows. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathcal{L}(P,Q)$ as an influence in the $\{P,Q\}$-extension, expand over $T_{\rm SAW}$ paths and bound each path weight by $\delta^\ell$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10.3
nodes.statement:
First, we show that the following entry-wise inequality  egin{align} \mathcal{J} \leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq k}\delta^{\ell+k}\cdot ( ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k} )^{\ell}\cdot \UpR )_{\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}}\enspace, \end{align} where $\UpR$ is the involution defined in \eqref{def:OfInvolutation}, while $\left( ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k} )^{\ell}\cdot \UpR ight)_{\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}}$ is the principal submatrix of $( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k} )^{\ell}\cdot \UpR$ induced by the elements in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$. Consider $P,Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, which are compatible. Let $w$ and $u$ be the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Consider $\gext{G}{P,Q}$, the $(P,Q)$-extension of graph $G$ and let $T_{P,Q}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P,Q},w)$. From the definition of matrix $\mathcal{J}$, we have  egin{align} \mathcal{J}(P,Q)&=\sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 2k}\delta^{\ell}\cdot \abs{\widehat{	t A}(u,\ell)} \enspace, \end{align} where recall that $\widehat{	t A}(u,\ell)$ is the set of copies of vertex $u$ in $T_{P,Q}$ which correspond to self-avoiding walks of length $\ell$ in $\gext{G}{P,Q}$. The vertex $u$ is the starting vertex of $Q$. Note that the compatibility assumption for $P$ and $Q$ implies ${m dist}_{G}(w,u)\geq 2k$. Hence the copies of $u$ in $T$ are at distance $\geq 2k$ from the root. For $\ell\geq 2k$, we obtain a bound on $\abs{\widehat{	t A}(u,\ell)}$ in terms of the $k$-non-backtracking matrix $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}$. W.l.o.g. let $P=v_0, \ldots, v_{k}$ and $Q=x_0,\ldots, x_{k}$. The cardinality of set $\widehat{	t A}(u,\ell)$ is equal to the number of self-avoiding walks $R=z_0,\ldots, z_{\ell}$ in $\gext{G}{P,Q}$, satisfying the following condition: for $0\leq i \leq k$, we have  egin{itemize} \item $z_{i}$ is a copy of vertex $v_{i}$ and $z_{\ell-{i}}$ is a copy of $x_{i}$. \end{itemize} Recall that the additional vertices that $\gext{G}{P,Q}$ has compared to $G$ are split-vertices, each of which is of degree $1$. No split-vertex can be a part of a self-avoiding walk from $w$ to $u$. Hence, every self-avoiding walk $R$ in $\gext{G}{P,Q}$ that satisfies the above condition also appears in $G$. Furthermore, since every self-avoiding walk of length $\ell$ from $w$ to $u$ in $G$ can also be considered as a $k$-non-backtracking walk of length $\ell-k$ from $P$ to $Q^{-1}$, we conclude that  egin{align}
onumber \abs{\widehat{	t A}(u,\ell)} &\leq ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k} )^{\ell-k}(P,Q^{-1}) = ( ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell-k} \cdot \UpR ) (P,Q) \enspace. \end{align} Walk $Q^{-1}$ corresponds to $Q$ reversed, i.e., $Q^{-1}=x_{k},x_{k-1}, \ldots, x_0$. Plugging the above inequality into \eqref{eq:RedefInfmatrixBP-Q}, we get that \eqref{eq:Final4prop:CJVskNBM} is true for compatible walks $P$ and $Q$. For non-compatible $P,Q$, the definition of $\mathcal{J}$ specifies that $\mathcal{J}(P,Q)=0$. This implies that \eqref{eq:Final4prop:CJVskNBM} is true even for non-compatible $P$ and $Q$ since we always have $( ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell-k} \cdot \UpR ) (P,Q)\geq 0$. All the above establish that \eqref{eq:Final4prop:CJVskNBM} is true. Furthermore, \eqref{eq:Final4prop:CJVskNBM}, the fact that both $\mathcal{J}$ and $\left( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}ight)^{\ell-k}\cdot \UpR$ have non-negative entries and the triangle inequality imply  egin{align}
onumber 
orm{ \mathcal{J}}{2} & \leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq k}\delta^{\ell+k}\cdot 
orm{ (( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell} \cdot \UpR )_{\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}}}2 \leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq k}\delta^{\ell+k}\cdot 
orm{ ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell} \cdot \UpR }{2} \leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq k}\delta^{\ell+k}\cdot 
orm{ ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell} }{2} \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} The second inequality follows from Cauchy’s interlacing theorem. Note that matrix $(\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell} \cdot \UpR$ is symmetric due to \eqref{eq:DefPTInvarianceFormalB}. The third inequality follows since $
orm{ ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell} \cdot \UpR }{2}\leq 
orm{ ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2}\cdot 
orm{ \UpR }{2}$ while, for the involutionary matrix $\UpR$, we have $
orm{ \UpR}{2}=1$. \Cref{prop:CJVskNBM} follows. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Count self-avoiding walks between compatible walks by entries of $H_{G,k}^{\ell-k}R$, then use the triangle inequality, interlacing and $\|R\|_2=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11.1
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\||\mathcal{L}|\|_{2s}\le\sum_\ell\|\mathcal{D}_\ell\|_{2s}$; dominate $\mathcal{D}_\ell q$ by vectors built from $H_{G,k}^{\ell-k}R$ (Proposition 12.1), whose 2-norm is controlled by symmetry of $H^{\ell-k}R$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 12.1
nodes.statement_short: Pass from $f$ to $z$ via extension weights (Claim 12.2), then a potential-weighted tree recursion with Hölder below level $\ell-k$ and contraction above bounds $z$ by $g$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 13.2
nodes.statement:
We use \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} and identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P}, u)$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}=T_{m SAW}(G,u)$. Recall that the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ in $\applegreen{T}$ arise from $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$. Also, the edge-weights $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ arise from $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$. Having identified $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}$, we endow $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ with the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha(e)\}_{e\in \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$. Hence now we have two sets of weights for $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. Also, recall that set $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ consists of each vertex in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ which is either a copy of vertex $v\in P$, or a copy of a split-vertex in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$. We start with the following claim.  egin{claim} For any edge $f$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$, at distance $\ell >10$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, if $\upalpha(f)=0$, then $\upalpha_{P}(f)=0$. \end{claim} \Cref{claim:AlphaPZero} implies that \eqref{eq:prop:StableSSM} is true for any edge $f$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ at distance $\ell>10$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ such that $\upalpha(f)=0$. For the rest of the proof, we consider edge $f$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ such that $\upalpha(f)
eq 0$ which is at distance $\ell \geq \ell_0$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, where the quantity $\ell_0>10$ is specified later in the proof. Let edge $f=\{v,x\}$ while w.l.o.g. assume that $v$ is a child of $x$. Also, let $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ be the children of $v$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. We take $f$ at distance $\ell>10$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. This implies that vertex $v$ has the same set of children in both trees $\applegreen{T}$ and $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. If $v$ had children in $\applegreen{T}$ which are not in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, then according to \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU}, we would have had $v\in  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$. But since $v\in \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} (statement ef{stat:B-lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}) implies that $v\in  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. This cannot happen since we assume that $f$ is at distance at least $10$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. Hence, $v$ indeed has the same set of children in both trees $\applegreen{T}$ and $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. Let function $\Phi_d:\mathbb{R}^d	o \mathbb{R}$ be such that  egin{align} { f x} & \mapsto  rac{( eta \gamma-1) \cdot F_d({ f x})} {( eta \cdot F_d({ f x})+1)(F_d({ f x})+\gamma)}\enspace, \end{align} while $F_d({ f x})=F_d({ f x}_1, \ldots, { f x}_d)$ is defined in \eqref{eq:BPRecursion}. Recall that $d$ is the number of children of vertex $v$. For each child $v_{i}$, consider the ratios of marginals $ lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_{i}}$ and $\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L, \eta}_{v_{i}}$ defined as described in \Cref{sec:RecursionVsSpectralIneq}. Specifically, the ratio $ lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_{i}}$ is defined with respect to the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$, while the ratio $\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L, \eta}_{v_{i}}$ is defined with respect to the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$. Using \eqref{def:OfInfluenceWeights}, it is not hard to verify that we have $\upalpha(f)=\Phi_d( lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_1}, \ldots,  lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_d})$ and similarly $\upalpha_{P}(f)=\Phi_d(\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L,\eta}_{v_1},\ldots, \magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L, \eta}_{v_d})$. From the {\em mean value theorem}, there exists ${ f z}\in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that  egin{align} \upalpha_{P}(f)&=\upalpha(f) + \sum^{d}_{i=1} \left .  rac{\partial }{\partial { f x}_{i}}\Phi_d({ f x}) ight |_{{ f x}={ f z}} \cdot \left (\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L, \eta}_{v_{i}}- lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_{i}} ight )\enspace. \end{align} Recall that we take $f$ such that $\upalpha(f) 
eq 0$. Our $b$-boundedness assumption, for fixed $b>0$, and having $ \upalpha(f) 
eq 0$, imply that $\abs{\upalpha (f)}$ is a constant bounded away from zero. Hence, \eqref{eq:prop:StableSSM} is true if the sum on the r.h.s. in \eqref{eq:MeanValue4Alphas} is a sufficiently small constant. A standard calculation implies that for $i =1,\ldots, d$, we have  egin{align}  rac{\partial }{\partial { f x}_{i}}\Phi_d({ f x}) &= \Phi_d({ f x}) \cdot {	extstyle  rac{ eta\gamma-1}{( eta { f x}_{i}+1)({ f x}_{i}+\gamma)}} \cdot {	extstyle \left(1- rac{1+ eta\gamma+2F_d({ f x})}{ eta\gamma-1} \cdot \Phi_d({ f x}) ight) }\enspace. \end{align} The above implies that $ rac{\partial }{\partial { f x}_{i}}\Phi_d({ f x}) $ is bounded only if both $\Phi_d({ f x})$ and $F_d({ f x})$ are bounded for any ${ f x}\in [0,\infty]^d$ and $d\in [{\Delta}]$. From the definition of the functions $\Phi_d({ f x})$ and $F_d({ f x})$, it follows that they are indeed bounded, implying that $ rac{\partial }{\partial { f x}_{i}}\Phi_d({ f x}) $ is also bounded for $i =1,\ldots, d$. In light of all the above, \eqref{eq:prop:StableSSM} follows by showing that for any fixed number $\upkappa>0$, there is $\ell_0=\ell_0(\upkappa)$ such that for any edge $f$ at distance $\ell\geq \ell_0$ from set $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, we have  egin{align} \abs{ \magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L, \eta}_{v_{i}}- lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_{i}} } &\leq \upkappa & 	extrm{for } 1\leq i\leq d\enspace. \end{align} Note that assuming that $f$ is at distance $\ell$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ implies that the ball of radius $\ell-1$ from each vertex $v_{i}$ is inside tree $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. This follows from \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU,lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}. Furthermore, statement ef{stat:C-lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} in \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that there is a pair of configurations $\xi^{(i)}_1$ and $\xi^{(i)}_2$ at $N=L\cup \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, which only disagree at $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, such that  egin{align} \abs{ \magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{L, \eta}_{v_{i}}- lue{{R}}^{M, \sigma}_{v_{i}} } &\leq \abs{ \magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \xi^{(i)}_1}_{v_{i}}-\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \xi^{(i)}_2}_{v_{i}} } & 	extrm{for } 1\leq i\leq d \enspace, \end{align} where $\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \xi^{(i)}_1}_{z}$ and $\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \xi^{(i)}_2}_{z}$ are the ratios of marginals at vertex $z$ with respect to the Gibbs distributions $\mu^{N, \xi^{(i)}_1}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ and $\mu^{N, \xi^{(i)}_2}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$, respectively. We bound the r.h.s. of \eqref{eq:RealRatiosVsTPRatios} by using the following result.  egin{claim} For $\delta=  rac{1-\varepsilon}{\uprho}$, suppose that there is a $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential function ${\Psi}$ with respect to $( eta,\gamma,\lambda)$, where $\varepsilon,  eta,\gamma, \lambda,\uprho$ are defined in \Cref{prop:StableSSM}. Then, there are constants $c_A, c_B>0$ and $t_0>0$, such that for any vertex $z$ in tree $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ which is at distance $\ell\geq t_0$ from $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, the following is true: For $N=L\cup \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ and for {\em any} two configurations $\eta_1, \eta_2\in \{\pm 1\}^{N }$ that differ only at $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$, we have  egin{align} \abs{ \magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \eta_1}_{z} - \magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \eta_2}_{z}} \leq c_A \cdot \exp\left( -c_B \cdot \ell ight)\enspace, \end{align} where $\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \eta_1}_{z}$ and $\magenta{\overline{{R}}}^{N, \eta_2}_{z}$ are the ratios of marginals at vertex $z$ with respect to the Gibbs distributions $\mu^{N, \eta_1}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ and $\mu^{N, \eta_2}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$, respectively. \end{claim} We get \eqref{eq:Target4prop:StableSSM} from \eqref{eq:RealRatiosVsTPRatios} and \Cref{claim:Target4prop:StableSSM}. \Cref{prop:StableSSM} follows. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Mean value theorem on $\Phi_d$ reduces the claim to closeness of ratios at the children; this follows from exponential decay of boundary influence (Claim 13.6).

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 13.5
nodes.statement: The proof is not too different from that of \Cref{claim:SupportOfWeiS} In this proof, we identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}=T_{\rm SAW}(G,u)$. W.l.o.g., let edge $f$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ be such that $f=\{v,x\}$. Also, let $\uppi$ be the set of vertices that consists of $v,x$ and their children in $\applegreen{T}$. Arguing as in \Cref{claim:SupportOfWeiS}, the assumption of having $f$ at distance $>10$ from $\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$ implies that all elements in $\uppi$ are vertices in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. Our assumption for $b$-boundedness, for fixed $b>0$, implies that for edge $f$ in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, we either have $\upalpha(f)=0$, or $\abs{\upalpha(f)}$ is bounded away from zero. The same holds for $\upalpha_{P}(f)$. Furthermore, we have $\upalpha(f)=0$ (resp. $\upalpha_{P}(f)=0$) only if at least one of the vertices in $\uppi$ has a pinning under $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ (resp. $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$). Note that for the case where the parameter of the Gibbs distribution $\beta=0$, it is possible that by pinning one of the children of $v$ or $x$ we get $\upalpha(f)=0$ (resp. $\upalpha_{P}(f)=0$). Recall from \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}, statement \ref{stat:C-lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}, that the pinnings imposed by $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ and $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ on the vertices in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ can only differ on the vertices in $L\setminus M\subseteq \byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}$. But since $L\setminus M\subseteq \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, we have that $L\setminus M\subseteq \magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$, i.e., since statement \ref{stat:B-lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} in \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$. Taking $f$ at a sufficiently large distance from $\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$, e.g., distance greater than $10$, we have that $\uppi\not\subset \magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$. Hence, if the two distributions $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ and $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ impose pinnings to vertices in set $\uppi$, these pinning should be identical. This leads us to conclude that if $\upalpha(f)=0$, this is because $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ fixes the configuration of a vertex in $\uppi$. But then, $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ imposes identical pinning to $\uppi$. Hence, we also have $\upalpha_{P}(f)=0$. All the above conclude the proof of \Cref{claim:AlphaPZero}. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Far from $\overline{\tt A}_P$ both pinnings agree on the neighbourhood of $f$, so a zero weight in one forces a zero weight in the other.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 13.6
nodes.statement:
In this proof, we identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}=T_{m SAW}(G,u)$. Firstly, we upper bound the number of paths in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ from vertex $z$ to the set of vertices $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ as a function of $\ell$, i.e., the distance of $z$ from the set. If $z$ is a copy of vertex $\widehat{z}$ in $\gext{G}{P}$, then the paths from $z$ to $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ correspond to the self-avoiding walks from $\widehat{z}$ to the set of vertices $P\cup \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$. Let $K(\ell)$ be the number of these walks. We assume that $\ell\geq t_0$ for a large constant $t_0$, e.g., $t_0>100k$. Note that $K(\ell)$ is upper bounded by the number of self-avoiding walks in $G$ from vertex $\widehat{z}$ to $P$. Furthermore, since each self-avoiding path of length $\ell>k$ is also a $k$-non-backtracking walk, we have  egin{align} K(\ell) &\leq\sum
olimits_{W,Q}\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}^{\ell-k}(W,Q) \enspace. \end{align} Variable $W$ varies over the walks in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$ which emanate from vertex $\widehat{z}$. Variable $Q$ varies over $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$ such that its last vertex is in $P$. The exponent $\ell-k$ has to do with how we measure distances between $k$-non-backtracking walks with $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}$. A crude estimation implies that the number of summands in \eqref{eq:KEllVsNBMGPEntry} is $\leq (k+2)\cdot {\Delta}^{k}$. We have  egin{align} K(\ell) &\leq (k+2)\cdot {\Delta}^{k} \cdot \max
olimits_{W,Q}\{ \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}^{\ell-k}(W,Q)\} \enspace. \end{align} Furthermore, \Cref{claim:SigmaLVsPathNumber,lemma:SingSequenConv} imply that for any $\zeta\in (0,1)$, there exists integer $\hat{r}_0=\hat{r}_0(N,{\Delta}, k, \zeta)>1$ such that for any $r \geq \hat{r}_0$ we have  egin{align} \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}^{r}(W,Q) \leq \left( (1+\zeta)\cdot \uprho ight)^{r}\enspace. \end{align} Recall that $
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$. Combining \eqref{eq:KELLVMaxHGKWQ} and \eqref{eq:FromClaim5758}, for $\ell\geq \max\{\hat{r}_0,k\}$, we have  egin{align} K(\ell) & \leq (k+2)\cdot {\Delta}^{k}\cdot \left( (1+\zeta)\cdot \uprho ight)^{\ell-k} \enspace. \end{align} We choose $\zeta$ such that $\zeta=(1+\varepsilon/2)(1-\varepsilon/2)$, where $\varepsilon$ is from the parameter $\delta$ of the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential function ${\Psi}$, i.e., recall that we have $\delta=  rac{1-\varepsilon}{\uprho}$. We choose $t_0$ to be the maximum between the quantities $2\varepsilon^{-1}\log((k+2)\cdot {\Delta}^{k})$ and $\hat{r}_0$. With our choices of $\zeta$ and $t_0$, for any $\ell\geq t_0$, we have $K(\ell)\leq \left((1+\varepsilon/2)\cdot \uprhoight)^{\ell}$. With the above in mind, standard arguments imply that for \eqref{eq:ClaimTarget4prop:StableSSM}, it suffices to show that there exists a differentiable, increasing potential function $\Upxi:[-\infty,+\infty]	o(-\infty,+\infty)$ such that  egin{align} \phi\left( F({ f z})ight)\cdot \sum^d_{i=1}  rac{1}{\phi({ f z}_{i})}\cdot \left.  rac{\partial}{\partial { f x}_{i}}F({ f x})ight|_{{ f x}={ f z}} \cdot { f m}_{i} &\leq \left(  rac{1-\varepsilon}{\uprho}ight)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot 
orm{ { f m}}{\darkmagenta{s}}\enspace, \end{align} where $\phi=\Upxi'$. Using the standard chain rule for derivatives, (see also \cite{VigodaSpectralInd}) we conclude that \eqref{eq:SSMCondition4Stability} is true by using $\Upxi={\Psi}\circ\log$, where ${\Psi}$ is the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential function. \Cref{claim:Target4prop:StableSSM} follows. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the number of walks to $P$ by entries of $H_{G,k}^{\ell-k}$ growing like $((1+\varepsilon/2)\uprho)^\ell$, then a standard potential-function contraction argument gives exponential decay.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: Combining \Cref{thrm:GoodPotentialHC}, \Cref{thrm:NonBacktrackingPotentialSpIn} and \Cref{claim:InterpretGoodPotentialHC}, with our assumption that ${\Delta}$ and $\uprho$ being $\Theta(1)$, we have \begin{align} \nonumber {\rho} {\textstyle \left( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} \right)} &= O(1) \enspace, \end{align} for any $\Lambda\subset V$ and $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^{\Lambda}$. Furthermore, our assumptions about $\lambda$ imply that $\mu$ is $b$-marginally bounded, for fixed $b>0$. Considering all the above, \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusHash} follows as a corollary from \Cref{thrm:SPINLOGN}. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorem 14.1, Theorem 3.7 and Claim 14.2 to get $O(1)$ spectral independence, then apply Theorem 5.4.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.7
nodes.statement: The proof of \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusAdj} is almost identical to that of \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusHash}. Combining \Cref{thrm:GoodPotentialHC}, \Cref{thrm:AdjacencyPotentialSpIn} and \Cref{claim:InterpretGoodPotentialHC}, with our assumption about ${\Delta}$ and ${\varrho}$ being $\Theta(1)$, we have \begin{align} \nonumber {\rho} \left( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} \right) &=O(1)\enspace, \end{align} for any $\Lambda\subset V$ and $\tau\in \{\pm 1\}^{\Lambda}$. Furthermore, our assumptions about $\lambda$ imply that $\mu$ is $b$-marginally bounded, for fixed $b>0$. Considering all the above, \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusAdj} follows as a corollary from \Cref{thrm:SPINLOGN}. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorem 14.1, Theorem 3.6 and Claim 14.2 to get $O(1)$ spectral independence, then apply Theorem 5.4.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement:
To prove \Cref{thrm:HC4CCK}, we use the following proposition.  egin{restatable}{proposition}{CcLccVsHSPradius} For integers $k,N>0$ and graph $G=(V,E)$, we have that $
orm{(\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{2} \leq \left( \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}ight)^{N+k}$. \end{restatable} The proof of \Cref{prop:HSPRadCCLCC} appears in \Cref{sec:prop:HSPRadCCLCC}. Given the parameters $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$, let $z=z(\varepsilon, \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})>0$ be such that  egin{align} {\lambda_c}((1+z)\goldenbrown{\upd}_k)= (1-\varepsilon/3){\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_k) \enspace. \end{align} Such $z$ exists and it is unique, since ${\lambda_c}(x)$ is monotonically decreasing in $x$. \Cref{prop:HSPRadCCLCC} implies that there exists $M=M(z,\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})$ such that for any $N\geq M$, we have  egin{align} 
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2} \leq \left( \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}ight)^{ rac{N+k}{N}}\leq (1+z)\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}\enspace. \end{align} Let $\uprho=
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^M}{1/M}{2}$, where $M$ is defined above. From \eqref{eq:Base4thrm:HC4CCK} and \eqref{eq:Base4thrm:HC4CCKBB} we have  egin{align} {\lambda_c}(\uprho) &\geq (1-\varepsilon/3){\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_k) \enspace. \end{align} For the above, we use once more that ${\lambda_c}(x)$ is monotonically decreasing in $x$. \Cref{thrm:HC4CCK} follows by noting that the above implies that for $\lambda<(1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_k)$ we also have that $\lambda<(1-\varepsilon/3){\lambda_c}(\uprho)$. For such $\lambda$, \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusHash} implies that there is a constant $C>0$, such that Glauber dynamics on the Hard-core model on $G$ has mixing time at most $C n\log n$. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Choose $N$ large so that $\|H_{G,k}^N\|_2^{1/N}\le(1+z)\upd_k$ (Proposition 14.3) and apply Theorem 1.2 using monotonicity of $\lambda_c$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 14.3
nodes.statement:
Let integer $M>1$ which we will specify later. Let a length $k \cdot M$ walk $P=w_0, \ldots, w_{k \cdot M}$ in $G$. We say that $P$ is $k$-wise self-avoiding, if the sub-walk $P_{i}=w_{i\cdot k}, w_{i\cdot k+1}, \ldots, w_{i\cdot k+k}$ is self-avoiding, for all $i=0,\ldots, M-1$. Note that $P$ is not necessarily a self-avoiding walk since the same vertex $v$ can appear in both $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$, for $i
eq j$. For each $v\in V$, let $\uppi_{k}(v, k M)$ be the set of $k$-wise self-avoiding walks of length $k \cdot M$ that emanate from $v$. Let $\upchi_{k,M}=\sup\{ \uppi_{k}(v, k M)\ |\ v\in V\}$. It is an easy exercise to show that  egin{align} \upchi_{k, M} & \leq (\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})^{k M}\enspace. \end{align} Furthermore, let $Q=x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k M}$ be a $k$-non-backtracking walk in $G$. $Q$ is also a $k$-wise self-avoiding walk. To see this, note that for all $j=0,\ldots, k\cdot(M-1)$, the sub-walk $x_{j},\ldots, x_{j+k}$ in $Q$ is self-avoiding. For $Q$ to be $k$-wise self-avoiding, we only need the sub-walks $x_{j},\ldots, x_{j+k}$ to be self-avoiding, for $j$ being a multiple of $k$. Hence, $Q$ is a $k$-wise self-avoiding walk. For $W, S\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}$, i.e., two self-avoiding walks of length $k$ in $G$, recall that $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}^{k (M-1)}(W, S)$ is equal to the number of $k$-non-backtracking walks of length $k\cdot (M-1)$ that start from $W$ and end at $S$. Every $k$-non-backtracking walk of length $k\cdot (M-1)$ from $W$ to $S$ is also a $k$-wise self-avoiding walk of length $k\cdot M$ starting at $v$, the first vertex in $W$. Hence, we have  egin{align} \sum
olimits _{S\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{k}}\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}^{k(M-1)}(W, S) \leq \uppi_{k}(v, k M) \leq \upchi_{k, M} \enspace. \end{align} From all the above, we obtain  egin{align}
onumber 
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR }{\infty}= 
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}}{\infty} &\leq \upchi_{k,M}= (\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})^{k M}\enspace, \end{align} where $\UpR$ is the involution defined in \eqref{def:OfInvolutation}. For any integer $\ell>0$, we have that  egin{align} 
orm{ ( (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR )^{\ell}}{\infty} &\leq 
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR}{\ell}{\infty} \leq (\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})^{k\cdot M\cdot \ell} \enspace. \end{align} Recall that $(\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR$ is a symmetric matrix, e.g., see \eqref{eq:DefPTInvarianceFormalB}. From Gelfand's formula e.g., see \cite{SIAM-LAlg}, we get  egin{align}
onumber 
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR }{2} = \lim_{\ell	o\infty} 
norm{ {	extstyle ( (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR )^{\ell} } }{1/\ell}{\infty} & \leq \lim_{\ell 	o \infty} \left ((\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})^{k\cdot M\cdot \ell} ight)^{1/\ell} = (\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})^{k\cdot M} \enspace. \end{align} where the second derivation follows from \eqref{eq:HRLInfBound}. Since $\UpR$ is an involution, we have $
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}\cdot \UpR}{2}=
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}}{2}$. From the above, we conclude that $
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{k(M-1)}}{2} \leq \left(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}ight)^{k\cdot M}$. \Cref{prop:HSPRadCCLCC} follows by setting $M= rac{N}{k}+1$. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Bound row sums of $H_{G,k}^{k(M-1)}$ by counts of $k$-wise self-avoiding walks, at most $\upd_k^{kM}$, then Gelfand's formula on the symmetric $H^{k(M-1)}R$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.5
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 15.1 gives $(1-\varepsilon)/\uprho$-contraction, Theorem 3.4 gives $O(1)$ spectral independence, Theorem 5.4 gives optimal mixing.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.8
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 15.1 gives $(1-\varepsilon)/\varrho$-contraction, Theorem 3.2 gives $O(1)$ spectral independence, Theorem 5.4 gives optimal mixing.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: The proof of \Cref{thrm:Ising4CCK} is conceptually similar to \Cref{thrm:HC4CCK}. We are using \Cref{prop:HSPRadCCLCC} once more in this proof. It is straightforward to show that for any $z<\hat{z}$, we have ${\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\hat{z},\delta)\subset {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(z,\delta)$. Similarly, for any $\delta<\hat{\delta}$, we have ${\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(z,\hat{\delta})\subset {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(z,\delta)$. Given the parameters $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and $\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}$, let $z=z(\varepsilon, \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})>0$ be such that \begin{align} {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon)= {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}((1+z)\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon/3)\enspace. \end{align} Furthermore, \Cref{prop:HSPRadCCLCC} implies that there exists $M=M(z,\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k})$ such that for any $N\geq M$, we have \begin{align} \nnorm{(\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2} \leq \left( \goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}\right)^{\frac{N+k}{N}}\leq (1+z)\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}\enspace. \end{align} Let $\uprho=\nnorm{(\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^M}{1/M}{2}$, where $M$ is defined above. The above relations imply that \begin{align} {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon)\subseteq {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\uprho, \varepsilon/3)\enspace. \end{align} \Cref{thrm:Ising4CCK} follows by noting that the above relation implies that for $\beta\in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\goldenbrown{\upd}_{k}, \varepsilon)$, we also have $\beta\in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(\uprho, \varepsilon/3)$. For such $\beta$ and for $\lambda>0$, \Cref{thrm:Ising4CCK} implies that there is a constant $C>0$, such that Glauber dynamics on the Ising model on $G$ has mixing time at most $C n\log n$. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 14.3 to compare $\uprho$ with $\upd_k$, nest the uniqueness intervals, and apply the $H_{G,k}$ mixing bound for the Ising model.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 14.1
nodes.statement:
Recall that the ratio of Gibbs marginals ${R}^{\Lambda, 	au}_{u}$, defined in \Cref{sec:RecursionVsSpectralIneq}, is possible to be equal to zero, or $\infty$. Typically, this happens if vertex $u$ with respect to which we consider the ratio is pinned, i.e., $u \in \Lambda$, or has a neighbour in $\Lambda$. When we deal with the Hard-core model, there is a standard way to avoid these infinities and zeros in our calculations and make the derivation much simpler. Suppose we have the Hard-core model with fugacity $\lambda>0$ on a tree $T$, while at the set of vertices $\Lambda$ we have a pinning $	au$. Then, it is elementary that this distribution is identical to the Hard-core model with the same fugacity on the tree (or forest) $T'$ which is obtained from $T$ by removing every vertex $w$ which either belongs to $\Lambda$, or has a neighbour in $ \Lambda$ which is pinned to 1. From now on, for the instances we consider, assume that we have applied the above steps and removed any pinnings. It is useful to write down the functions that arise from the tree recursions in \Cref{sec:RecursionVsSpectralIneq}, specifically for the Hard-core model with fugacity $\lambda$. Recall that, in this case, we have $ eta=0$ and $\gamma=1$. In the following definitions, we assume that there are no pinnings. For integer $d\geq 1$, we have $F_d:\mathbb{R}^d_{>0}	o (0, \lambda)$ such that for any ${ f x}=({ f x}_1, \ldots, { f x}_d)$, we have {\small  egin{align} { f x}\mapsto \lambda \prod
olimits_{i\in [d]} rac{1}{{ f x}_{i}+1} \enspace. \end{align} } We also define $F_{d,{m sym}}:\mathbb{R}_{>0}	o (0, \lambda)$ the {\em symmetric} version of the above function, that is  egin{align} x&\mapsto F_d(x,x,\ldots, x) \enspace. \end{align} We also have $H_d:\mathbb{R}^d	o \mathbb{R}$ such that for any ${ f x}=({ f x}_1, \ldots, { f x}_d)$, we have {\small  egin{align} { f x} \mapsto \log \lambda+\sum
olimits_{i\in [d]} \log\left(  rac{1}{\exp({ f x}_{i})+1} ight) \enspace. \end{align} } For $ rac{\partial }{\partial { f x}_{i}}H_d({ f x})=h({ f x}_{i})$, we have $h:\mathbb{R} 	o \mathbb{R}$ such that {\small  egin{align} { f x} \mapsto - rac{e^{{ f x}_{i}}}{e^{{ f x}_{i}}+1} \enspace. \end{align} } Finally, the set of log-ratios $J$, defined in \eqref{eq:DefOfRatiorange}, satisfies that  egin{align} J=(-\infty, \log(\lambda)) \enspace. \end{align} Set $S_{{\Psi}}$, i.e., the image of ${\Psi}$, satisfies $S_{{\Psi}}=(-\infty, \infty)$. \Cref{thrm:GoodPotentialHC} follows by showing that ${\Psi}$ satisfies the Contraction and the Boundedness conditions of \Cref{def:GoodPotential}, for the parameters indicated in the statement. We start with the {\em Contraction}. The claim follows. \end{proof} In light of \Cref{claim:OnePotVsOtherPot}, \eqref{prop:Target4PotContractsA} follows by showing that for any ${ f m}=({ f m}_1, \ldots, { f m}_d) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}_{ \geq 0}$ and ${ f z}=({ f z}_1, \ldots, { f z}_d)\in \mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}$ we have  egin{align} {\psi} (F_{d}({ f z})) 	imes \sum

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.3
nodes.statement:
The proofs of \Cref{thrm:HarndessTransHCNBM,thrm:HarndessTransIsingNBM} are almost identical. We only show how to prove \Cref{thrm:HarndessTransHCNBM} and we omit the proof of \Cref{thrm:HarndessTransIsingNBM}. For a graph $G=(V,E)$ and $\lambda>0$, consider the Hard-core model with fugacity $\lambda$. We define $\mathcal{Z}(G,\lambda)$, the {\em partition function} of this distribution by  egin{align} \mathcal{Z}(G,\lambda)&=\sum
olimits_{\sigma}\lambda^{|\sigma|}\enspace, \end{align} where $\sigma$ varies over all the independent sets of $G$. For the proof of \Cref{thrm:HarndessTransHCNBM} we use the following result.  egin{theorem}[\cite{GSV16Hardness,SS14}] Unless ${m NP} = {m RP}$, for the Hard-core model, for all ${\Delta}\geq 3$ for all $\lambda>{\lambda_c}({\Delta}-1)$ there does not exist an FPRAS for the partition function with fugacity $\lambda$ for graphs of maximum degree at most ${\Delta}$. \end{theorem} \Cref{thrm:HC4SPRadiusHash} yields (via \cite{JVV86,SVV09}) an FPRAS for estimating the partition function $\mathcal{Z}(G,\lambda)$ with running time $O^*(n^2)$, for any $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\uprho)$. Recall that $\uprho=
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}$. Also, recall that $O^*()$ hides multiplicative $\log n$-factors. The negative part, i.e., the non-existence of FPRAS for $\lambda\geq (1+\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(\lceil \uprhoceil)$, follows from \Cref{thrm:HarndessCounting}. For graph $G$, such that $
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$, it is standard that ${\Delta}\geq \lceil \uprho ceil +1$. Then, it suffices to apply \Cref{thrm:HarndessCounting} for graphs $G$ with $
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}=\uprho$ and maximum degree at most ${\Delta}=\lceil \uprho ceil +1$. The above concludes the proof of \Cref{thrm:HarndessTransHCNBM}.
nodes.statement_short: Positive part from Theorem 1.2 via counting-to-sampling reductions; negative part from the hardness Theorem 17.1 applied to graphs of maximum degree $\lceil\uprho\rceil+1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.1
nodes.statement: For $G=(V,E)$, the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and integer $k\geq 1$, we introduce the $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}\times (V\setminus \Lambda)$ matrix ${\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$ such that, for any $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$ and $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$, the entry ${\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda, \tau}_G(P, u) $ is defined as follows: Letting $w$ be the starting vertex of walk $P$, we have \begin{align} {\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda, \tau}_{G,k}(P, u) &=0 \enspace, \end{align} if vertices $u$ and $w$ are at distance $<2k$. Consider $u$ and $w$ which are at distance $\geq 2k$. Let $\upzeta^{P}$ be the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. We have \begin{align} {\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda, \tau}_{G,k}(P, u) &= \upzeta^{P}_{u}(+1\ |\ (w,+1)) - \upzeta^{P}_{u}(+1 \ |\ (w,-1)) \enspace, \end{align} where $\upzeta^{P}_{u}$ is the marginal of $\upzeta^{P}$ at vertex $u$. Letting ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$ be the influence matrix induced by $\upzeta^{P}$, \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrixB} implies \begin{align} {\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda, \tau}_{G,k}(P, u) &={\mathcal{I}}^{P}(w,u)\enspace. \end{align} In light of all the above, \Cref{thrm:InflVsExtInfl} follows as a corollary from the following two results. \begin{lemma} There is an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}\times (V\setminus \Lambda)$ matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_A$ such that \begin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G = \UpD_{k} \cdot\left({\mathcal{N}}_A \circ {\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k} \right)+ {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G, <2k} \enspace. \end{align} Furthermore, there is a fixed number $C_A>0$, which is independent of $\Lambda$ and $\tau$, such that, for any $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ and any $v\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have $|{\mathcal{N}}_A(P,v)|\leq C_A$. \end{lemma} In \eqref{eq:lemma:FromCalI2CalF}, the matrices $ {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G, <2{k}}$ and $\UpD_{k}$ are defined in \eqref{eq:DefOfCISmallerK} and \eqref{def:Vertex2EdgeMatrixEntryBB}, respectively. Also, ${\mathcal{N}}_A \circ {\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$ is the Hadamard product of the two matrices. The proof of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF} appears in \Cref{sec:lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. \begin{lemma} There exists an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}\times \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$ matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_B$ such that \begin{align} {\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k} =\left( \applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k} \circ {\mathcal{N}}_B \right)\cdot \UpC_{k} \enspace. \end{align} Furthermore, there is a fixed number $C_B>0$, which is independent of $\Lambda$ and $\tau$, such that for any $Q,P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, we have $\abs{{\mathcal{N}}_B(P,Q)} \leq C_B$. \end{lemma} In \eqref{eq:lemma:FromCalF2CalH}, matrix $\UpC_k$ is defined in \eqref{def:Edge2VertexMatrixEntryBB}. The proof of \Cref{lemma:FromCalF2CalH} appears in \Cref{sec:lemma:FromCalF2CalH}. \Cref{thrm:InflVsExtInfl} follows as a corollary from \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF,lemma:FromCalF2CalH}. Specifically, ${\mathcal{N}}$ is given by the Hadamard product ${\mathcal{N}}={\mathcal{N}}_C \circ{\mathcal{N}}_B$, where ${\mathcal{N}}_B$ is from \Cref{lemma:FromCalF2CalH} and ${\mathcal{N}}_C$ is the $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}\times \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ matrix such that for any $P,Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ we have ${\mathcal{N}}_C(P,Q)={\mathcal{N}}_A(P,u)$, where $u$ is the starting vertex of $Q$. Matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_A$ is from \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. We conclude that \Cref{thrm:InflVsExtInfl} is true for $\widehat{C}=C_A\cdot C_B$. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Compose Lemma 18.1 ($\mathcal{I}$ via $\mathcal{F}$) and Lemma 18.2 ($\mathcal{F}$ via $\mathcal{L}$) through Hadamard products of bounded matrices.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 18.1
nodes.statement:
In this proof, we use the properties of extensions from \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw,lemma:GibbsWeightsTpVsP}. Also, we abbreviate $\UpD_{k}$, ${\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k}$, ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G, <2k}$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G}$ to $ \UpD$, ${\mathcal{F}}$, ${\mathcal{I}}_{<2k}$ and ${\mathcal{I}}$, respectively. Firstly, we note that the matrices at the two sides of the equation in \eqref{eq:lemma:FromCalI2CalF} are of the same dimension, i.e., they are $(V\setminus \Lambda)	imes (V\setminus \Lambda)$. We show that their corresponding entries are equal to each other. For any $v\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}_{<2{k}}(v,v)&=1& 	extrm{and}&& \left(\UpD\cdot \left({\mathcal{N}}_A \circ{\mathcal{F}} ight)ight)(v,v)&=0 \enspace. \end{align} The equality on the right is true because $\left(\UpD\cdot \left({\mathcal{N}}_A \circ{\mathcal{F}} ight)ight)(v,v)=\sum_{P}\UpD(v,P)\cdot{\mathcal{N}}_A(P,v)\cdot {\mathcal{F}}(P,v)$ and the variable $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ runs over walks that emanate from $v$. For such walks ${\mathcal{F}}(P,v)=0$. Hence, for any matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_A$ the above is true. From the definition of ${\mathcal{I}}$ and \eqref{eq:FirstEqInlemma:FromCalI2CalF} we conclude that ${\mathcal{I}}$ and $ {\mathcal{I}}_{<2k}+\UpD\cdot\left({\mathcal{N}}_A \circ {\mathcal{F}} ight)$ have ones at their diagonal. Now, we focus on the off-diagonal elements. Let  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}_{\geq 2k} &={\mathcal{I}}-{\mathcal{I}}_{<2k}\enspace. \end{align} It suffices to show that there exists an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}	imes V\setminus \Lambda$ matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_A$, with its entries bounded as specified in the statement of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}, such that for any $u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda$, which are different from each other, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}_{\geq 2k}(w,u) &= \sum
olimits_{P} {\mathcal{N}}_A(P,u) \cdot {\mathcal{F}}(P,u) \enspace, \end{align} where $P$ varies in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$, such that its first vertex is $w$. For vertices $w,u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ at distance $< 2k$, The definition of ${\mathcal{F}}$ implies that for $P$ emanating from $w$, we have $ {\mathcal{F}}(P,u)=0$. Also, we have ${\mathcal{I}}_{\geq 2k}(w,u)=0$. We conclude that for pairs of vertices $w,u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ at distance $< 2k$, \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalI2CalF} is true for any choice of matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_A$. We consider $w$ and $u$ at distance $\geq 2k$ from each other. Let $ yzantine{T}=T_{{m SAW}}(G, w)$. Also, let $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ be the collection of weights over the edges of $ yzantine{T}$ we obtain by applying the $T_{m SAW}$-construction on the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$. Then, \Cref{prop:Inf2TreeRedaux} implies  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}_{\geq 2k}(w,u) &=\sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 2k} \sum
olimits_{W=(e_1, \ldots, e_{\ell}) \in  yzantine{T}} \prod
olimits_{1 \leq i\leq \ell}\upalpha(e_{i}) \enspace, \end{align} where $W$ varies over the length-$\ell$ paths in $ yzantine{T}$ from the root of the tree to the copies of vertex $u$. For each $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, which emanates from vertex $w$, consider $\deeppink{T_{P}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},w)$. Using \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw}, we identify each $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ as a subtree of $ yzantine{T}$, while note that both trees have the same root. Recall also the weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ on the edges of $ yzantine{T}$ that are induced by the $T_{m SAW}$-construction on $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$. Since $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ is a subtree of $ yzantine{T}$, we endow $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ with the edge-weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}_{e\in \deeppink{T_{P}}}$. Each path $W$ in $ yzantine{T}$ that emanates from the root and is of length $\geq 2k$ belongs to exactly one of the subtrees $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ of $ yzantine{T}$ we define above. Using this observation, we write \eqref{eq:IfVsWeightscFVsVi} as follows:  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}_{\geq 2k}(w,u)&=\sum
olimits_{P} \sum
olimits_{\ell \geq 2k} \sum
olimits_{W=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}) \in \deeppink{T_{P}}} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell }\upalpha(e_i) \enspace, \end{align} where variable $P$ varies over the walks in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanate from vertex $w$ and variable $W$ varies over the length-$\ell$ paths in $\deeppink{T_{P}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},w)$ from the root of the tree to the copies of vertex $u$. For each $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$ whose first vertex is $w$, and $\deeppink{T_{P}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},w)$, we let $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}_{e\in \deeppink{T_{P}}}$ be the collection of weights over the edges of $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ specified with respect to the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$. The definition of matrix ${\mathcal{F}}$ in \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrix} and \Cref{prop:Inf2TreeRedaux} imply  egin{align} {\mathcal{F}}(P, u)&=\sum
olimits_{\ell \geq 2k}\sum
olimits_{W=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}) \in \deeppink{T_{P}}} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell} \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) \enspace, \end{align} where $W$ varies over the length-$\ell$ paths from the root to the copies of $u$ in $\deeppink{T_{P}}$. Letting $P=x_0,\ldots,x_k$, there is a path $R_{P}=u_0,\ldots, u_{k}$ in tree $\magenta{T}$, which emanates from the root such that $u_{i}$ is a copy of $x_{i}$, for all $0\leq i \leq k $. We have that $R_{P}$ is in $ \deeppink{T_{P}}$, too. Furthermore, all paths $W\in \deeppink{T_{P}}$ of length $\ell\geq 2k$ that emanate from the root of $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ overlap with $R_{P}$ in their first $k$ edges. The above observation implies that fixing $\ell\geq 2k$ and path $W=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell})$, the corresponding summand in \eqref{eq:FVsITs} trivially satisfies  egin{align} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell} \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) &= \UpK 	imes \prod
olimits_{k< i\leq \ell } \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) \enspace, \end{align} where $\UpK=\prod
olimits_{e \in R_{P}} \upalpha_{P}(e)$. In a previous step, we endowed each $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ with the edge weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}_{e\in \deeppink{T_{P}}}$ since it is a subtree of $ yzantine{T}$. Overall now, for each $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ we have two sets of edges weights i.e., we have $\{\upalpha(e)\}_{e\in \deeppink{T_{P}}}$ and $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}_{e\in \deeppink{T_{P}}}$. \Cref{lemma:GibbsWeightsTpVsP} implies that for any edge $e\in \deeppink{T_{P}}$, which is at distance $\geq k$ from the root of $\deeppink{T_{P}}$, we have  egin{align} \upalpha_{P}(e)&=\upalpha(e) \enspace. \end{align} Combining \eqref{eq:IfVsWeightscFVsViCC} and \eqref{eq:ProdWeigtPTPBreak} we get the following: fixing $\ell\geq 2k$ and path $W=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell})$, the corresponding summand in \eqref{eq:FVsITs} satisfies  egin{align} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell} \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) &= \UpK 	imes \prod
olimits_{k< i\leq \ell } \upalpha(e_{i}) \enspace. \end{align} We define the $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}	imes V\setminus \Lambda$ matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_A$ such that for each $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ and $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{N}}_A(P,u) = \left \{  egin{array}{lcl} 1 &\quad &	extrm{if distance from $u$ to the starting vertex of $P$ is $<2k$}\ \prod_{e\in R_{P}} rac{\upalpha(e)}{\upalpha_{P}(e)+\mathds{1}\{\upalpha_{P}(e)=0\}} &&	extrm{otherwise}\enspace, \end{array} ight . 
onumber \end{align} where $R_{P}$ is the path in $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ defined earlier. The above definition of ${\mathcal{N}}_A$ implies  egin{align} {\mathcal{N}}_A(P,u)\cdot {\mathcal{F}}(P, u)&= \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 2k} \sum
olimits_{W=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell})\in \deeppink{T_{P}}} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell }\upalpha(e_{i}) \enspace, \end{align} where $W$ varies over the paths in $\deeppink{T_{P}}$ from the root to the copies of vertex $u$ at distance $\ell$ from the root. Verifying the above equality is a matter of simple calculations when $\upalpha_{P}(e)
eq 0$ for all $e\in R_{P}$. That is, it follows from \eqref{eq:FVsITs}, \eqref{eq:ProdWeigtPTPBreakNew} and the definition of ${\mathcal{N}}_A$. When there is at least one $e\in R_{P}$ such that $\upalpha_{P}(e)=0$, then it is not hard to see that we also have $\upalpha(e)=0$; hence both sides in \eqref{eq:IfVsWeightscFVsViDD} are equal to zero. All the above imply that \eqref{eq:IfVsWeightscFVsViDD} is true. Then, plugging \eqref{eq:IfVsWeightscFVsViDD} into \eqref{eq:IfVsWeightscFVsViBB}, we obtain \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. Hence, we conclude that \eqref{eq:lemma:FromCalI2CalF} is true. The assumption that $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$ is $b$-marginally bounded implies that there is $\upc \in (0,1)$, bounded away from zero such that we either have $\upalpha_{P}(e)=0$, or $\upc\leq \abs{\upalpha_{P}(e)} \leq 1$ and similarly for $\upalpha(e)$. Hence, for any $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ and any vertex $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have $| {\mathcal{N}}_A(P, u)| \leq \max\{1,\upc^{-k}\}$. We conclude that \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF} is true for $C_A=\max\{1,\upc^{- k}\}$. \hfill $\square$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 18.2
nodes.statement:
In what follows, we abbreviate ${\mathcal{F}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k}$ and $\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k}$ to ${\mathcal{F}}$ and $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$, respectively. Firstly, we note that the matrices at the two sides of the equation in \eqref{eq:lemma:FromCalF2CalH} are of the same dimension, i.e., they are $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}	imes (V\setminus \Lambda)$. \Cref{lemma:FromCalF2CalH} follows by showing that there is an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}	imes \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_B$, with entries bounded as specified in the statement of \Cref{lemma:FromCalF2CalH}, such that for any $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda, k}$, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{F}}(P, u) &= \sum
olimits_{Q} {\mathcal{N}}_B(P, Q)\cdot osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q) \enspace, \end{align} where $Q$ varies over all walks in $ \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanate from vertex $u$. Consider vertices $w, u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ at distance $\geq 2k$ and $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ which emanates from $w$. We start by showing that for such $P$ and $w, u$, \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalF2CalH} is true. Let $\upzeta^{P}$ be the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_{G}$. Let ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$ be the influence matrix induced by $\upzeta^{P}$. From \eqref{eq:SemExtIndVsInfM}, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{F}}(P, u) &={\mathcal{I}}^{P}(w,u) ={\mathcal{W}} \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{P}(u,w) \enspace, \end{align} where ${\mathcal{W}}={\mathcal{W}}(P, u)= rac {\upzeta^{P}_{u}(+1)\cdot \upzeta^{P}_{u}(-1 )} {\upzeta^{P}_{w}(+1)\cdot \upzeta^{P}_{w}(-1)+\mathds{1}\{\upzeta^{P}_{w}(+1)\in \{0,1\}\}}$. To verify the second equality in \eqref{eq:CFReverse} note the following: when $\upzeta^{P}_{u}(+1), \upzeta^{P}_{w}(+1)
otin \{0,1\}$, the second equality in \eqref{eq:CFReverse} is true due to \Cref{claim:InfSymmetrisation}. When at least one of $\upzeta^{P}_{u}(1), \upzeta^{P}_{w}(1)$ is in $\{0,1\}$, the definitions of ${\mathcal{F}}$ and the influence matrix ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$ imply ${\mathcal{F}}(P, u)=0$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}(u,w)=0$. Hence, the second equality in \eqref{eq:CFReverse} is true. The $b$-marginal boundedness assumption implies  egin{align} 0\leq {\mathcal{W}}(P,u) & \leq b^{-2} \enspace. \end{align} 
oindent For $Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanates from $u$, let $\upzeta^{P,Q}$ be the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_{G}$. Note that $P$ and $Q$ are compatible because we assume that $u$ and $w$ are at distance $\geq 2k$; hence, $\upzeta^{P,Q}$ is well-defined. In what follows, denote ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ the influence matrix induced by $\upzeta^{P,Q}$.  egin{claim} There is an $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}	imes (V\setminus \Lambda)$ matrix $\widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A$ such that for $w, u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ with ${m dist}_{G}(w,u)\geq 2k$ and any $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanates from $w$, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{P}(u,w) &=\sum
olimits_{Q} \widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q, w) \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q} (u,w) \enspace, \end{align} where $Q$ varies over the walks in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, which emanate from $u$. Furthermore, we have  egin{align} \max
olimits_{Q,z} \{ |\widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q,z)| \} & \leq C_A\enspace, \end{align} where $C_A$ is specified in the statement of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. \end{claim} The definition of matrix $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$ and in particular \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrixEquivalent}, imply ootnote{The definition of the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$ imply that ${\mathcal{I}}^{Q,P}={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$.} that, for any $P, Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanate from the vertices $w$ and $u$, respectively, we have  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q} (u, w)= osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)\enspace. \end{align} Combining \eqref{eq:CalEllAsInfluence} and \eqref{eq:CFReverseSplit}, we obtain  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{P}(u,w) &= \sum
olimits_{Q} \widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q, w) \cdot osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)\enspace, \end{align} where recall that $Q$ varies over the walks in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ which emanate from $u$. Working as in \eqref{eq:CFReverse}, we use \eqref{eq:CalEllAsInfluence} to obtain that for any $Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanates from $u$, we have  egin{align} osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q, P) &= \widehat{{\mathcal{W}}} \cdot osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)\enspace, \end{align} where $\widehat{{\mathcal{W}}}=\widehat{W}(P,Q)= rac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1)\cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)\cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1 )+\mathds{1}\{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)\in \{0,1\}\}}$. The $b$-marginal boundedness assumption implies  egin{align} 0\leq \widehat{{\mathcal{W}}}(P,Q) \leq b^{-2}\enspace. \end{align} We get \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalF2CalH} by plugging \eqref{eq:CFReverseSplitAA} and \eqref{eq:CHReverse} into \eqref{eq:CFReverse} while setting  egin{align} {\mathcal{N}}_B(P, Q) &={\mathcal{W}}(P,u) \cdot \widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q,w) \cdot \widehat{{\mathcal{W}}}(P, Q)\enspace. \end{align} Recall that $u$ is the first vertex of path $Q$. Plugging \eqref{eq:Bound4CN1}, \eqref{eq:CFReverseSplitBB} and \eqref{eq:CalN2Bound} into \eqref{eq:CLVsCIPQ} we obtain that $|{\mathcal{N}}_B(P, Q)| \leq b^{-4}\cdot C_A$. We consider \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalF2CalH} for $u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda$ which are at distance $< 2k$ and $P\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanates from $w$. For such $u,w$ and $P$, we have  egin{align} \left(\left( osegold{{\mathcal{L}}} \circ {\mathcal{N}}_B ight)\cdot \UpC_{k}ight)(P,u)&=0 & 	extrm{and} &&{\mathcal{F}}(P,u)&=0\enspace. \end{align} The equality on the left is true because $\left(\left( osegold{{\mathcal{L}}} \circ {\mathcal{N}}_B ight)\cdot \UpC_{k}ight)(P,u)= \sum_{Q} osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q) \cdot {\mathcal{N}}_B(P,Q) \cdot \UpC_{k}(Q,u)$ and the variable $Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ varies over the walks that emanate from $u$. In this case, we have $osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)=0$ since $P$ and $Q$ are not compatible. The equality on the right follows from the definition of matrix ${\mathcal{F}}$. Hence, for any choice of matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_B$, the above is true. For matrix ${\mathcal{N}}_B$ to be well defined, for $u,w$ at distance $<2k$ and any $P, Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanate from $w$ and $u$, respectively, we let ${\mathcal{N}}_B(P,Q)=1$. This choice of ${\mathcal{N}}_B$ and \eqref{eq:LNCVsFNonCompatiblePQ} imply that \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalF2CalH} is also true for any $u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda$ which are at distance $< 2k$ and $P$ that emanates from $w$. Hence \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalF2CalH} is true for any $u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda$. We conclude that \Cref{lemma:FromCalF2CalH} is true for $C_B=\max\{1, b^{-4}\cdot C_A\}$. \hfill $\square$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13.1
nodes.statement:
The setting in this proof is the same as in the proof of \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU}. Recall that we have vertices $w,u$ in graph $G$ such that ${m dist}_{G}(u,w)\geq 2k$ and a self-avoiding path $P$ of length $k$ that emanates from vertex $w$; hence, we have $u
otin P$. Let $\magenta{\Omega}$ be the set of walks in $G$ which correspond to the vertices in $\applegreen{T}=T_{m SAW}(G,u)$. Also, let $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ be the set of walks in $\gext{G}{P}$ which correspond to the vertices in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$. We use the same map $\iris{\upphi}:\magenta{\Omega}_{P}	o \magenta{\Omega}$ as in the proof of \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU}. That is,  egin{enumerate}[(a)] \item For each $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r}\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ such that $v_{r}
otin \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ we set $\iris{\upphi}(W)=W$. \item For each $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r}\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ such that $v_{r}\in \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$, we set $\iris{\upphi}(W)=W_{P}$, where $W_{P}=z_0, \ldots, z_{r}$ is such that $z_{i}=v_{i}$ for $i=0, \ldots, r-1$, while the split-vertex $v_{r}$ is generated from $z_{r}$. \end{enumerate} We let $\widehat{\magenta{\Omega}} \subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ be the image set of $\iris{\upphi}$. Let $\widehat{T}$ be the subtree of $\applegreen{T}$ induced by the vertices that correspond to the walks in $\widehat{\magenta{\Omega}}$. We showed in the proof of \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} that we can identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}$, in particular, we identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ as the subtree $\widehat{T}$ of $\applegreen{T}$, using $\iris{\upphi}$. Every vertex in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ corresponds to two walks, one walk in $\gext{G}{P}$ and another in $G$, e.g., the walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ and the walk $\iris{\upphi}(W)\in \widehat{\magenta{\Omega}}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$. Furthermore, we apply the $T_{m SAW}$-construction on $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$ and obtain the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ for tree $\applegreen{T}=T_{m SAW}(G,u)$. We proceed to identify the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}$ that correspond to the vertices in $M$. Specifically, consider the following subsets of $\magenta{\Omega}$,  egin{enumerate}[(i)] \item set $\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ consists of all self-avoiding walks whose last vertex is in $\Lambda$, \item set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ consists of all walks $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}$ such that $v_0, \ldots, v_{r-1}$ is self-avoiding and $v_{r}$ repeats, while $W\cap P
eq \emptyset$, \item set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}$ consists of all walks $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}$ such that $v_0, \ldots, v_{r-1}$ is self-avoiding and $v_{r}$ repeats, while $W\cap P= \emptyset$. \end{enumerate} The $T_{m SAW}$-construction implies that set $M$ consists of the vertices that correspond to the walks in the three aforementioned categories. Also, we use the $T_{m SAW}$-construction for the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$ and get the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$ for tree $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{m SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$. We proceed to identify the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ that correspond to the vertices in $L$. Consider the following subsets of $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$,  egin{enumerate}[(i)] \setcounter{enumi}{3} \item set $\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ consist of all self-avoiding walks whose last vertex is in $\Lambda$, \item set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ consists of all self-avoiding walks whose last vertex is in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$, \item set $\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ consists of all walks $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}$ such that $v_0, \ldots, v_{r-1}$ is self-avoiding and $v_{r}$ repeats, while $W\cap P
eq \emptyset$. \end{enumerate} It is not hard to verify that set $L$ consists of the vertices that correspond to the walks of the above three categories. We use all the above to prove statements ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUA}-ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUD} of \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}. We start with statement ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUA}. For each vertex $v\in M\cap L$, there are two alternatives. In the first one, vertex $v$ corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}$ and $\iris{\upphi}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}$. In the second alternative, vertex $v$ corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$ and $\iris{\upphi}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$. To see the above, note that for each walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}\cup\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$, the definition of $\iris{\upphi}$ implies that we should have $\iris{\upphi}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$. On the other hand, for each walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ we have $\iris{\upphi}(W)
otin (\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)} \cup\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)})$. This is because $\iris{\upphi}(W)$ is a self-avoiding walk in $G$ from $u$ to a vertex in $P$. Hence, every vertex $v$ which corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ does not belong to $M$. Also, for every $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$, we have that $\iris{\upphi}^{-1}(W)$ is not defined, implying that the vertex $v$ which corresponds to walk $W$ does not belong to $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$; hence it does not belong to $L$. Statement ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUA} follows by noting that the definition of the $T_{m SAW}$-construction implies that all vertices in $M\cap L$ take on the same pinning, i.e., there are no copies of split-vertices in this intersection. As far as statement ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUB} is concerned, note that each vertex $v\in  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P} \cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ can only correspond to a self-avoiding walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$ which ends at a vertex in $P$. The definition of $\iris{\upphi}$ implies that $\iris{\upphi}^{-1}(W)$ is well-defined and corresponds to a self-avoiding walk in $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ whose last vertex is either in $P$ or in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$. Hence, it follows from the definition of set $\magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$ that $v\in \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P}$. This proves ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUB}. We proceed to prove statement ef{stat:C-lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}. The previous discussion shows that each vertex $v\in L\setminus M$ corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$. Furthermore, the definition of $\iris{\upphi}$ implies that the last vertex of walk $\iris{\upphi}(W)$ is in $P$. Hence, we have $v\in  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$. We conclude that $L\setminus M\subseteq  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$. If vertex $v\in M\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}$, then the definition of $\iris{\upphi}$ implies that $\iris{\upphi}^{-1}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}$; hence $v\in L$. Similarly, if vertex $v\in M\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$, then it also corresponds to walk $\iris{\upphi}^{-1}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$; hence $v\in L$. We conclude that $M\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}\subseteq L$ by noting that there is no vertex $v\in M\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ which corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ (this was also noted in the proof of ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUA}). The two conclusions that $L\setminus M\subseteq  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$ and that $M\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}\subseteq L$ imply that statement ef{stat:C-lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} is true. We proceed to prove statement ef{statement:lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromUD}. This follows directly by recalling that all vertices in $T\setminus \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ are descendants of the vertices in $ yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$. Hence, after pinning the vertices in $L\cup  yzantine{{	t A}}_{P}$, the vertices in $T\setminus \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ have no effect on the configurations of the vertices in $T\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. All the above conclude the proof of \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU}. \hfill $\square$
