It remains to show that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:MySpectralMatrixNorm} is true.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the weighted norm bound (7.4) via Theorem 7.1 with $D=\Xi^{1/s}$

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 7.1 to the row sum $q(w)$
nodes.statement: For $w\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we let $\mathbold{q}(w)$ be equal to the absolute row sum for the row of matrix $\Upxi^{-1/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda, \tau}_G \cdot \Upxi^{1/\darkmagenta{s}}$ that corresponds to vertex $w$. \Cref{thrm:InflNormBound4GeneralD} and \eqref{def:AdjMatrixEigenvals} imply \begin{align} \mathbold{q}(w) & \leq 1+ \frac{c}{\left(\upphi_1(w)\right)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}}} \cdot \left( \sum\nolimits_{z \in N(w)}\left(\upphi_1(z)\right)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}}+ \sum\nolimits_{\ell \geq 2} \left( \delta^{\ell-1} \cdot \left(\UpC\cdot{\UpA}^{\ell-1}_G\cdot \upphi_1\right) (wz) \right)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} \right) \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 7.1 to the row sum $q(w)$

nodes.name: Use the eigenvector identity to collapse walk sums into...
nodes.statement: Recalling that $\upphi_1$ is the principal eigenvector of ${\UpA}_G$, \eqref{eq:PFT4thrm:AdjacencyPotentialSpIn} implies \begin{align} \UpC\cdot{\UpA}^{\ell-1}_G\cdot \upphi_1 &= {\varrho}^{\ell-1} \cdot \UpC\cdot \upphi_1\enspace. \end{align} Plugging the above into \eqref{eq:Base4Proofthrm:PowerMatrixTopologicalNorm} and rearranging, we get \begin{align} \mathbold{q}(w) & =1+ c \cdot \sum\nolimits_{\ell\geq 1} \left(\delta \cdot {\varrho} \right)^{{(\ell-1)}/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot \sum\nolimits_{z\in N_G(w)}\left( {\textstyle \frac{\upphi_1(z)}{\upphi_1(w)} } \right)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Use the eigenvector identity to collapse walk sums into $\varrho^{\ell-1}$

nodes.name: Hölder's inequality bounds the neighbour sum by...
nodes.statement: We need to bound the rightmost sum in the equation above. Letting $d=\abs{N_G(w)}$ and applying H\"older's inequality, we get \begin{align} \sum\nolimits_{z\in N_G(w)}\left( {\textstyle\frac{\upphi_1(z)}{ \upphi_1(w)} }\right)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} & \leq \left( \sum\nolimits _{z\in N_G(w)} {\textstyle \frac{\upphi_1(z)}{ \upphi_1(w)}} \right)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} d^{1-(1/\darkmagenta{s})}\ = \ {\Delta}^{1-(1/\darkmagenta{s})} \cdot {\varrho}^{1/\darkmagenta{s}}\enspace, \end{align} where the last equality follows from the observations that $\sum_{z\in N_G(w)}\upphi_1(z)={\varrho}\cdot \upphi_1(w)$ and $d^{1-(1/\darkmagenta{s})}\leq {\Delta}^{1-(1/\darkmagenta{s})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hölder's inequality bounds the neighbour sum by $\Delta^{1-1/s}\varrho^{1/s}$

nodes.name: Combine to get (7.4) for every $w$
nodes.statement: Plugging \eqref{eq:fthrm:PowerMatrixTopologicalNormTempB} into \eqref{eq:fthrm:PowerMatrixTopologicalNormTempA} we get \begin{align} \mathbold{q}(w) &\leq 1+ c \cdot {\Delta}^{1-(1/\darkmagenta{s})} \cdot {\varrho}^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot \sum\nolimits_{\ell \geq 0} \left(\delta \cdot {\varrho} \right)^{\ell/\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace . \nonumber \end{align} The above holds for any $w\in V\setminus \Lambda$, implying that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:MySpectralMatrixNorm} is true. \Cref{thrm:AdjacencyPotentialSpIn} follows.

nodes.name: Potential derivatives are non-zero on the path
nodes.statement: Our assumptions for the potential function ${\Psi}$ imply that, for every $e_{i}\in P$, we have $\uppsi(e_{i})\neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Potential derivatives are non-zero on the path

nodes.name: Telescoping rewrite of the weight
nodes.statement: Using a simple telescopic trick, we get \begin{align} \abs{{\tt weight}(P)}&= \prod^{\ell}_{i=1}\frac{\uppsi(e_{i})}{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \ = \ \uppsi(e_{\ell})\cdot \frac{\abs{\upalpha(e_1)}}{\uppsi(e_1)}\cdot \prod^{\ell}_{i=2}\frac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace. \nonumber \end{align} The claim follows.

nodes.name: Bound the first factor by Max to get (7.25)
nodes.statement:
For brevity, we let  egin{align}
onumber {	t Max}& =\max_{ ar{e}, \hat{e} \in T} \left\{ {	extstyle \uppsi( ar{e}) \cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(\hat{e})} }{\uppsi(\hat{e})}} ight\} \enspace. \end{align} Recall that $\ell>1$. From the definition of $\mathcal{H}_{\ell} $ in \eqref{eq:DefOfCalHL} and \Cref{claim:AddPotentialA} we have  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} &= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_\ell) \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \left( \uppsi(e_{\ell})\cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(e_1)} }{\uppsi(e_1)} ight)\cdot \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell} rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} For $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $\ell\geq 0$, recall that ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$ is the set of paths $P$ from the root of $T$ to the set of copies of vertex $u$ which are at level $\ell$ of the tree such that ${	t weight}(P)
eq 0$. Also, recall that ${	t A}(u,\ell)$ is the set of copies of $u$ at level $\ell$ in $T$ that are connected to the root with a path $P\in {\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$. Noting that $\left( \uppsi(e_{\ell})\cdot  rac{\abs{\upalpha(e_1)}}{\uppsi(e_1)} ight)\leq {	t Max}$, we get  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} &\leq {	t Max}\cdot \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_\ell) \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell} rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})}\cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the first factor by Max to get (7.25)

nodes.name: Rewrite the root value as Max times the children sum (7.26)
nodes.statement: As far as ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{\rm root}$ is concerned, recalling \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeights}, we have \begin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{\rm root} &= {\tt Max}\cdot \sum\nolimits_{1\leq j\leq r} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} \enspace, \end{align} where $z_1, \ldots, z_{r}$ are the children of the root, for some integer $r>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the root value as Max times the children sum (7.26)

nodes.name: State the closed form (7.27) for $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}_v$
nodes.statement:
We show that for any vertex $v$ at level $h=1,\ldots, \ell-1$ of the tree $T$, we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &=\sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, \end{align} where ${\mathcal{P}}(v,u, \ell)$ is the set of paths of length $\ell-h+1$ from the parent of vertex $v$ to ${	t A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{v}$.

nodes.name: Derive the claim from (7.27) by summing over the root's children
nodes.statement:
Before proving that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true, let us show how it implies \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD}. For every child $z_{j}$ of the root, \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} implies  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} & = \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}) \in {\mathcal{P}}(z_{j}, u, \ell) } \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} Summing the above over all the children of the root, we get  egin{align} \sum
olimits_{z_{j}} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} & = \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots e_{\ell}) \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1})}{\uppsi(e_{i})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} For the above, we use the observation that the sets ${\mathcal{P}}(z_j,u,\ell)$'s partition ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$, i.e., we have $\cup_{z_{j}}{\mathcal{P}}(z_{j},u,\ell)={\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$, while for distinct ${j}, i$ the sets ${\mathcal{P}}(z_{j},u,\ell)$ and ${\mathcal{P}}(z_{i},u,\ell)$ do not intersect. Plugging \eqref{eq:GoodExpression4Rzj} into \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeightsRepeat4HlVsRroot}, we see that ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root}$ is equal to the r.h.s. of the inequality in \eqref{eq:basis4HlAtHlVsRroot}. This implies that $\mathcal{H}_{\ell} \leq {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root}$, which also proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Derive the claim from (7.27) by summing over the root's children

nodes.name: Set up induction on the level $h$
nodes.statement: We conclude the proof of \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} by showing that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true. To this end, we use induction on the level $h$ of vertex $v$ in \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl}. The basis of the induction corresponds to taking $h=\ell-1$. For the inductive step, we assume that there is $h\leq \ell-1$ such that that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true. We then prove that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is also true for any vertex $v$ at level $h-1$ of tree $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on the level $h$

nodes.name: Base case $h=\ell-1$
nodes.statement:
We start with the basis and show \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} for a vertex $v$ at level $\ell-1$. As per standard notation, let $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ be the children of $v$. These children are vertices at level $\ell$. From \eqref{eq:SRecurBaseWeights} and \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821}, we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &= \sum
olimits_{j} rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{ \upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} 
onumber\ &=\sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{j} rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{ \upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \mathds{1}\{v_{j} \in {	t A} (u,\ell )\}\cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, \end{align} where we let $b_{v}$ be the edge that connects $v$ to its parent at $T$, while edge $b_{j}$ connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. For the second equality, we substitute ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}}$ by using \eqref{eq:SRecurBaseWeights}. For each $u \in V\setminus \Lambda$ in \eqref{eq:FinalofBaseHlVsRvInter}, the summand $ rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \mathds{1}\{v_{j} \in {	t A} (u,\ell )\}$ is non-zero only if the edges $b_{v}$ and $b_{j}$ form a path which belongs to set ${\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$, i.e., we have $(b_{v},b_{j})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$. We use this observation and write \eqref{eq:FinalofBaseHlVsRvInter} as follows:  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&=\sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,e_2) \in {\mathcal{P}}(v, u, \ell)}  rac{\uppsi(e_{1}) }{\uppsi(e_2)} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_2)} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} It is not hard to see that \eqref{eq:FinalofBaseHlVsRv} corresponds to \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} for $h=\ell-1$. This concludes the proof of the base of the induction.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis at level $h$
nodes.statement: The induction hypothesis is that there exists $1<h\leq \ell-1$, such that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true for any vertex at level $h$ of tree $T$.

nodes.name: Inductive step from level $h$ to $h-1$
nodes.statement:
We show that the hypothesis implies that \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} is true for any vertex $v$ at level $h-1$. As per standard notation, we let $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ be the children of $v$, while edge $b_{v}$ connects $v$ to its parent and edge $b_{j}$ connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. From \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821} we have  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &= \sum
olimits_{j}  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} The children of $v$ are at level $h$. Using the hypothesis, we substitute each ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}}$ using \eqref{eq:Target4InductionRvVsHl} and get  egin{align}
onumber {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{j}  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})}\cdot \sum
olimits_{P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v_{j}, u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} It is elementary that for any $1\leq j\leq d$ and for every path $P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v_{j}, u, \ell)$, there is exactly one path $Q=(\overline{e}_1, \ldots, \overline{e}_{\ell-h+2})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$, with $\overline{e}_2=\{v,v_{j} \}$, such that  egin{align} 
onumber \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+2}  rac{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(\overline{e}_{i})} &=  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace \end{align} and vice versa. Combining the two relations above, we get  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{Q=(\overline{e}_1,\ldots, \overline{e}_{\ell-h+2})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v, u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+2}  rac{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, 
onumber \end{align} which proves the inductive steps and concludes the inductive proof. \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} follows.

nodes.name: Expand $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}_v$ by the recursion
nodes.statement: As per standard notation, we let $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ be the children of $v$, while edge $b_{v}$ connects $v$ to its parent and edge $b_{j}$ connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. From \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821} we have \begin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} &= \sum\nolimits_{j} \frac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} \enspace. \nonumber \end{align}

nodes.name: Substitute the hypothesis for the children
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the hypothesis for the children

nodes.name: Path bijection completes the inductive step
nodes.statement:
It is elementary that for any $1\leq j\leq d$ and for every path $P=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell-h+1})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v_{j}, u, \ell)$, there is exactly one path $Q=(\overline{e}_1, \ldots, \overline{e}_{\ell-h+2})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v,u,\ell)$, with $\overline{e}_2=\{v,v_{j} \}$, such that  egin{align} 
onumber \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+2}  rac{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(\overline{e}_{i})} &=  rac{\uppsi(b_{v} )}{\uppsi(b_{j})}\cdot \abs{\upalpha(b_{j})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+1}  rac{\uppsi(e_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(e_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace \end{align} and vice versa. Combining the two relations above, we get  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{Q=(\overline{e}_1,\ldots, \overline{e}_{\ell-h+2})\in {\mathcal{P}}(v, u, \ell)} \prod
olimits_{2\leq i\leq \ell-h+2}  rac{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i-1}) }{\uppsi(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(\overline{e}_{i})} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace, 
onumber \end{align} which proves the inductive steps and concludes the inductive proof. \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Path bijection completes the inductive step

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 10.1 with $\delta=(1-\varepsilon)/\uprho$
nodes.statement:
\Cref{thrm:L2InflRedux2KNBTM} implies that for $\delta = rac{1-\varepsilon}{\uprho}$, there are constants $C_1,C_2>0$ such that  egin{align} 
orm{ {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G}}{2} &\leq C_1+C_2 \cdot \sum
olimits_{\ell \geq k} \delta^{\ell} \cdot 
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2} \enspace, \end{align} where recall that $\uprho=
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}$.

nodes.name: Claim 5.8 controls $\|H^\ell\|_2^{1/\ell}$ beyond $\ell_0$
nodes.statement: \Cref{lemma:SingSequenConv} implies that there is a bounded number $\ell_0=\ell_0(N,\varepsilon, {\Delta})>k$ such that, for any $\ell \geq \ell_0$, we have \begin{align} \nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{1/\ell}{2} & \leq (1+{\varepsilon}/{2}) \uprho\enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Split the sum at $\ell_0$
Bound the finite head by a constant
nodes.statement:
Since $\ell_0$ and $C_1,C_2$ are bounded numbers, there is ${C}_0>1$, which is a bounded number, too, such that  egin{align} C_1+C_2 \cdot \sum
olimits_{k \leq \ell < \ell_0} \delta^{\ell} \cdot 
orm{ ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2} \leq {C}_0 \enspace. \end{align} For the above, we use the observation that, for any $0<\ell<\ell_0$, we have that $
orm{( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2} \leq ({\Delta}-1)^{\ell}$, while ${\Delta}$ is also a bounded number.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the finite head by a constant

nodes.name: Bound the tail by a geometric series $2C_2\varepsilon^{-1}$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the tail by a geometric series $2C_2\varepsilon^{-1}$

nodes.name: Combine with $\widehat C=2C_2+C_0$
nodes.statement: \Cref{thrm:NonBacktrackingInfinityMixing} follows by plugging \eqref{eq:Sum4BelowL0} and \eqref{eq:Sum4AboveL0} into \eqref{eq:Base4thrm:NonBacktrackingInfinityMixing} and setting $\widehat{C}=2C_2+{C}_0$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 9.2
nodes.statement: When there is no danger of confusion, in this proof, we abbreviate ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ and $\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$ to ${\mathcal{I}}$ and $\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$, respectively. From \Cref{proposition:CINorm2VsCLNorm2}, there are constants $c_1, c_2>0$ such that \begin{align} \norm{ {\mathcal{I}}}{2} \leq c_1+c_2\cdot \norm{ \abs{ \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}} }}{2} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Reduce to bounding $\||\mathcal{L}|\|_2$
nodes.statement:
\Cref{thrm:NonBacktrackingPotentialSpIn} follows by bounding appropriately $
orm{ \abs{ osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}_{k} }}{2}$. To this end, we use the following claim.  egin{claim} There is a constant $c_3>0$ such that $
orm{ \abs{ \applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k} }}{2} \leq c_3\cdot 
orm{ \abs{ \applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G,k} }}{2\darkmagenta{s}}$. \end{claim}

nodes.name: Theorem 11.1 with Claim 11.2 gives (11.2)
nodes.statement:
\Cref{thrm:InfNormBoundHConj} and \Cref{claim:Ll2VsLl2s} imply that there exists a fixed number ${c}_4\geq 1$, such that  egin{align} 
orm{ \abs{ osegold{{\mathcal{L}}} }}{2} &\leq {c}_4\cdot \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq k} \left( {	extstyle \left( rac{1-\varepsilon/2}{\uprho}ight)^{\ell}} \cdot 
orm{ ( \cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2} ight)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}}\enspace. \end{align} where recall that $
norm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^N}{1/N}{2}= \uprho$.

nodes.name: Claim 5.8 controls large powers
nodes.statement: \Cref{lemma:SingSequenConv} implies that there is a bounded integer $\ell_0=\ell_0(N,\varepsilon, {\Delta})>0$ such that, for any $\ell\geq \ell_0$, we have \begin{align} \nnorm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{1/\ell}{2} \leq (1+\varepsilon/4) \uprho\enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Bound the finite head by $c_5$
nodes.statement:
Since $\ell_0$ is bounded, there exists a constant $c_5>0$ such that  egin{align} {c}_4\cdot \sum
olimits_{k \leq \ell < \ell_0} \left( {	extstyle \left( rac{1-\varepsilon/2}{\uprho}ight)^{\ell}} \cdot 
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2} ight)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}} \leq c_5\enspace. \end{align} For the above, we use that $
orm{ (\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k})^{\ell}}{2} \leq 
norm{\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}}{\ell}{2}\leq ({\Delta}-1)^{\ell}$.

nodes.name: Sum the geometric tail and conclude
nodes.statement:
Plugging \eqref{eq:CorFromlemma:SingSequenConvBB} and \eqref{eq:CorFromlemma:SingSequenConv} into \eqref{eq:ExtInfN2sBoundWithDistL}, we obtain  egin{align} 
orm{ \abs{ osegold{{\mathcal{L}}} } }{2} &\leq c_5+ {c}_4\cdot \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq \ell_0} \left( {	extstyle (1+\varepsilon/4)(1-\varepsilon/2) } ight)^{\ell/\darkmagenta{s}} \ \leq \ c_5+ rac{c_4}{1-(1-\varepsilon/4)^{1/\darkmagenta{s}}} \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} \Cref{thrm:NonBacktrackingPotentialSpIn} follows by plugging the above into \eqref{eq:L2BoundInflNoNuMatrix} and setting $C=c_1+c_2\cdot (c_4+c_5)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the geometric tail and conclude

nodes.name: Express $\mathcal{L}(P,Q),\mathcal{L}(Q,P)$ as influences in the...
nodes.statement: For what follows, we abbreviate $\applegreen{{\mathcal{L}}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G,k}$ to $\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}$. Consider $P, Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ which are compatible. Let $w$ and $u$ be the starting vertices of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Then, as already noticed in \eqref{def:EdgeInflMatrixEquivalent}, we have \begin{align} \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)&={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(w,u), & \textrm{and} && \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)&={\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(u, w)\enspace, \end{align} where the influence matrix ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ is with respect to $\upzeta^{P,Q}$, the $\{P, Q\}$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Note that ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{Q,P}$ correspond to the same influence matrix.

nodes.name: Claim 5.1 relates $\mathcal{L}(P,Q)$ and $\mathcal{L}(Q,P)$ by...
nodes.statement: A useful observation is that \Cref{claim:InfSymmetrisation} and \eqref{eq::InfNormHStartVsH-HVsI} imply that if $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)\notin \{0,1\}$, then we have \begin{align} \sqrt{ \frac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1) } }\cdot \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)&= \sqrt{\frac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} } \cdot \rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)\enspace. \end{align} If at least one of $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)$ is in $\{0,1\}$, then we have $\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P,Q)=\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(Q,P)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.1 relates $\mathcal{L}(P,Q)$ and $\mathcal{L}(Q,P)$ by marginal ratios

nodes.name: Define the symmetric non-negative matrix $\mathcal{M}$
nodes.statement: Let the $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}\times \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ matrix ${\mathcal{M}}$ be defined as follows: For $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ with starting vertex $w$ and $Q \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ with starting vertex $u$, such that $P$ and $Q$ are compatible while $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)\notin \{0,1\}$, we let \begin{align} {\mathcal{M}}(P,Q)&= \sqrt{ \frac{\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(-1)} {\upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1) \cdot \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(-1) } } \cdot \abs{\rosegold{{\mathcal{L}}}(P, Q)} \enspace. \end{align} On the other hand, if at least one of $\upzeta^{P,Q}_{w}(+1), \upzeta^{P,Q}_{u}(+1)$ is in $\{0,1\}$, then we let ${\mathcal{M}}(P,Q)=0$. Also, we let ${\mathcal{M}}(P,Q)=0$ when $P$ and $Q$ are not compatible. ${\mathcal{M}}$ has non-negative entries, while \eqref{eq::InfNormHStartVsH-HVsIBB} implies that it is symmetric.

nodes.name: Compare norms of $|\mathcal{L}|$ and $\mathcal{M}$ within $b^{-2}$...
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, we have  egin{align} 
orm{ \abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}}}{2} &\leq b^{-2} \cdot 
orm{ {\mathcal{M}} }{2} \leq b^{-2} \cdot 
orm{ {\mathcal{M}}}{2\darkmagenta{s}} \leq b^{-4} \cdot 
orm{ \abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}}}{2\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace. \end{align} The first inequality follows by noting that \eqref{eq:DefOfHatL} and the $b$-marginal boundedness assumption imply that $\abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}} \leq b^{-2} \cdot {\mathcal{M}}$, where the comparison is entry-wise. The second inequality follows since ${\mathcal{M}}$ is symmetric. Similarly to the first inequality, the third inequality follows by noting that \eqref{eq:DefOfHatL} and the $b$-marginal boundedness assumption imply that ${\mathcal{M}}$ has non-negative entries, while ${\mathcal{M}} \leq b^{-2}\cdot \abs{osegold{{\mathcal{L}}}}$, where the comparison is entry-wise. \Cref{claim:Ll2VsLl2s} follows for $c_3=b^{-4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare norms of $|\mathcal{L}|$ and $\mathcal{M}$ within $b^{-2}$ factors; conclude with $c_3=b^{-4}$

nodes.name: Expand $f_{q,\ell}(P)$ over paths in $T_{P,Q}$
nodes.statement:
The definition of $\upf_{\iris{{ f q}}, \ell}$ implies that, for any $P \in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$, we have  egin{align} \upf_{\iris{{ f q}}, \ell}(P)&=\sum
olimits_{Q\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}: P,Q 	extrm{ compatible}}\iris{{ f q}}(Q)\cdot \sum
olimits_{W=(e_1, \ldots, e_{\ell})} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell} \abs{\upalpha_{P,Q}(e_{i})} \enspace, \end{align} where $W$ varies over the paths from the root to the vertices in ${	t A}(Q,\ell)$ in tree $\cadmiumgreen{T_{P,Q}}$. The edge weights of path $W$ are obtained using $\zeta^{P,Q}$, the $\{P,Q\}$-extension of the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$.

Regroup into $\mathcal{C}_\ell q=z_{q,\ell}$

Plugging the above into \eqref{eq:Base4claim:CQLVsCKL}, we obtain  egin{align}
onumber \upf_{\iris{{ f q}}, \ell}(P) &\leq \widehat{c}^{\ 1/\darkmagenta{s}}_1 \cdot (1+\varepsilon/3)^{\ell/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot \sum
olimits_{Q\in\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}: P,Q	extrm{ compatible}}\iris{{ f q}}(Q)\cdot \sum
olimits_{W=(e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell})} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell-k} \abs{ \upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \& = \widehat{c}^{\ 1/\darkmagenta{s}}_1 \cdot (1+\varepsilon/3)^{\ell/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot \sum
olimits_{Q\in\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}: P,Q	extrm{ compatible}} \iris{{ f q}}(Q)\cdot {\mathcal{C}}_{\ell}(P, Q) 
onumber \ & =\widehat{c}^{\ 1/\darkmagenta{s}}_1\cdot (1+\varepsilon/3)^{\ell/\darkmagenta{s}} \cdot \upz_{\iris{{ f q}},\ell}(P) 
onumber \enspace. \end{align} For the second equality we use the definition of matrix ${\mathcal{C}}_{\ell}$. The third equality follows from the definition of $\upz_{\iris{{ f q}},\ell}$ in \eqref{eq:DefOfZQELL} and recalling that for $P$ and $Q$ which are not compatible we have ${\mathcal{C}}_{\ell}(P, Q)=0$. \Cref{claim:CQLVsCKL} follows.

nodes.name: Fix the path $W$ and recall the two weight systems
nodes.statement: We consider path $W=e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}$ from the root of $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P}, u)$ to a copy of vertex $w$. Note that we specify $W$ it terms of its edges. Recall the two sets of edge-weights for $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, i.e., set $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ is induced by the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$, and set $\{ \upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ is induced by the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$. Also, recall that set $\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$ consists of each vertex in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ which is either a copy of a vertex $v\in P$, or a copy of a split-vertex of $v\in P$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the path $W$ and recall the two weight systems

nodes.name: Define $\upalpha_{\min},\upalpha_{\max}$, bounded away from zero
nodes.statement: Let $\upalpha_{\rm min}=\min_{e}\{ \abs{\upalpha_{P} (e)}, \abs{{\upalpha}(e)} \}$, where $e$ varies over the set of edges in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ such that $ \upalpha_{P} (e), \upalpha(e)\neq 0$. Similarly, we define $\upalpha_{\rm max}=\max_{e}\{\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e)}, \abs{\upalpha(e)}\}$ where $e$ varies over the same set of edges. It is an easy exercise to show that our assumption about $b$-marginal boundedness, for fixed $b>0$, implies that $\upalpha_{\rm min}$ and $\upalpha_{\rm max}$ are constants bounded away from zero.

nodes.name: Partition the edges of $W$ into $H$, $K$, $R$
nodes.statement:
Consider $\ell_0$ as specified in \Cref{prop:StableSSM}. Let set $H$ consist of the edges $e_{i} \in W$ such that $i>\ell-k$. Also, let set $K$ consist of the edges $e_{i}\in W$ such that $1\leq i \leq \ell-k$ and ${m dist}(e_{i}, \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P} )<\ell_0$. Similarly, let set $R$ consist of the edges $e_{i}\in W$ such that $1\leq i \leq \ell-k$ and ${m dist}(e_{i}, \magenta{\overline{{	t A}}}_{P} )\geq \ell_0$. We have  egin{align} \prod
olimits_{1\leq i\leq \ell}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} &= \prod
olimits_{e_{i}\in H}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{e_{i} \in K}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \cdot \prod
olimits_{e_{i} \in R}\abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: State Claim 13.3
nodes.statement: For our subsequent arguments, we use the following result. \begin{claim} For $W=e_1,\ldots, e_{\ell}$ and $\{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})\}$, $\{\upalpha(e_{i})\}$, the following is true: if $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})\neq 0$, then we have $\upalpha(e_{i})\neq 0$, for each $e_{i}\in K\cup R$. \end{claim}

nodes.name: Bound weights on $H$ by 1 and on $K$ by...
nodes.statement: For $\upalpha_{P}(e_i)$ such that $e_{i}\in H$, we use the standard bound \begin{align} \abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} &\leq 1\enspace. \end{align} For each edge $e_{i}\in K$, we have \begin{align} \abs{ \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) } \leq \frac{\upalpha_{\rm max}}{\upalpha_{\rm min}} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \ \leq \ (1+\varepsilon/3)^{{1}/{\darkmagenta{s}}} \cdot \frac{\upalpha_{\rm max}}{\upalpha_{\rm min}} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace. \end{align} We use \Cref{claim:SupportOfWeiS} for the first inequality. The second inequality uses that $1<(1+\varepsilon/2)^{{1}/{\darkmagenta{s}}}$ for $\varepsilon, \darkmagenta{s}>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound weights on $H$ by 1 and on $K$ by $\upalpha_{\max}/\upalpha_{\min}$ times the original

nodes.name: Proposition 13.2 bounds weights on $R$
nodes.statement: \Cref{prop:StableSSM} implies that, for every $e_{i} \in R$, we have \begin{align} \abs{ \upalpha_{P}(e_{i}) } \leq (1+\varepsilon/3)^{{1}/{\darkmagenta{s}}}\cdot \abs{ \upalpha(e_{i})} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Combine the three bounds (13.6)
nodes.statement: Plugging \eqref{eq:WeightEllUBound}, \eqref{eq:WeightPVsWeightClose3LM} and \eqref{eq:WeightPVsWeightFarfromLM} into \eqref{eq:splitProdHatBetas}, we get \begin{align} \prod^{\ell}_{i=1} \abs{\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})} &\leq \left( \frac{\upalpha_{\rm max}}{\upalpha_{\rm min}} \right)^{\abs{K}} \cdot \prod^{\ell-k}_{i=1} (1+\varepsilon/3)^{{1}/{s}} \cdot \abs{\upalpha(e_{i})}\enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: State Claim 13.4 on $|K|$
nodes.statement: For the cardinality of set $K$, we use the following claim. \begin{claim} There are at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$ edges in path $W$ that are at distance $<\ell_0$ from set $\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$. \end{claim}

nodes.name: Bound $|K|$ and set $\widehat c_1$
nodes.statement: The above implies that $\abs{K}\leq (k+1) \cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$. Hence, \Cref{thrm:ProdWideHatBetaVsBeta} follows from \eqref{eq:Final4thrm:ProdWideHatBetaVsBeta} by setting $\widehat{c}_1=\left( \frac{\upalpha_{\rm max}}{\upalpha_{\rm min}} \right)^{(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}}$.

nodes.name: Identify $\overline T$ inside $T$ and recall the two weight systems
nodes.statement: We use \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} and identify $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P},u)$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}=T_{\rm SAW}(G,u)$ such that both trees have the same root. Then, $W$ is also a path in $\applegreen{T}$ starting from the root. Having $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ as a subtree of $\applegreen{T}$, we endow the subset of edges of $\applegreen{T}$ that correspond to those of $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ with the edge weights $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}$. Note that we do not necessarily have $\upalpha_{P}(e)$ for all edges $e\in \applegreen{T}$. Also, recall that the set of weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ and $\{\upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ are induced by $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ and $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\overline T$ inside $T$ and recall the two weight systems

nodes.name: Define $\uppi_i$ and list observations (i)-(iv)
nodes.statement: For $e_{i}\in W$, let $e_{i}=\{x_{i},z_{i}\}$ while let $\uppi_{i}$ be the set that consists of $x_{i}, z_{i}$ and their children in $\applegreen{T}$. Furthermore, we have the following observations: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$, \item \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} implies that each vertex in $\applegreen{T} \setminus \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ corresponds to a descendant of a vertex in $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}$, \item \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $M \cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}} \subseteq L$, \item \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that the pinnings $\sigma$ and $\eta$ agree on the assignment in $L\cap M$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Define $\uppi_i$
nodes.statement: For $e_{i}\in W$, let $e_{i}=\{x_{i},z_{i}\}$ while let $\uppi_{i}$ be the set that consists of $x_{i}, z_{i}$ and their children in $\applegreen{T}$. Furthermore, we have the following observations: \begin{enumerate}[(i)]

nodes.name: (i) $A_P\cap\overline T=\overline A_P$
nodes.statement: \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$,

nodes.name: (ii) extra vertices descend from $A_P$
nodes.statement: \Cref{lemma:Subtree4TSawU} implies that each vertex in $\applegreen{T} \setminus \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ corresponds to a descendant of a vertex in $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}$,

nodes.name: (iii) $M\cap\overline T\subseteq L$
nodes.statement: \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that $M \cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}} \subseteq L$,

nodes.name: (iv) pinnings agree on $L\cap M$
nodes.statement: \Cref{lemma:BoundaryTVsBoundaryTPFromU} implies that the pinnings $\sigma$ and $\eta$ agree on the assignment in $L\cap M$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Zero weights arise only from fixed configurations in $\uppi_i$
nodes.statement: Since we assume that our Gibbs distributions are $b$-marginally bounded, we can have $\upalpha(e_{i})=0$ (resp. $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})=0$) only if at least one vertex in $\uppi_{i}$ has a fixed configuration under $\mu^{M,\sigma}_{\applegreen{T}}$ (resp. $\mu^{L,\eta}_{\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}}$). Note that for Gibbs distributions with parameter $\beta=0$, it is possible that a pinning on a child of $x_{i}$ or $z_{i}$ determines the configuration of its parent with probability 1, implying that $\upalpha(e_{i})=0$ (resp. $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})=0$).
nodes.statement_short: Zero weights arise only from fixed configurations in $\uppi_i$

nodes.name: Rule out vertices of $\uppi_i$ outside $\overline T$
nodes.statement: Consider $1\leq i \leq \ell-k$. If there is $v\in \uppi_{i}$ which is not in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, this means that at least one of $x_{i}$ and $z_{i}$ is in $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}$, i.e., due to observation \ref{obs:TminusBarTVsAp}. But then, since $x_{i},z_{i}\in \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$, observation \ref{obs:APBarTVsBarAp} implies that the parent of $v$, i.e., one of $x_{i}, z_{i}$, is in $\byzantine{{\tt A}}_{P}\cap \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}=\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$. Since $i\leq \ell-k$, if any of $x_{i},z_{i}$ is in $\magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$, then it should be a split-vertex in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$, which means that is of degree $1$. This can only happen if $i=1$, however in this case we have $x_{i},z_{i}\notin \magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$ because the root is a copy of vertex $u$ which is at distance at least $k$ from any copy of a vertex $v\in \magenta{\overline{{\tt A}}}_{P}$. We then conclude that this event cannot happen.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out vertices of $\uppi_i$ outside $\overline T$

nodes.name: Pinnings agree on $\uppi_i$, so supports agree
nodes.statement: Hence, all elements in $\uppi_{i}$ are vertices in $\overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$. The fact that $e_{i}\in \overline{\cadmiumgreen{T}}$ and observations \ref{obs:PinMVsBarTVsPinL} and \ref{obs:PinMVsPinLIntesection} imply that if any vertex in $\uppi_{i}$ is pinned, then the pinning is the same under both $\sigma,\eta$. Hence, if $\upalpha_{P}(e_{i})\neq 0$, then we also have that $\upalpha(e_{i})\neq 0$. \Cref{claim:SupportOfWeiS} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Pinnings agree on $\uppi_i$, so supports agree

nodes.name: Distances from $P\cup S_P$ in $G_P$ match distances from $P$ in $G$
nodes.statement: It is not hard to verify that the number of edges at distance $\ell$ from the vertices in $P\cup \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ in $\gext{G}{P}$ is the same as the number of edges at distance $\ell$ from the vertices in $P$ in graph $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Distances from $P\cup S_P$ in $G_P$ match distances from $P$ in $G$

nodes.name: Geometric-series count of nearby edges
nodes.statement: Furthermore, it is not hard to check that there are at most ${\Delta}^{\ell+1}$ edges in $G$ which are at distance $\ell$ a from vertex $v\in P$. A simple geometric series calculation implies that the total number of edges at distance $<\ell_0$ from all vertices $v\in P$ is at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$. Recall that there are in total $k+1$ vertices in $P$.

nodes.name: Each nearby edge appears at most once in $W$
nodes.statement: Hence, we conclude that the number of edges at distance $<\ell_0$ from the vertices in $P\cup \cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ in $\gext{G}{P}$ is at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$. The claim follows by noting that each one of these, at most $(k+1)\cdot {\Delta}^{\ell_0+1}$ edges can have at most one copy in path $W$.
nodes.statement_short: Each nearby edge appears at most once in $W$

nodes.name: Substitute $\chi$ and $h$ and rearrange
nodes.statement:
The claim follows by using simple rearrangements. We have  egin{align} {\mathcal{J}}_{d}({ f m}, { f z}) &= \chi\left(\log F_{d}({ f z}) ight) \sum
olimits_{j\in [d]}  rac{ \abs{ h(\log { f z}_j )}}{ \chi\left( \log { f z}_j ight)} 	imes { f m}_j 
onumber\ &= \sqrt{ rac{F_{d}({ f z})}{1+F_{d}( f z)}} \sum^{d}_{j=1} \sqrt{ rac{{ f z}_j}{1+{ f z}_j}}	imes { f m}_j \ &= \sqrt{ rac{1}{F_{d}({ f z})(1+F_{d}( f z))}} \sum^{d}_{j=1} \sqrt{{ f z}_j(1+{ f z}_j) }	imes rac{ F_{d}( f z)}{1+{ f z}_j} 	imes { f m}_j \enspace. 
onumber \end{align} In \eqref{eq:AppOfFX}, we substitute $\chi$ and $h$ according to \eqref{def:XPotentialFunction} and \eqref{def:GradientRecHC}, respectively.

nodes.name: Rewrite with $\psi$ and $|\partial_iF_d|$
nodes.statement: Using the definition of ${\psi} $ from \eqref{def:PotentialFunction}, we get that \begin{align} {\mathcal{J}}_{d}({\bf m}, {\bf z}) &= {\psi}(F_{d}({\bf z})) \sum\nolimits_{j\in [d]}\frac{1}{ {\psi}({\bf z}_j)} \times \frac{ F_{d}(\bf z)}{1+{\bf z}_i} \times {\bf m}_j \enspace. \nonumber \end{align} The above implies \eqref{eq:SubCondVsPotentials}, i.e., since $\left| \frac{\partial }{\partial {\bf x}_i}F_{d}({\bf x}) \right|=\frac{F_{d}({\bf x})}{1+{\bf x}_i}$, for any $i\in [d]$. The claim follows.

nodes.name: Reuse equality (18.8) for the extended distributions
nodes.statement: The claim follows by utilising the equality in \eqref{eq:Target4lemma:FromCalI2CalF} from the proof of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. We apply this equality with respect to the influence matrices ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$, ${\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}$, i.e., instead of matrices ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{P}$ that are considered there.
nodes.statement_short: Reuse equality (18.8) for the extended distributions

nodes.name: Apply it to $\mathcal{I}^P$ and $\mathcal{I}^{P,Q}$
nodes.statement: More specifically, we have \begin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{P}(u,w) &=\sum\nolimits_{Q} \widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q, w) \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{P,Q}(u,w) \enspace, \end{align} where $Q$ varies over the walks in $\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_{\Lambda,k}$ that emanate from vertex $u$ and matrix $\widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A$ is defined as in \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}, with respect to the Gibbs distributions $\upzeta^{P}$ and $\upzeta^{P,Q}$.

nodes.name: The same bound $C_A$ holds
nodes.statement: Applying the same arguments as in the proof of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}, we obtain $\max_{Q,z}\{ |\widehat{{\mathcal{N}}}_A(Q,z)\}| \leq C_A$, where $C_A$ is specified in the statement of \Cref{lemma:FromCalI2CalF}. Note that the bound $C_A$ depends only on the parameters $k$ and $b$ for the marginal boundedness. \Cref{claim:CFReverseSplit} follows.

nodes.name: Reduce to a bijection between walk sets $\Omega$ and $\Omega_P$
nodes.statement: Our result follows by showing that there is an appropriate bijection $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ from the vertex set of $\capri{t}_{P}$ to that of $\blue{T_{P}}$ that allows us to identify $\capri{t}_{P}$ with $\blue{T_{P}}$. Since the vertices in $\capri{t}_{P}$ correspond to the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}$ and the vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$ correspond to the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$, we equivalently establish the bijection $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ from set $\magenta{\Omega}$ to $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a bijection between walk sets $\Omega$ and $\Omega_P$

nodes.name: Define the removed and added edge sets $\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}_P$
nodes.statement: For concreteness, let $P=x_0, \ldots, x_{k}$, while $x_0=w$. Let set ${\mathcal{O}}$ consist of each edge $e$ in $G$, which does not connect two consecutive vertices in $P$ but has at least one end in the set $\{x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k-1}\}$. Similarly, let set ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$ consist of each edge in $\gext{G}{P}$ which is between a split-vertex in set $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$ and another vertex of $\gext{G}{P}$. The only edges in $G$ that do not appear in $\gext{G}{P}$ are exactly those in set ${\mathcal{O}}$. Similarly, the only edges in $\gext{G}{P}$ that do not appear in $G$ are exactly those in set ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$. This implies that the elements in $\magenta{\Omega} \cap \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ correspond to the walks that do not use edges from sets ${\mathcal{O}}$ and ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the removed and added edge sets $\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}_P$

nodes.name: $\Omega^{(a)}=\Omega^{(a)}_P$ and $\Omega^{(c)}=\Omega^{(c)}_P$
nodes.statement: The definitions of the two trees $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$ imply that \begin{align}\nonumber \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}&=\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P} & \textrm{and} &&\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}&=\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P} \enspace. \end{align} To see this, recall that we have $P=x_0, \ldots, x_{k}$. Then each $W=v_{0}, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}$ corresponds to a self-avoiding walk that emanates from vertex $w$, while $v_{i}=x_{i}$, for $i=0,\ldots, \min\{k,r \}$. It is immediate to check that each such walk $W$ also belongs to $\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P}$ and vice versa. This implies that $\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}=\magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}_{P}$. With a very similar argument, we also get $\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}=\magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$.

nodes.name: Define the map swapping final vertices with split-vertices
nodes.statement: It is only the walks in $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ and $\magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ that use edges from ${\mathcal{O}}$ and ${\mathcal{O}}_{P}$, respectively. For each walk $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$, there is a walk $W_{P}=z_0, \ldots, z_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ such that $v_{i}=z_{i}$ for $i=0,\ldots, r-1$, while $z_{r}$ is a split-vertex that is generated by vertex $v_{r}$ and vice versa. This holds since the definition of $\gext{G}{P}$ implies that when constructing $\gext{G}{P}$, we substitute the edge $\{v_{r-1}, v_{r}\}\in{\mathcal{O}}$ with the edge $\{z_{r-1}, z_{r}\}\in {\mathcal{O}}_{P}$. Considering all the above, we specify $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ that \begin{align} \cadmiumorange{\uph}(W) &= \left\{ \begin{array}{lcl} W && \textrm{if } W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}\enspace, \\ W_{P} && \textrm{if } W \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)} \enspace, \\ \end{array} \right . \end{align} where $W_{P}$ is as described in the paragraph above \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}.
nodes.statement_short: Define the map swapping final vertices with split-vertices

nodes.name: The map is a bijection respecting copies
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that for each $W_{P}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}$ there is a unique $W \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ such that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}$. This observation and \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection} imply that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ is a bijection from $\magenta{\Omega}$ to $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. Using the correspondence between sets $\magenta{\Omega}$, $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ and the sets of vertices of trees $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$, respectively, we identify $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ as a bijection from the set of vertices in $\capri{t}_{P}$ to those in $\blue{T_{P}}$. For vertex $u$ in $\capri{t}_{P}$ that corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, we have that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(u)$ is a vertex in $\blue{T_{P}}$ that corresponds to walk $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. From \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}, it is easy to verify that if $u$ is a copy of $v$ in $G$, then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(u)$ must be a copy of $v$ or a split-vertex in $\gext{G}{P}$ generated by $v$.
nodes.statement_short: The map is a bijection respecting copies

nodes.name: Adjacency preservation
nodes.statement: We now show that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ preserves adjacencies. That is, for two vertices $x$, $z$ in $\capri{t}_{P}$ which are adjacent, we have that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ are two adjacent vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$. Suppose $x$ and $z$ correspond to walks $W, \overline{W}\in \magenta{\Omega}$, respectively. W.l.o.g., suppose walk $ W$ extends walk $\overline{W}$ by one vertex. Then, the vertices $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ correspond to walks $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})$, respectively. The definition of $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ implies that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)$ extends $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})$ by one vertex. To see this, note that in this setting we have $\overline{W}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}$ while $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, hence we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})=\overline{W}$. If $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$, then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W$ implying that $W$ extends $\overline{W}$. If on the other hand we have $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}$, where $W_{P}$ is defined as in the paragraph above \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}. It is easy to verify that $W_{P}$ extends $\overline{W}$ in this case too. Hence, $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ are two adjacent vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$. This implies that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ preserves adjacencies between the two trees, $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$.

nodes.name: Restate what adjacency preservation means
nodes.statement: That is, for two vertices $x$, $z$ in $\capri{t}_{P}$ which are adjacent, we have that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ are two adjacent vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$.

nodes.name: Take adjacent vertices and their walks
nodes.statement: Suppose $x$ and $z$ correspond to walks $W, \overline{W}\in \magenta{\Omega}$, respectively. W.l.o.g., suppose walk $ W$ extends walk $\overline{W}$ by one vertex. Then, the vertices $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ correspond to walks $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Take adjacent vertices and their walks

nodes.name: Case check that images still extend each other
nodes.statement: The definition of $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ implies that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)$ extends $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})$ by one vertex. To see this, note that in this setting we have $\overline{W}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}$ while $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, hence we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(\overline{W})=\overline{W}$. If $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(a)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$, then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W$ implying that $W$ extends $\overline{W}$. If on the other hand we have $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ then $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}$, where $W_{P}$ is defined as in the paragraph above \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}. It is easy to verify that $W_{P}$ extends $\overline{W}$ in this case too.
nodes.statement_short: Case check that images still extend each other

nodes.name: Adjacency is preserved
nodes.statement: Hence, $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(x)$ and $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(z)$ are two adjacent vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$. This implies that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ preserves adjacencies between the two trees, $\capri{t}_{P}$ and $\blue{T_{P}}$.

nodes.name: The bijection identifies $t_P$ with $T_P$
nodes.statement: From all the above, we conclude that $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ has all the necessary properties to allow us to identify $\capri{t}_{P}$ with $\blue{T_{P}}$. \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw} follows.

nodes.name: Set up both Gibbs distributions and weight systems on $T_P$
nodes.statement: Let $\mu^{M,\sigma}$ be the Gibbs distribution on $T=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$ induced by the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction on $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Similarly, let the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{K,\eta}_P$ on $\blue{T_{P}}=T_{\rm SAW}(\gext{G}{P},w)$ be induced by the same construction with respect to the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Consider the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ and $\{ \upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ induced by the two Gibbs distributions $\mu^{M,\sigma}$ and $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ respectively. Note that the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ are on the edges of $T$, while the edge-weights $\{ \upalpha_{P}(e)\}$ are on the edges of $\blue{T_{P}}$. Using \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw}, we identify $\blue{T_{P}}$ as a subtree of $T$, and we endow the edges of $\blue{T_{P}}$ with the edge-weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}_{e\in \blue{T_{P}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up both Gibbs distributions and weight systems on $T_P$

nodes.name: Reduce to one edge at depth $\ge k$
nodes.statement: Fix an edge $e=\{x,z\}$ in $\blue{T_{P}}$ such that $z$ is the child of $x$. Suppose $e$ is at distance $\geq k$ from the root. \Cref{lemma:GibbsWeightsTpVsP} follows by showing that $\upalpha(e)=\upalpha_{P}(e)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to one edge at depth $\ge k$

nodes.name: Weights depend only on the pinning below the edge
nodes.statement: The edge weights $\upalpha(e)$ and $\upalpha_{P}(e)$ only depend on the parameters of the initial Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and the pinnings $(M,\sigma)$ and $(K,\eta)$ that the two Gibbs distributions $\mu^{M,\sigma}$, $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ impose, respectively, at the vertices of $T_{z}$. As per standard notation, $T_{z}$ is the subtree of $\blue{T_{P}}$ that consists of vertex $z$ and its descendants. Since $z$ is also a vertex in $T$, it is not hard to verify that the subtree of $T$ which consists of $z$ and its descendants is exactly the same as $T_{z}$. This is due to the assumption that edge $e$ is at distance $\geq k$ from the root of $T$. Since, by definition, both $\mu^{M,\sigma}$ and $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ have the same parameters, it suffices to show the pinnings $(M\cap \blue{T_{P}},\sigma)$ and $(K,\eta)$ are identical. Here, we let $(M\cap \blue{T_{P}},\sigma)$ stand for the restriction of pinning $(M,\sigma)$ to the vertices in $\blue{T_{P}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Weights depend only on the pinning below the edge; reduce to equal pinnings

nodes.name: Describe the pinned sets $M\cap T_P$ and $K$ by walk types
nodes.statement: Let set $\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}$ consist of the self-avoiding walks in $\magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}$ whose last vertex is in set $\Lambda$. Similarly, we define $\magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P} \subseteq \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}_{P}$. The $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction implies that set $M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$ consists of the vertices that correspond to the walks in $ \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda} \cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$. Similarly, set $K$ in $\mu^{K,\eta}_{P}$ consists of the vertices that correspond to the walks in $ \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}_{P}\cup \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Describe the pinned sets $M\cap T_P$ and $K$ by walk types

nodes.name: Show $M\cap T_P\subseteq K$ with matching pins, walk type by walk type
nodes.statement: We start by showing that $M\cap \blue{T_{P}} \subseteq K$ while for every $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, we have $\sigma(v)=\eta(v)$. Since we identify $\blue{T_{P}}$ as a subtree of $T$, each vertex in $\blue{T_{P}}$ corresponds to two walks, one from set $\magenta{\Omega}$ and one from set $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$. Particularly, for vertex $v\in \blue{T_{P}}$ which corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}$, it also corresponds to walk $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)\in \magenta{\Omega}_{P}$, where $\cadmiumorange{\uph}$ is the bijection between $\magenta{\Omega}$ and $\magenta{\Omega}_{P}$ described in \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection}, i.e., the proof of \Cref{lemma:TsawPVsTsaw}. Each vertex $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, which corresponds to a walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}\subseteq \magenta{\Omega}^{(\alpha)}$, also corresponds to the same walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_P$ since \eqref{def:OfUPHBijection} implies $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{\Lambda}_{P}$. We then obtain that vertex $v\in K$. Furthermore, the pinning rules of the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction imply $\eta(v)=\sigma(v)=\tau(v)$. Recall that $\tau$ is from the pinning of the initial Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. Arguing as above, for each vertex $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, which corresponds to walk $W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}$, we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(c)}_{P}$. Hence, we obtain that $v\in K$. For such vertex $v$, the pinning rules of the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction imply that $\eta(v)=\sigma(v)$. Each vertex $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$ which corresponds to walk $W=v_0, \ldots, v_{r} \in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$ also corresponds to walk $W_{P}=z_0, \ldots, z_{r}$ such that $v_{i}=z_{i}$ for $0\leq i \leq r-1$, while $z_{r}$ is a split-vertex in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P} $generated by vertex $v_{r}$. That is, we have $\cadmiumorange{\uph}(W)=W_{P}\in \magenta{\Omega}^{(b)}$. This implies that $v\in K$. For vertex $v$ in the paragraph above, the pinning $\sigma(v)$ is induced by the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction on $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, while the pinning $\eta(v)$ is because we consider the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$, which pins the split-vertices in $\cadmiumgreen{\UpS}_{P}$. From the description of the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction and the definition of the $P$-extension of $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}$ it not hard to verify that $\eta(v)=\sigma(v)$, e.g., see \eqref{eq:DefOfTau_x}. All the above imply that $M\cap \blue{T_{P}} \subseteq K$, while for each $v\in M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, we have $\sigma(v)=\eta(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $M\cap T_P\subseteq K$ with matching pins, walk type by walk type

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion by the same argument
nodes.statement: With a very similar line of arguments, we also deduce that $K \subseteq M\cap \blue{T_{P}}$, while for each $v\in K$, we have $\sigma(v)=\eta(v)$. We omit these arguments because they are almost identical to those we presented above.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse inclusion by the same argument

nodes.name: Pinnings coincide, so weights agree
nodes.statement: We conclude that the two pinnings $(M\cap \blue{T_{P}},\sigma)$ and $(K,\eta)$ are identical. Consequently, we have that $\upalpha(e)=\upalpha_{P}(e)$ for any edge $e$ at distance $\geq k$ from the root of $\blue{T_{P}}$. \Cref{lemma:GibbsWeightsTpVsP} follows.

nodes.name: Compute $D_kD_k^T$ entrywise
Diagonal entries at most $\Delta^k$
nodes.statement:
We conclude that $\UpD_{k} \cdot \MTR{\UpD}_{k}$ is a non-negative and diagonal matrix. For $w\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have $(\UpD_{k} \cdot \MTR{\UpD}_{k} )(w,w) \leq {\Delta}^{k}$. Hence, we have $ 
orm{ \UpD_{k} \cdot \MTR{\UpD}_{k}}{2} \leq {\Delta}^{k}$, which implies that $
orm{ \UpD_{k}}{2} \leq {\Delta}^{k/2}$. Working similarly, we get $ 
orm{ \UpC_{k}}{2}\leq {\Delta}^{k/2}$. \Cref{claim:2NormBoundforVVsEdge-AAA} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal entries at most $\Delta^k$; same for $C_k$

nodes.name: Dominate $|\mathcal{I}_{<2k}|$ by the distance-$2k$ adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: Let ${\UpA}^{(2k)}$ be a $(V\setminus \Lambda)\times (V\setminus \Lambda)$, zero-one matrix such that for any $w,u\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have \begin{align} {\UpA}^{(2k)}(w,u)&=\mathds{1}\{{\rm dist}_{G}(w,u)\leq 2k\}\enspace. \end{align} Noting that each entry in ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G, <2k}$ is in the interval $[-1,1]$, we have \begin{align} \abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G, <2k}} &\leq {\UpA}^{(2k)}\enspace, \end{align} where the inequality is entrywise.
nodes.statement_short: Dominate $|\mathcal{I}_{<2k}|$ by the distance-$2k$ adjacency matrix

nodes.name: Chain of norm inequalities via Lemma B.2 and symmetry
nodes.statement:
We have  egin{align} 
orm{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G, <2k}}{2}&\leq 
orm{ \abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G, <2k}} }{2} \leq 
orm{{\UpA}^{(2k)}}{2} \leq 
orm{{\UpA}^{(2k)}}{\infty}\enspace. \end{align} The first inequality above is elementary, e.g. see \Cref{lemma:AbsoluteVs2Norm}. The second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:AbsInfLes2kVsAGPow2k}. The last inequality follows by noting that matrix ${\UpA}^{(2k)}$ is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of norm inequalities via Lemma B.2 and symmetry

nodes.name: Bound the $\infty$-norm by a ball count
nodes.statement: Since $G$ is of maximum degree ${\Delta}$, we have that $\norm{{\UpA}^{(2k)}}{\infty}\leq \frac{{\Delta}^{2k+1}-1}{{\Delta}-1}$. The claim follows by plugging the bound on $\norm{{\UpA}^{(2k)}}{\infty}$ into \eqref{eq:FinalEq2Norm4BoundedNoOfIL-AAA}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the $\infty$-norm by a ball count

nodes.name: Introduce the symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma$
nodes.statement: Let $\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ be the $(V\times \Lambda)\times (V\times \Lambda)$ covariance matrix defined with respect to $\mu^{\Lambda, \tau}$. That is, for any $u,v\in V\setminus \Lambda$ we have \begin{align}\nonumber \Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(v,u) &=\mu^{\Lambda, \tau}_{(v,u)}((+1,+1))-\mu^{\Lambda, \tau}_{v}(+1)\cdot \mu^{\Lambda, \tau}_{u}(+1)\enspace. \end{align} A straightforward observation is that $\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ is symmetric. W.l.o.g. in this proof, assume that the diagonal entries of $\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ are non-zero.

nodes.name: $M(v,v)=\sqrt{\Sigma(v,v)}$ and...
nodes.statement: Note that for any $v\in V\setminus \Lambda$ we have that \begin{align} \UpM(v,v)= \sqrt{\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(v,v)}\enspace. \end{align} Furthermore, it is standard to show, e.g. see \cite{VigodaSpectralInd}, that $\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ and ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ satisfy that ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(u,v)= \frac{\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(u,v)}{\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(u,u)}.$

nodes.name: Symmetry of $\Sigma$ and rearrangement
nodes.statement: Since $\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$ is symmetric, this relation implies that \begin{align}\nonumber \Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(u,u) \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(u,v) & =\Upsigma^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(v,v) \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(v,u) \enspace. \end{align} Then, a simple rearrangement and \eqref{eq:UpMVsCovMat} imply that \begin{align}\nonumber \textstyle \frac{\UpM(u,u)}{\UpM(v,v) } \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(u,v)& \textstyle = \frac{\UpM(v,v)}{\UpM(u,u) } \cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G(v,u) \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Identify the entries of $M\mathcal{I}M^{-1}$
nodes.statement: The l.h.s. in the above equation corresponds to the entry $(\UpM\cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G \cdot \UpM^{-1})(u,v)$, while the r.h.s. corresponds to $(\UpM\cdot {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_G \cdot \UpM^{-1})(v,u)$. The claim follows.

nodes.name: Define the test vector $x$
nodes.statement: In what follows, we abbreviate $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}$ to $\byzantine{\UpH}$. Let the vector ${\bf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{\iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_k}$ be such that for any $R\in \iris{{\mathcal{E}}}_k$ we have \begin{align} {\bf x}(R)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left( \mathds{1}\{R=P\} + \mathds{1}\{R=Q^{-1}\} \right)\enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Expand the quadratic form and use symmetry of $H^\ell R$
nodes.statement: We have that \begin{align} \nonumber {\bf x}^T (\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR){\bf x}&=\frac{1}{2}\left((\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR)(P,Q^{-1}) +(\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR)(Q^{-1}, Q^{-1})+(\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR)(P,P)+ (\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR)(Q^{-1}, P) \right)\enspace. \end{align} Recalling the definition of matrix $\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell}\cdot \UpR$, we have \begin{align} \nonumber \byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell}(P,Q) =(\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell}\cdot \UpR)(P,Q^{-1})=(\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR)(Q^{-1},P) \enspace, \end{align} the last equation follows since $\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR$ is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the quadratic form and use symmetry of $H^\ell R$

nodes.name: Quadratic form bounded by the top eigenvalue $\sigma_{k,\ell}$
nodes.statement: All the above imply that \begin{align} \nonumber \byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell}(P,Q) \leq {\bf x}^T \cdot (\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR) \cdot {\bf x} \leq \norm{ \byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell} \cdot \UpR}{2}=\sigma_{k,\ell} \enspace. \end{align} The last inequality above follows from the fact that $\byzantine{\UpH}^{\ell}\cdot \UpR$ is symmetric, with maximum eigenvalue $\sigma_{k,\ell}$. The claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic form bounded by the top eigenvalue $\sigma_{k,\ell}$

nodes.name: Write $\ell=Nt+r$ and use submultiplicativity (A.3)
nodes.statement:
In what follows, we abbreviate $\cadmiumgreen{\UpH}_{G,k}$ to $ yzantine{\UpH}$ Let the integers $t=\lfloor  rac{\ell}{N} floor$ and $r\geq 0$ be such that $\ell= N\cdot t+r$. We have  egin{align} \left( \upsigma_{k,\ell} ight)^{1/\ell}& = 
norm{  yzantine{\UpH}^{\ell}}{ rac{1}{\ell}}{2} \leq 
norm{  yzantine{\UpH}^{\ell-r}}{ rac{1}{\ell}}{2} \cdot 
norm{  yzantine{\UpH}^{r}}{ rac{1}{\ell}}{2} \leq 
norm{  yzantine{\UpH}^{\ell-r}}{ rac{1}{\ell-r}}{2} \cdot 
norm{  yzantine{\UpH}^{r}}{ rac{1}{\ell}}{2} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Bound the $Nt$ part by $\sigma_{k,N}^{1/N}$
Remainder factor tends to 1
nodes.statement: Noting that $\nnorm{ \byzantine{\UpH}^{r}}{\frac{1}{\ell}}{2}\leq ({\Delta}-1)^{\frac{r}{\ell}}$ and recalling that ${\Delta}$ is bounded, there is fixed $\ell_0$ such that for $\ell>\ell_0$ we have $\nnorm{ \byzantine{\UpH}^r}{\frac{1}{\ell}}{2}\leq (1+z)$. \Cref{lemma:SingSequenConv} follows.

nodes.name: Reduce to the bound (A.5)
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that any $d>0$ and any ${\bf y}\in [-\infty, +\infty]^d$ we have \begin{align} \norm{\nabla H_d ({\bf y})}{\infty} &\leq \frac{|\beta-1|}{\beta +1} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: (A.5) implies (15.2) by maximising over the uniqueness interval
nodes.statement: Before showing that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:SI4Ising} is true, let us show how it implies \eqref{eq:lemma:IsingInfNormBound}. That is, we show that for any $\beta \in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(R,\varepsilon)$, we have that $\frac{|\beta-1|}{\beta +1}\leq \frac{1-\zeta}{R}$. Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{|x-1|}{x+1}$ defined on the closed interval $\left[\frac{R-1}{R+1}, \frac{R+1}{R-1} \right]$. Taking derivatives, it is elementary to verify that $f(x)$ is increasing in the interval $1< x < \frac{R+1}{R-1}$, while it is decreasing in the interval $\frac{R-1}{R+1}< x <1$. Furthermore, noting that $f(1)=0$, it is direct that {\small \begin{align}\nonumber \sup\nolimits_{\beta \in {\mathbb{U}_{\rm Ising}}(R,\varepsilon)}f(\beta)= f\left(\frac{R-1+\varepsilon}{R+1-\varepsilon}\right)= f\left(\frac{R+1-\varepsilon}{R-1+\varepsilon}\right) =\frac{1-\varepsilon}{R} \enspace. \end{align} } We conclude that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:SI4Ising} implies \eqref{eq:lemma:IsingInfNormBound}.
nodes.statement_short: (A.5) implies (15.2) by maximising over the uniqueness interval

nodes.name: Reduce to a bound on $|h|$
nodes.statement: It remains to show that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:SI4Ising} is true. Since $\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{i}}H_d(x_1, \ldots, x_d)=h(x_{i})$, it suffices to show that for any $x\in [-\infty, +\infty]$ we have that {\small \begin{align} \abs{ h(x)} &\leq \frac{\abs{1-\beta } }{1+\beta} \enspace. \end{align} }

nodes.name: Write $|h(x)|$ explicitly for the Ising model
nodes.statement: For the distribution we consider here, the function $h(\cdot)$ is given by \begin{align} h(x) & =-\frac{(1-\beta^2) \exp(x)}{(\beta \exp(x)+1)(\exp(x)+\beta)} \enspace. \end{align} From the above we get that {\small \begin{align} \abs{h(x)} & = \frac{\abs{1-\beta^2}\exp(x)}{(b \exp(x) +1)(b+ \exp(x))} \ = \ \frac{\abs{1-\beta^2 }}{\beta^2+1 +\beta (\exp(-x)+\exp(x) ) } \enspace. \nonumber \end{align} }
nodes.statement_short: Write $|h(x)|$ explicitly for the Ising model

nodes.name: Use $e^x+e^{-x}\ge2$
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to verify that $\phi(x)=e^{-x}+e^{x}$ is convex and for any $x\in [-\infty, +\infty]$ and attains its minimum at $x=0$, i.e., we have that $\phi(x)\geq 2$. Consequently, we get {\small \begin{align} \nonumber \abs{h(x)} & \leq \frac{\abs{1-\beta^2}}{\beta^2+1 +2\beta } \ = \ \frac{\abs{1-\beta}}{1+\beta} \enspace, \end{align} } for any $x\in [-\infty, +\infty]$. The above proves that \eqref{eq:TargetB4thrm:SI4Ising} is true and concludes our proof.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $\Delta_c$ gives the left inequality
nodes.statement: It elementary to verify that the function ${\Delta_c}(x)$ is decreasing in $x$. This implies that for any $\lambda\leq (1-\varepsilon){\lambda_c}(R)$, we have ${\Delta_c}(\lambda)\geq {\Delta_c}({\lambda_c}(R))=R$. Particularly, this implies that there is $0<z<1$, which only depends on $\varepsilon$ such that ${\Delta_c}(\lambda) \geq \frac{R}{(1-z)}$. This proves the leftmost inequality in \eqref{eq:claim:InterpretGoodPotentialHC}.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $\Delta_c$ gives the left inequality

nodes.name: Bound $\lambda/(1+\lambda)<\lambda_c(R)$
nodes.statement: As far as the rightmost inequality is concerned, we have \begin{align} \textstyle \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda} \leq \lambda < {\lambda_c}(R) \enspace. \end{align} The first inequality follows since $\lambda>0$, while the second follows since $\lambda<{\lambda_c}(R)$.

nodes.name: $\lambda_c(R)\le e^3/R$ via $1+x\le e^x$
nodes.statement: From the definition of ${\lambda_c}(\cdot)$, we have {\small \begin{align} {\lambda_c}(R)& =\frac{R^{R}}{(R-1)^{(R+1)}}\ = \ \frac{1}{R}\left( 1+\frac{1}{R-1}\right)^{R+1} \ \leq \ \frac{1}{R}\exp\left(\frac{R+1}{R-1}\right) \ \leq \ \frac{e^3}{R} \enspace. \end{align} } For the one before the last inequality we use that $1+x\leq e^{x}$. For the last inequality we note that $\frac{R+1}{R-1}$ is decreasing in $R$, hence, for $R\geq 2$, we have that $\frac{R+1}{R-1}\leq 3$.

nodes.name: Combine for the right inequality
nodes.statement: Plugging the above bound into \eqref{eq:Base4Righteq:claim:InterpretGoodPotentialHC}, gives the rightmost inequality in \eqref{eq:claim:InterpretGoodPotentialHC}. The claim follows.

nodes.name: Symmetric case via Lemma B.1
nodes.statement: If $\UpD$ is symmetric, then ${\rho}(\UpD)=\norm{ \UpD}{2}$ and ${\rho}(\abs{\UpD}) = \norm{ \abs{ \UpD}}{2}$. Hence, \Cref{lemma:AbsoluteVs2Norm} follows as a corollary from \Cref{lemma:MonotoneVsSRad}.

nodes.name: General case via $DD^T$
nodes.statement:
Let us consider the general case, i.e., where $\UpD$ is not necessarily symmetric. Let $\overline{\UpD}$ be the standard matrix transpose of $\UpD$. We have that  egin{align} 
norm{ \UpD}{2}{2} = 
orm{ \UpD\cdot \overline{\UpD}}{2} &\leq 
orm{ \abs{ \UpD\cdot \overline{\UpD}}}{2} \leq 
orm{ \abs{\UpD} \cdot \abs{\overline{\UpD}}}{2}=
norm{ \abs{\UpD}}{2}{2}\enspace. \end{align} The first inequality follows by noting that $\UpD\cdot \overline{\UpD}$ is a symmetric matrix. The second inequality follows by noting that $\abs{ \UpD\cdot \overline{\UpD}}\leq \abs{ \UpD} \cdot \abs{\overline{\UpD}}$. \Cref{lemma:AbsoluteVs2Norm} follows.

nodes.name: Write the 2-norm as a supremum
The supremum is attained at a non-negative vector
nodes.statement: Since the entries of $\UpD$ are assumed to be non-negative, it is elementary to verify that supremum, above, is achieved for ${\bf z}$ whose entries are non-negative.
nodes.statement_short: The supremum is attained at a non-negative vector

nodes.name: Entrywise domination of $Dx$ by $Bx$
nodes.statement:
Let ${ f x}\in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ be such that $
orm{ { f x}}{2}=1$ and $
orm{ \UpD \cdot { f x}}{2}=
orm{ \UpD}{2} $, while let ${ f v}=\UpD{ f x}$ and ${ f w}=\UpB{ f x}$. Since the entries of $\UpB$ are assumed to be non-negative, while $\UpD\leq \UpB$, for any $i\in [N]$ we have that ${ f w}(i)\geq { f v}(i)$. Clearly, this implies that  egin{align} 
orm{ \UpD}{2}=
orm{ { f v}}{2} \leq 
orm{ { f w}}{2} \leq 
orm{ \UpB}{2}\enspace. \end{align} The above concludes the proof of \Cref{lemma:MonotonicityVs2Norm}.

nodes.name: Define $B=\sum_\ell(\delta A_G)^\ell$ and bound...
nodes.statement:
Recalling that $\delta=(1-\varepsilon)/{\varrho}$, let ${{\UpB}}$ be the $V	imes V$ matrix defined by  egin{align} {{\UpB}}&= \sum
olimits_{0\leq \ell \leq n} \left( \delta \cdot {\UpA}_Gight)^{\ell} \enspace. \end{align} Since the adjacency matrix ${\UpA}_G$ is symmetric, ${{\UpB}}$ is symmetric, as well. We have  egin{align}
onumber {ho}\left ({{\UpB}} ight ) & = 
orm{ {{\UpB}}}{2} = 
orm{ \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0}(\delta\cdot {\UpA}_G)^{\ell}}{2} \leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0} \delta^{\ell} \cdot 
orm{ ({\UpA}_G)^{\ell}}{2} \leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0}(1-\varepsilon)^{\ell} =\varepsilon^{-1} \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Cauchy interlacing for the principal submatrix
nodes.statement: Let ${{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda}$ be the principal submatrix of ${{\UpB}}$, which is obtained by removing rows and columns that correspond to the vertices in $\Lambda$. Cauchy’s interlacing theorem, e.g., see \cite{MatrixAnalysis}, implies that \begin{align} {\rho}\left ({{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda} \right )&\leq {\rho}\left ({{\UpB}} \right ) \leq \varepsilon^{-1}\enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy interlacing for the principal submatrix

nodes.name: Reduce to entrywise domination (6.4)
nodes.statement: \Cref{thrm:AdjacencyInfinityMixing} follows by showing that ${\rho}( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} ) \leq {\rho}\left( {{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda} \right)$. To this end, it suffices to show \begin{align} \abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} (w,u)}&\leq {{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda}(w,u) & \forall u,w\in V\setminus \Lambda \enspace. \end{align} To see why the above implies ${\rho}( {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} ) \leq {\rho}\left( {{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda} \right)$ see \Cref{lemma:MonotoneVsSRad} in the Appendix, It is immediate that for any $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$, we have $\abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G}(u,u) } =1$. Also, we have ${{\UpB}}(u,u)\geq 1$, as the summand in \eqref{eq:DefOfPowerAdj} for $\ell=0$ corresponds to the identity matrix. This proves that \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:AdjacencyInfinityMixing} is true when $u=w$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to entrywise domination (6.4); handle the diagonal

nodes.name: Expand $\mathcal{I}(w,u)$ over $T_{\rm SAW}$ paths (Proposition 5.9)
nodes.statement:
Fix $w,u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ such that $w
eq u$. Let $T=T_{m SAW}(G,w)$ and let $\{ \upalpha(e)\}$ be the weights on the edges of $T$ specified as in \eqref{def:OfInfluenceWeights} with respect to $\mu^{\Lambda,	au}_G$. \Cref{prop:Inf2TreeRedaux} implies  egin{align} {\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G}(w,u) &=\sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0}\sum
olimits_{P\in {\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)}\prod
olimits_{e\in P}\upalpha(e)\enspace, \end{align} where set ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$ consists of the paths of length $\ell$ from the root of $T$ to ${	t A}(u)$.

nodes.name: Each edge weight is at most $\delta$
nodes.statement: The $\delta$-contraction assumption implies that $\abs{\upalpha(e)} \leq \delta$, for each $e\in T$. Then, from \eqref{eq:AdjacencyInfinityMixingTsawConstruction}, we have \begin{align} \abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,\tau}_{G} (w,u)}&\leq \sum\nolimits_{\ell\geq 0} \abs{{\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)} \cdot \delta^{\ell} \enspace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Each edge weight is at most $\delta$

nodes.name: Count paths by walks: $|\mathcal{P}(u,\ell)|\le A^\ell_G(w,u)$
nodes.statement: Let ${\rm SAW}_{\ell}(w,u)$ be the set of walks of length $\ell$ from $w$ to $u$, in graph $G$, that correspond to the elements in ${\tt A}(u)$. Let ${\rm Walks}_{\ell}(w,u)$ be the set of walks of length $\ell$ from $w$ to $u$, in graph $G$. We have ${\rm SAW}_{\ell}(w,u)\subseteq {\rm Walks}_{\ell}(w,u)$ i.e., since each element in ${\rm SAW}_{\ell}(w,u)$ is also a walk in graph $G$ from $w$ to $u$. We have \begin{align}\nonumber \abs{{\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)} &= \abs{{\rm SAW}_{\ell}(w,u)} \leq \abs{{\rm Walks}_{\ell}(w,u)} = {\UpA}^{\ell}_G(w,u) \enspace. \end{align} The last equality is from \eqref{eq:NoOfWalksVSA2L}.

nodes.name: Entrywise domination holds off the diagonal
nodes.statement:
Plugging the above bound into \eqref{eq:AdjacencyInfinityMixingInlEntryBoundDelta}, we get  egin{align}
onumber \abs{{\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda,	au}_{G} (w,u)} &\leq \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0} \delta^{\ell} \cdot {\UpA}^{\ell}_G(w,u)={{\UpB}}_{V\setminus \Lambda}(w,u) \enspace. \end{align} Hence, \eqref{eq:Target4thrm:AdjacencyInfinityMixing} is also true when $w
eq u$. \Cref{thrm:AdjacencyInfinityMixing} follows. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: Entrywise domination holds off the diagonal

nodes.name: Set up $T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$ and path weights
nodes.statement: We abbreviate ${\mathcal{I}}^{\Lambda, \tau}_G$ to ${\mathcal{I}}$ and the diagonal element $\UpD (u,u)$ to $\UpD (u)$. Let $T=T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$, while consider the weights $\{\upalpha(e)\}$ over the edges of $T$ obtain by applying the $T_{\rm SAW}$-construction to the Gibbs distribution $\mu^{\Lambda,\tau}_G$. For every path $P$ of length $\ell\geq 0$ that starts from the root of tree $T$, i.e., $P=e_1, \ldots e_{\ell}$, let \begin{align} {\tt weight}(P) & = \prod\nolimits_{1\leq i \leq \ell }\upalpha(e_{i}) \enspace. \end{align} Note that we have written path $P$ using its edges.
nodes.statement_short: Set up $T_{\rm SAW}(G,w)$ and path weights

nodes.name: Claim 7.2 and its proof
Define $\mathcal{P}(u,\ell)$, ${\tt A}(u,\ell)$ and $\mathcal{H}_\ell$
nodes.statement:
For $u\in V\setminus \Lambda$ and $\ell\geq 0$, let ${\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$ be the set of paths $P$ from the root of $T$ to the set of copies of vertex $u$ which are at level $\ell$ of the tree such that ${	t weight}(P)
eq 0$. Also, let ${	t A}(u,\ell)$ be the set of copies of $u$ at level $\ell$ in $T$ that are connected to the root with a path $P\in {\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)$. Let  egin{align} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} & = \sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \sum
olimits_{P \in {\mathcal{P}}(u, \ell) } \abs{ {	t weight}(P ) } \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align}

nodes.name: Proposition 5.9 bounds row sums by $\sum_\ell\mathcal{H}_\ell$
nodes.statement:
Recalling that \Cref{prop:Inf2TreeRedaux} implies  egin{align} 	extstyle \left( \UpD^{-1}\cdot {\mathcal{I}}\cdot \UpD ight) (w,u) & = rac{1}{\UpD(w)} \cdot \sum
olimits_{\ell \geq 0} \sum
olimits_{P \in {\mathcal{P}}(u,\ell)}{	t weight}(P) \cdot \UpD(u)\enspace, \end{align} we have  egin{align} \sum
olimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda } \abs{\left( \UpD^{-1}\cdot {\mathcal{I}}\cdot \UpD ight) (w,u)} & \leq  rac{1}{\UpD(w)} \sum
olimits_{\ell\geq 0} \mathcal{H}_{\ell} \enspace . \end{align}

nodes.name: Define the recursion $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}_v$
nodes.statement:
Fix $\ell> 1$. For a vertex $v$ at level $h$ of $T$, where $h=0, \ldots, \ell$, let the quantity ${{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}$ be defined as follows: For $h=\ell$, we let  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} & = \sum
olimits_{u \in V\setminus \Lambda} \mathds{1}\{v \in {	t A} (u,\ell)\} \cdot \UpD(u) \enspace. \end{align} For a vertex $v$, which is at level $0< h <\ell$ such that vertices $v_1, \ldots, v_d$ are its children, we let  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}&= \uppsi(b_{v})\cdot \sum
olimits_{j}  rac{\abs{\upalpha(b_{j})}}{\uppsi(b_{j})} \cdot {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_{j}} \enspace, \end{align} where $b_{v}$ is the edge that connects $v$ to its parent, while $b_{j}$ is the edge that connects $v$ to its child $v_{j}$. Since we assume that $h>0$, $v$ has a parent, hence $b_{v}$ is well-defined. Also, recall $\uppsi(\cdot)$ from \Cref{claim:AddPotentialA}. Finally, for $h=0$, i.e., $v$ and the root of $T$ are identical, we let  egin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v}\ = \ {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{m root} & = \max_{ ar{b},\hat{b}\in T} \left\{ {	extstyle \uppsi\left( ar{b}ight) \cdot  rac{\abs{ \upalpha\left(\hat{b}ight)}}{\uppsi\left(\hat{b}ight)}} ight\} \cdot \sum
olimits_{z_{j}} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_{j}} \enspace, \end{align} where $z_1, \ldots, z_{r}$ are the children of the root of $T$.

nodes.name: State Claim 7.3
nodes.statement: \begin{claim} For any $\ell> 1$, we have $\mathcal{H}_{\ell} \leq {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{\rm root}$. \end{claim} The proof of \Cref{claim:CEllVsCalD} appears immediately after the proof of \Cref{thrm:InflNormBound4GeneralD}.

nodes.name: Boundedness bounds the root factor by $c$
nodes.statement: The Boundedness property of the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential ${\Psi}$, together with \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeights} imply \begin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{\rm root} & \leq c \cdot \sum\nolimits_{z_j} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{z_j} \enspace. \end{align} \noindent
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness bounds the root factor by $c$

nodes.name: Contraction gives level-wise $\ell_s$ decay (7.18)-(7.19)
nodes.statement: The Contraction property of the $(\darkmagenta{s},\delta,c)$-potential ${\Psi}$ and \eqref{eq:SRecurStepHC1821} imply that, for every vertex $v$ at level $0<h<\ell$, we have \begin{align} \left( {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} \right) ^{\darkmagenta{s}} & \leq \delta \cdot \sum\nolimits_{v_j} \left( {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v_j} \right)^{\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace, \end{align} where recall that $v_1,\ldots, v_d$ are the children of $v$. Then, \eqref{eq:SubContVsDeltaKWeights} and \eqref{eq:SRecurBaseWeights}, imply \begin{align} \left ( {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{v} \right)^{\darkmagenta{s}} & \leq \delta^{\ell - h }\cdot \sum\nolimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \abs{{\tt A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{v}} \cdot \left ( \UpD(u)\right)^{\darkmagenta{s}} \enspace , \end{align} where, recall that ${\tt A}(u,\ell)\subseteq {\tt A}(u)$ is the set of copies of vertex $u$ in $T$ that are at level $\ell$. $T_{v}$ is the subtree of $T$ that includes $v$ and its descendants.

nodes.name: Count copies by walks $CA^{\ell-1}_G$
nodes.statement: Applying \eqref{eq:SubContVsDeltaKWeights1821} for the children of the root and plugging the result into \eqref{eq:SRecurTopWeightsB}, we get \begin{align} {{\mathcal{R}}}^{(\ell)}_{\rm root} & \leq c\cdot \sum\nolimits_{z_{j}} \left( \delta^{\ell-1} \cdot \sum\nolimits_{u\in V\setminus \Lambda} \abs{{\tt A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{z_{j} }} \cdot \left ( \UpD(u)\right )^{\darkmagenta{s}} \right )^{1/{\darkmagenta{s}}} \enspace, \end{align} where note that each $z_{j}$ is at level $h=1$ of $T$. Suppose that $z_{j}$ is a copy of vertex $z$ in $G$. Then, since $\ell>1$, we have \begin{align} \abs{{\tt A}(u,\ell)\cap T_{z_j}} \leq \left( \UpC\cdot {\UpA}^{\ell-1}_G\right)(wz,u)\enspace, \end{align} where recall matrix $\UpC$ from \eqref{def:SingleEdgeM}, while ${\UpA}_G$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$.
